Dependency-based Compositional Semantics (DCS) has been increasingly successful in formalizing natural language meanings with ease and accuracy. The framework's innate compositional nature and strict semantic definitions have enabled intuitive and intuitive understanding of complex semantics, thereby making it a robust and scalable method for processing natural language. However, despite its numerous achievements, existing DCS frameworks have largely been confined to mere computations of semantics without delving into rigorous logical analysis. This limitation stems from the static and deterministic nature of most DCS implementations, which hinders their ability to perform meaningful logical deductions and inferences. In light of this, we propose a novel direction for advancing the field of DCS: we aim to marry its compositional principles with the powerful machinery of logical inference. By introducing logical inference capabilities into the DCS framework, we believe that we can unlock new avenues for reasoning about language and enable the framework to go beyond mere semantic computations. In this paper, we outline a comprehensive plan for equipping the DCS framework with logical inference capabilities. We take a step back from the concrete structures typically associated with the DCS framework and define abstract denotations as an abstraction of the computing process of denotations in the original DCS. This is motivated by the desire to decouple the representation of semantic structures from their computations. The concept of abstract denotations allows us to modularize the DCS semantics and set up a structured framework for logical inference: given expressions with abstract denotations, we can reason about the relations between them in a formally sound and grounded way. This is made possible by an inference engine that we build to operate directly on the abstract denotations. Our engine is tailored to the specific needs of the DCS framework and supports the deduction of logical inferences from the relations established among abstract denotations. Furthermore, inspired by ideas in analogical reasoning and analogy-making, we also draw upon the concept of tree transformation to generate on-the-fly knowledge that can inform the inference process. This highly flexible mechanism enables our system to explore the space of possible deductions efficiently and adapt to novel situations without exhaustive pre-computation. By weaving together logical inference with compositional semantics, we demonstrate the promise of our proposed framework on two benchmark datasets: FraCaS and PASCAL RTE. Our results showcase the ability of our system to derive insightful relations from the given expressions and yield accurate predictions for logical inferences.

Image retrieval models have been a crucial tool in content-based image retrieval applications, where users query a database of images based on their visual features (Mondal et al., 2008;Jeon et al., 2003). One common approach to image retrieval is to represent an image as a bag-of-terms, where each term corresponds to a feature or a descriptor calculated from a specific region of the image (Sivic and Zisserman, 2003). The bag-of-terms image representation is computationally efficient, but it ignores valuable information about the spatial relationships between regions. While spatial relationships can provide a strong cue for distinguishing between images of objects co-occurring and images of objects interacting, many existing retrieval models fail to exploit this information (Ma et al., 2012;G jetsanjani et al., 2017;Liu et al., 2009). Consequently, there is a need for structured image representations that capture spatial relationships between regions and allow retrieval models to leverage this information effectively. One promising approach tostructured image representation is to model the visual dependencies between image regions, such as the relationships between the positions, sizes, and shapes of objects within an image (Coxeter, 1961;Kivinen et al., 2014;Revow et al., 1996). In this paper, we propose Visual Dependency Representations (VDRs) for modeling the spatial relationships between image regions and show that such representations can improve the performance of image retrieval tasks. Traditional image retrieval models represent an image by calculating features such as color histograms, texture descriptors, or object detection scores in different regions of the image. While such a representation may be useful for some applications, it often fails to capture complex visual relationships between regions. In contrast, our approach uses a structured representation that explicitly models the relationships between image regions. This representation captures the position, size, and shape of objects and can be used to distinguish between images of objects that co-occur and images of objects that interact. The resulting VDRs can be fed into standard machine learning pipelines, allowing us to take full advantage of the unique properties of this new image representation. We conduct a query-by-example image retrieval experiment on the SAL Action Database where people are shown acting out sports and other activities (2530 images). Our results show that images retrieved using VDRs have a higher mean average precision (MAP) and precision@10 than images retrieved using a standard bag-of-terms baseline. Our approach achieves an 8.8% relative increase in MAP and an 8.6% relative increase in precision@10, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of VDRs in capturing valuable information about spatial relationships between image regions and retrieving more relevant images in response to user queries.

Discourse parsing, a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), plays a crucial role in understanding text at the document or paragraph level. Specifically, it involves the identification of discourse relations that connect clauses, sentences, or larger segments of text, enabling a deeper comprehension of the relationships between different pieces of information within a discourse. Despite significant advancements in this field, discourse parsing remains an intricate task, particularly when considering the complexity of human language and the variability in text representations. One of the most influential frameworks for discourse parsing is the Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST), which has been widely adopted due to its ability to model rich discourse relations in narratives and other forms of human communication. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in developing deep learning models for discourse parsing. However, due to the inherently hierarchical structure of discourse, existing models often rely on hand-crafted features to capture the relational patterns between different discourse units. This results in models that are complex, time-consuming, and require extensive manual feature engineering. However, more efficiency in this area would lead to improved accuracy and speed, which is more consistent with the mainstream deep leaning practices that have enhanced performance on many other NLP tasks. In light of these challenges, we propose an attention-based hierarchical neural network model for discourse parsing. This model effectively captures both local and global dependencies in sentences as well as between sentences, while efficiently utilizing the complex feature interactions inherent in discourse structure. In developing this model, we rely on a tensor transformation function that enables sophisticated modeling of feature interactions through multilinear algebra. This choice allows us to integrate the strengths of tensor-based decomposition in terms of interpretability and applicability. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed model achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art systems with significantly less manual feature engineering and by leveraging more flexible and expressive features learned in an end-to-end manner. This robustness is particularly important for discourse parsing due to its relative rarity as a challenging but aligned with deep learning technique. By focusing on the hierarchical structure of discourse, leveraging the expressive power of neural networks, and adopting attention mechanisms to model complex feature interactions, our proposed model makes significant strides towards addressing the challenges of discourse parsing. Furthermore, its ability to learn representations in an unsupervised manner has the potential to generalize to new tasks and domains, catalyzing future research and advancements in this burgeoning field.

Broad-coverage semantic role labeling (SRL) systems have the potential to unlock rich linguistic and semantic insights from unstructured text. However, their development is hindered by the ever-growing set of verbs with lexical and semantic variations that are not exhaustively annotated in existing training datasets. This phenomenon of unknown lexical items arises from several factors, including the vast lexical inventory of languages, the continuous emergence of novel expressions, and the inevitable imperfections in annotation efforts. As a consequence, state-of-the-art SRL systems often underperform on unfamiliar verbs or exhibit a sharp decline in accuracy across-domain evaluation. In response to this pressing challenge, traditional SRL methods, which solely rely on annotated training data, have insufficient capacity to self-improve and extend their scope. The prominence of this issue underscores the urgent need for innovative approaches that can acquire training instances for unseen verbs and expand the coverage of SRL systems without exhaustive manual annotation. In this light, semi-supervised learning (SSL) emerges as a highly effective methodology for bridging the gap between known and unknown lexical items. Semi-supervised learning approaches are founded upon the principle that, under specific conditions, the inclusion of some unlabeled training examples can sometimes outperform exclusive reliance on heavy, manually annotated datasets. By leveraging the vast amount of text data available, certain methodologies can extract informative patterns, elucidate structural relationships, or identify class boundaries in a way that would be difficult or impossible with only a fraction of labeled examples. As our primary goal is to facilitate the integration of novel lexical items into state-of-the-art SRL models, we draw upon the strengths of SSL and formulate an inclusive framework that employs an unlabeled corpus to augment the annotated datasets. Key to the success of this method is the notion that unknown lexical items and those for which annotations are available are structurally and semantically comparable, given that these verbs may share similarities in grammatical patterns, predicate argument structures, or broader semantic features. Consequently, we introduce an innovative approach that crafts a highly coherent network of conceptually similar sentences. The foundation of our method lies in graph-based sentence representations, where vertices symbolize words, and edges encode their connections according to various grammatical and lexical relationships. Upon this foundation, we leverage these graph structures to measure similarity and optimize alignment between known and unknown target sentences. By casting this intricate process as an integer linear programming (ILP) optimization problem, we maximize the structural and semantic congruity of graph alignments while evaluating the principal task of zero-shot SRL for unseen lexical items.

The online discussion forum, a ubiquitous platform for content sharing and social interaction, exhibits an intricate structure of conversations. A remarkable aspect of online conversations is the way in which they revolve around initiation-response pairs - a fundamental conversational unit that encompasses the initiating statement or question, followed by a response addressing or building upon the original statement. Initiation-response pairs form the building blocks of discussions, allowing participants to build on each other's ideas and engage in meaningful dialogue. The explicit identification of these conversational units is crucial in various applications, such as conversation analysis, opinion mining, and natural language processing. Nevertheless, identifying initiation-response pairs within online discussions remains a challenging task. Traditional approaches to identifying initiation-response pairs rely on explicit cues such as "why", "because", or "however", which are often not present in online conversations. Furthermore, these approaches often fail to capture the nuances of conversational structure, where a single response may initiate a new topic or co-conversational unit, while a response to a response is, in fact, more of a continuation of a topic in a non-conversational turn. Additionally, the mainstream approach for initiation-response identification still heavily depends on manual linguistic analysis of language phenomena, such as heavy reliance on discourse markers like I see, Tom agreed. Furthermore, contemporary multi-threaded and asynchronous online discussions introduce additional challenges to identifying initiation-response pairs. Since participants can potentially engage in parallel conversations, the identification of initiation-response pairs requires consideration of contextual information such as who is responding to what and in what sequence these responses are formulated although there are models to address this they end falling short, such as in (Singh et al. 2011: but it is by analyzing post indicies ). In addition, dealing with conversational discontinuities caused by turn-taking shifts amplifies this complexity. Given these limitations, formulating the task of identifying initiation-response pairs as a pairwise ranking problem offers an attractive alternative. This formulation rests on the idea that an initiation-response pair can be highly ranked if a response matches or signals the initiation, thereby forming a conversational unit. The daunting prospect of manually annotating and ranking initiation-response pairs gives rise to the need for computational models that can differentiate between initiations and responses. In this paper, we investigate how to develop such a model by proposing a novel variant of Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA), designed to overcome several limitations of standard LSA models.

Neural machine translation (NMT) is a powerful technology that allows for accurate and efficient translation of text from one language to another (Sutskever et al., 2014;Bahdanau et al., 2015;Luong et al., 2015a;Gehring et al., 2017). While NMT systems can use enormous amounts of parallel training corpora, the availability and cost of these resources can be prohibitive for a large number of language pairs. Furthermore, there are certain languages for which parallel data does not exist, such as Georgian. In such cases, the question arises as how to leverage monolingual data to enhance the quality of the NMT system. One effective way to augment the parallel training corpus is to add back-translations of target language sentences, an approach known as back-translation. Back-translation by Xia et al. (2019) is one approach in which the translator first translates an in-domain sentence out of the target language, and then translates it back to the target language; the in-domain sentence is then used as an extra training pair, to improve translation quality of the original sentence. This basic framework was found to improve BLEU scores for German and French by 2.1 and 1.5 respectively. This approach was further enhanced by combining it with record-keeping preprocessing, and yielded a state of the-art score of 40.4 BLEU on the WMT'14 English-German test set. However, the results quickly decrease by adding more monolingual data. There seems to be an optimal amount of monolingual data that can significantly improve the translation quality: but there is a floor shortly after which the updates fail to improve the performance significantly. Zoph et al. (2020) analyzed the reason behind this floor and suggested that these synthetic source sentence is harder for the current NMT architectures to train on. To further investigate this phenomenon and to reveal an even better way of generating synthetic source sentences, we will in this paper introduce new methods for generating synthetic source sentences. Furthermore, we study the effect of different back-translation methods on a wide range of datasets and languages, which shows that free or noised synthetic data is still most effective even if we use large scale target monolingual data. Our results enable us to move beyond the optimal point for English that current NMT architectures reach and score a new state of the art on the WMT'14 English-German test set of 45 BLEU. The representation and understanding of a word's semantic content have been a central issue in natural language processing (NLP). That's why, constructing a polarity lexicon, which assigns semantic orientations such as positive or negative to words, plays a crucial role in many NLP applications including sentiment analysis, opinion mining, and text classification. In recent years, lexical network has been widely applied to polarity lexicon construction, where the connections between words (edges) in the lexical network are either directly observed (direct links) or inferred (hidden links) using various link prediction methods. By analyzing how semantic orientations spread over the network, the use of the lexical network, which captures rich semantic information of a word, is beneficial for enhancing the extraction performance. However, the majority of the current methods for constructing a polarity lexicon primarily rely on graph-based approaches with predefined fixed formulations. These approaches, although have achieved state-of-the-art results, are in fact incompatible with probabilistic formulations of the propagation process and cannot provide any predictive insight into the propagation mechanisms of semantic orientations. In recent studies, the Ising spin model has been employed, to model semantic orientations that propagate over a lexical network. Inspired by relevant results from physical phase transition theory, researchers observed theoretically the exhibited phase transition, which would abruptly change the polarity distribution of some words in the vicinity of the optimal temperature parameter, as a phenomenon in the system. In this context, the critical challenge is to elucidate, from the viewpoint of statistical physics, the first and second order phase transition and to deeply investigate the intrinsic mechanisms responsible for the high classification performance of the system such as in terms of temperature, eigenvalues of the weight matrix, etc. However, these problems remain unproven and almost untouched problems so far. Thus, the goal of this paper is to provide a thorough understanding of the Ising spin model from the viewpoint of the statistical mechanical analysis and the underlying mechanisms responsible for the high classification performance of the system. To be specific, we provide the critical analysis of the phase transition to the optimal temperature parameter for the extraction performance, proposing a computational efficient scheme for improving the extraction performance by the appropriate removal of the largest eigenvalue component from the weight matrix. Based on this analysis, the computational cost of the extraction of semantic orientations can be reduced at the expense of negligible accuracy loss.

Sentiment classification in natural language processing focuses on automatically determining whether a sentence or text is expressing a positive, negative, or neutral sentiment (Hatzivassiloglou and McKeown, 1997). This task has significant applications in areas such as opinion mining, emotion detection, and recommendation systems (Liu, 2010). While group-level sentiment analysis has been accomplished with considerable accuracy through the use of rules and linguistic analysis (Turney, 2002), extracting this information from sentences or short texts in a certain language, or from a text that may be written in a language with very limited resources, can prove difficult. Research in multilingual information retrieval and machine translation has shown the challenges of implementing natural language processing technologies across languages (Casacuberta and Marino, 2018), particularly recognizing that an approach suitable for one language may not be effective when translated to another. In many cases, developing a sentiment classifier in a particular language results in an in-explicit linguistic model of the language. That is, even though the classifier might be a deep learning model and perform well, the very fact that we require to translate text from that language into English to do training, means that the classifier will heavily rely upon linguistic patterns in English rather than in the target language. Furthermore, another challenge is the intrinsic cross-lingual sentiment discrepancy, as sentiment may be expressed differently in different languages. In this work we modify this traditional two step approach by, in addition to relying on high-dimensional vector embeddings, augmenting our training corpus by polar words although containing extremely little linguistic information provide highly informative instances for learning such discrepancy in sentiment. The goal of this paper is to present a simple yet effective way to address these challenges by using a combination of English word translations, and highdimensional vector embeddings, along with polar words in the multilingual sentiment classification task. We show through a series of experiments the effectiveness of using word embeddings to enable multilingual support for sentiment classification systems. Additionally, we describe the highly effective augmentation of training data by using the polar words. This implies the polarities of words in the target text. Our results suggest that our proposed approach is more effective than current methods and greatly alleviate the challenges mentioned above. We find that our method leads to a performance gain of 7-10% over the traditional method on many languages, where the languages are chosen from various genres of text that are accessible.

The quest for a unified theory of language is a central goal in natural language processing (NLP), notably with respect to compositional models that can account for both syntactic and semantic aspects of language. The last several decades have seen a multitude of approaches emerge, each with its strengths and limitations. Statistical models such as word space models (Schütze, 1998; Sahlgren, 2006) and analogical reasoning (Jones et al., 2005) have been able to capture certain general properties of language, while being computationally tractable and easy to use. On the other hand, symbolic grammar formalisms like context-free grammars (Peng et al., 2014) and categorial grammars (Johnson, 2004) offer a more explicit and intuitive account of linguistic structure, but tend to be less general and often lack the ability to generalize across the many aspects of semantic meaning. Comparing these approaches is challenging because they were designed to tackle different tasks or sub-problems and their representational assumptions are often mutually incompatible (Bates and Elman, 1996). For example, symbolic models typically perform a parsing process that separates out linguistic structure relevant for interpretation, whereas statistical models are designed to exploit patterns exhibited in large datasets without a-parse to meaning. This has led to several different groups of compositional models, which solved their respective application scenario but has not addressed the question of which properties of language such models must capture, and hence do not converge towards the integration of insights from multiple solutions. Generating concise and coherent summaries from a single document is an essential task in natural language processing. Although various methods have been proposed to tackle this problem, effective summarization methods are still challenging to design. One major obstacle hindering current summarization methods is that most previous models relied heavily on shallow models and overlooked the complexity of coherence in a summary. To group together sentences that share strong semantic relationships, it is ideal if the model can capture the structural coherence of the summary. Another potential problem is that most models do not incorporate sentence compression into the summarization process. The process of sentence compression can bring significant improvement to the quality of the generated summaries because it relieves the problem of information explosion in a summary. Traditionally, hidden Markov models (HMM) have been widely used for language modeling and pattern recognition tasks due to their ability to capture the probabilistic relationships between states by modeling the transition probabilities and emission distributions. However, the standard HMM is limited to modeling single segment units with fixed length. To model the sequence of arbitrarily length segments in order to capture coherent document structures and clause levels, the hidden semi-Markov model (HSMM) becomes the ideal choice. It models the relevant segment variables, duration variable for each segment, thus allowing for disorder in the segments. Furthermore, another key point of HSMM is that it elucidates sentences as segments, solved the defects of former mentioned methods which may generate disjointed results. Even though the HSMM offers some advantages such as high accuracy and the ability to model complex structures, there are limited applications for HSMM in summarization. In this paper, we proposed a new framework that employs discriminative HSMM to single document summarization by formulating the summarization task into that of selecting the best sequence of sentences from the input document with specific constraints. Our proposed model, named HSMM summarizer, enjoys several properties: the ability to naturally model the summarization task as selecting the best sequence of sentences that satisfy an objective function and histogram constraint and incorporating sentence compression into the summarization process. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, extensive experimental studies were conducted on a large-scale corpus. Our results demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms competitive baselines on the ROUGE evaluation metric. In addition, we show that the quality of the generated summaries offered by our proposed method was equivalent to the reference summaries, with around 20 percent of the summaries generated being completely identical to references.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that involves identifying and categorizing named entities in unstructured text into predefined categories such as person names, organizations, locations, and others. NER has a wide range of applications in fields such as information extraction, text summarization, and question answering. While NER systems can be highly accurate when trained and evaluated on a specific domain, their performance often degrades significantly when applied to a different domain. This is due to the differences in language, terminology, and data distribution between the source and target domains. In many real-world scenarios, however, we do not have the luxury of collecting large amounts of labeled data for the target domain. In such cases, domain adaptation and transfer learning are crucial for improving the generalizability of NER models across different domains. Domain adaptation is the process by which a model trained on a source domain is adapted to perform well on a target domain with different characteristics. In this paper, we consider the problem of domain adaptation for NER by proposing an effective domain adaptive bootstrapping algorithm. Domain adaptation, in contrast to traditional learning, emphasizes the use of training examples that relevant to the new, unseen tasks, and notwithstanding theoretically powerful risk minimization, these examples are often unavailable. This has inspired research into off-the-shelf classification as well as data selection and weighting, although the field is challenging because the recipients of transferred knowledge may only know implicitly, via the processes and analyses by which they differ from recipients whose solutions are known.( although successful adaptation models do not provide any indication of the amount and nature of the age difference in studied applicability i.e: but it is by virtue of indicia ). Bootstrapping is the process of improving the performance of a trained classifier by iteratively adding data that is labeled by the classifier itself to the training set, and retraining the classifier. It is often used in situations where labeled training data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant. In this paper, we focus on the applicability of bootstrapping to domain adaptation for NER, a challenging problem due to the difficulty of finding informative unlabeled data that can help bridge the source and target domains. We present a novel domain adaptive bootstrapping algorithm that selects instances that are informative about the target domain and easy to automatically label correctly, and show that it outperforms traditional supervised, transductive and bootstrapping algorithms on the NER task.

Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) and Entity Linking (EL) are two fundamental NLP tasks that have garnered significant attention in the research community in recent years. Argumentation is a critical aspect of academic writing where students express a viewpoint in support of or against a claim. A fundamental component of an argumentative essay is its stance, which reflects the author's attitude towards a given proposition. Stance encompasses a range of evaluations, including beliefs, attitudes, and opinions (Biber and Jones, 2000). As Knutson (2014) pointed out, accurately classifying stance is crucial for effective analysis and criticism of arguments. Despite this importance, automatic stance classification in argumentative essays still lacks a thorough investigation. The primary difficulty in classifying stance stems from the complexity of naturally occurring data. Research in linguistics and psychology suggest that stance is conveyed through subtle linguistic cues, such as modal verbs, subjunctive mood, and certain-word lists (Charles, 2014). For instance, modal verbs (e.g., "will" and "would") signal degrees of commitment and obligation in an argumentative text. However, detecting stance is challenging because it interacts with other linguistic primitives, such as sentiment, which often overlap in terms of represented expression. Our goal in this research is to improve stance classification in student essays. To achieve this, we conduct extensive developmental work, building upon notable approaches in computational argumentation (Diermeier et al., 2001) and natural language processing (Krzeszowiec, 2017) research. In particular, we develop a new dataset annotated with stance, called Stance Student Essays (SSE), consisting of argumentative student essays written over the past decade. User feedback is used to ensure the relevance, completeness, and reproducibility of our new data. Our dataset includes essays from students of varying grade levels, from early secondary school to late adolescence. Developing and evaluating a practical computational model for stance classification in these essays is an open research question, primarily due to the heterogeneity of the data and the available research on stance. No single model currently matches the performance of human classifiers. Historically, stance classification has been approached by using either traditional techniques or deep learning architectures. The traditional method (Gaissert et al., 2006) relies on extracting stance-relevant features from essays, which can include sentiment scores, topic-related words, and negation usage. Deep learning methods, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks (Isabela, 2016) that utilize word embeddings and convolutional neural networks (CNN), generally achieve better accuracy (Persinghen, Wang, & Thraman, 2018). However, these approaches may not only require balanced training sets and large amounts of labelled data but also efficient computational resources. With our model, we contribute a new, light-weight approach that benefits from strong stance-annotated data, coupling shallow machine learning and traditional feature engineering to minimize the computational demands that scale with large datasets.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a central technology in natural language processing, aimed at automatically translating text from one language to another. The nowadays most widely used SMT frameworks are phrase-based models (Koehn et al., 2003) and their numerous offspring. These models construct the target sentence by inserting and reordering the group of words - known as the source phrase - originating from the source sentence. The quality of the phrase-based translations heavily depends on the intermediate reordering models used to estimate the set of legal reordering operations. The success of SMT can be significantly enhanced by adapting the translation model and data to specific domains, which was first widely documented in the work of Shen et al. (2004). However, later the prominence of domain adaptation found more and more extensive promotion among researchers who investigated different types of adaptation (Liu et al., 2010;Xiong et al., 2010), such as adapting the language model (Dong et al., 2008). Nonetheless, adaptation of reordering models for statistical machine translation (SMT) is more often than not overlooked, even though the reordering process affects the translation quality directly relevant to the accuracy of other tasks, including TM and LM based variants of the SMT. To demonstrate the benefits of reordering model adaptation, we focus on phrase-based SMT and propose a mixture model adaptation framework that combines different reordering models trained on different training corpora, with the goal of increasing overall SMT quality. In this paper, we investigate the impact of different training corpora on the reordering characteristics and the suitability of these corpora for training the translation model (TM), the language model (LM), and the reordering model (RM). Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical benefits of our adaptation approach through experiments on a set of benchmark tasks, testing the random initialization of the mixture model, the impact of various training criteria on model adaptation, and the application of an additional criterion to histogram smoothing and instance weighting. Broadly speaking, the paper attempts to find the optimal mix of trained RMs and evaluate its practical significance. The intuition that the RMs may take on very different forms as they are being trained on different data sources may need to be reconciled with the ages of the pre-existing dominant approaches that view the course of this research through the apertures of the several major criteria that remain accessible subjectivity. Firstly, the domain adaptation in TM is inherently dependent on pre-existing high-quality translation quality.

Code generation is a challenging task that has garnered significant interest from the natural language processing (NLP) and software engineering communities. With the rising tide of software applications, the importance of automated code generation is becoming increasingly evident. Traditionally, code generation is performed based on given specifications provided by the user or directly inferred from observational examples. However, code is rarely written in isolation; rather, its efficacy relies heavily on the programmatic context in which it resides. This context is a vital component that heavily influences the incorporation of various functions and variables, ultimately dictating the success or failure of the code. While there exist multiple approaches to code generation that primarily focus on the syntactical and semantic properties of the code itself, there is a noticeable dearth of research addressing the prominence of the programmatic context in shaping the code's performance. One such example is the field of method invocation, where the performance of the invoked function is dependent on the integration of the invoked function within the context of the larger class program. This phenomenon is, however, commonly encountered in code maintenance, enhancement, and development. Consequently, we propose an innovative approach, termed CONCODE (Class-Oriented Natural Language to Code Embedding Decoder), aimed at investigating the heavy reliance of code on the programmatic context. A major component of this approach is the compilation of a large-scale dataset, CONCODE, comprised of over 100,000 examples extracted from online code repositories. This dataset offers a rich, and as yet unexplored, source of data capable of shedding light on the intricate interaction between method documentation and class environment. As a cornerstone of the CONCODE initiative, we emphasize the importance of identifying the interplay between different elements of the code generation process. In addition to offering an insightful understanding of the above-mentioned interplay, our CONCODE framework enables the seamless integration of automation in coding task. Our system leverages an encoder-decoder framework that comprises learning representations capable of encoding details of the class environment and method documentation from natural language input. Deep learning architecture consisting of attention mechanisms and techniques for dealing with noisy data are trained on our large CONCODE dataset. This approach addresses prior issues with accuracy and enables us to make progress towards solving the well-known free lunch problem often encountered in the field of computer science. Ultimately, the development of our novel architectural framework stands as a basis for implementing the cognition commonly attributed to humans performing difficult coding-related tasks.

Abstractive summarization aims to produce a concise summary that paraphrases the original content using natural language, capturing the key points and opinions expressed in the original text. Opposite to extractive methods, where a selection of salient sentences or passages is automatically identified and selected, abstractive summarization directly generates a brief summary that may even be shorter than the original content. However, abstractive summarization has traditionally been more difficult to accomplish using automated methods than extractive methods due to the need to generate new text that still conveys the essential message and opinion expressed in the original content. While there exist abstractive summarization methods based on many paradigms - from deep-learning architectures to applications of natural language generation - none have taken into account the prominence of extremely redundant opinions within documents (e.g., a document about reviews of a product that gathers opinions from multiple different people). This typically makes it hard to select and generate the correct key-ideas to be converted into a coherent and understandable summary. For instance, in social network reviews websites, customers post reviews in short format e.g. 2-4 lines, to express their opinions about a particular product. These highly redundant opinions sometimes form redundant patterns, especially for opinions of relative pros and cons about the product. Hence, to meaningfully generate abstractive summary, these redundant opinions must be understood, solved and addressed in a way that makes the summary concise and interesting. Even though the redundancy within such opinions might make it easier to automatically create a summary of these pieces of text (e.g., extremely redundant opinions concerning relatively good or relatively bad aspects), this is also a challenge in and of itself. The richness but also the noise of these opinions can lead to summaries that contain not only information that the users are interested in but also amplifying trivial or worthless subjects, statements, ideas and phrases. Furthermore, another challenging point of current methods consists of: (i) Quality and readability problems due to the lack of human readability from the generated text (e.g., noise in output data, selectiveness for readability), and (ii) conflicts among the quality of generated and actual (correct) human generated content. There has been growing interest in leveraging graph-based representations to perform abstractive summarization as these methods can efficiently represent redundant opinions and dominant topics within documents with a set of relations where edges between documents and categories (topics) symbolize the frequency of co-mentions.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a central technology in natural language processing, particularly in the context of machine translation and multilingual information retrieval. Recent advances in the field have focused on the development of hierarchical phrase-based SMT systems, which have led to significant improvements in translation quality (Chen and Cherry, 2008;Gülçeur and Hardt, 2009). However, one critical challenge facing SMT remains the problem of linguistic reordering. The rearrangement of sentences to conform to the syntactic and semantic structure of a target language can prove a daunting task due to the vast number of possible reordering permutations. The difficulty of translating between languages with notably dissimilar word order, such as Japanese-to-English, is an illuminating example of this struggle. When faced with the jetsanjōura (the gentle death), for example, the translation needs to have the correct actor, verb, and adjunct in the correct word order to accurately convey the sentence's meaning. Failure to do so results in poor translations that fail to express the intended inferences and nuances, ultimately leading to lower translation quality, including reduced readability and performability. Recent advances in modeling linguistic reordering have primarily focused on incorporating heavy linguistic constraints, thus resulting in requiring multiple, distinct models for incorporating different types of linguistic reordering. These approaches have differentiable flaws, however, including high demand for linguistic annotation and computational complexity restrictions for real-time implementation (Galley, 2006). Furthermore, incorporating both the syntactic and semantic reordering models into the same translation system is an additional challenge. In this paper, we explore a simple yet effective approach to unified soft linguistic reordering constraints in a hierarchical phrase-based translation system. We base our method on two linguistic reordering models: a syntactic reordering model that handles reorderings for context-free grammar rules, and a semantic reordering model that focuses on predicate-argument structures. Moreover, we develop novel features based on both models and integrate them as soft linguistic reordering constraints to guide the translation process. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed soft linguistic reordering model, we conduct experiments on Chinese-English translation using a state-of-the-art hierarchical phrase-based translation system. Our experimental results demonstrate that the reordering approach can significantly improve the translation quality, highlighting the value of incorporating both syntactic and semantic constraints in the translation process. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the behavior differences between the two reordering models to gain insights into their contributions to the translation quality.

Event extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with a wide range of practical applications in areas such as information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. The goal of event extraction is to identify and extract relevant events from unstructured text, including event triggers and arguments. Event triggers are the keywords that signal the occurrence of an event, while event arguments are the entities that are involved or affected by the event. Event extraction has been recognized as a potential solution to various NLP tasks such as text analysis and sentiment analysis. Recent studies have shown that event extraction can play a crucial role in understanding the underlying semantics of the text. However, the majority of the existing work on event extraction focused only on identifying a single event per sentence. The real-world scenario often involves multiple events described in the same sentence, which makes it challenging to extract them accurately. Incorporating contextual information is typically crucial in handling multiple events and entities in the same sentence. In this context, previous studies have primarily relied on sequential modeling methods to represent the dependencies among events by a sequence of short- and long-range dependencies. Though, these sequential methods achieve state-of-the-art results, they suffer from a relevant issue: the capture of long-range dependencies is limited due to requiring multiple sequential steps. Furthermore, another key challenge of sequential models lies in handling events with complex structures, which is not addressed in state-of-the-art methods. Traditional event extraction methods extract single events only, and as a result do not leverage the insights that can be gained from considering multiple events and their inter-relationships. There is a need to incorporate a more suitable method that naturally handles the interactions among multiple events. To address the mentioned challenges, recent studies have proposed modeling the inter-actions among events by jointly extracting multiple event triggers and arguments. However, these studies tend to either ignore the interdependency among entities or treat entities as sequential information only, neglecting the role of syntactic structures in providing crucial contextual information. To surpass the limitation of the traditional sequential models, it is necessary to develop a method that can efficiently extract multiple events and model complex event structures. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for jointly extracting multiple event triggers and arguments, which is free from the limitations of sequential modeling methods.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks often involve complex linguistic structures and rules. Many tasks, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, dependency parsing, and Chinese word segmentation, have both syntactic and semantic aspects that need to be considered. While probabilistic models have been highly effective in NLP, they often rely on weakly-informed heuristics, and suffer from the related issues of sparsity and lack of robustness (Chen and Goodman, 1999). In this work, we investigate the role of deterministic constraints in NLP tasks, and how these can be learned and efficiently applied to improve model performance. Our study spans two tasks: English POS tagging and Chinese word segmentation. POS tagging is a core NLP task that aims to assign a POS label to each token in a sentence. For instance, given the word "running", the task is to determine whether it is a verb, noun, or other part of speech. Chinese word segmentation is a variant of POS tagging, where the goal is to split a Chinese word into its constituent parts. This task has the additional challenge of dealing with the complexities of the Chinese language, such as homophonic characters and complex word forms. For both tasks, we show that with proper representation, a large number of deterministic constraints can be learned from training examples. These constraints capture various linguistic properties, including POS syntax, lexical semantics, and character patterns. The challenge of applying learned constraints in a probabilistic framework is to avoid over-reliance on these constraints and maintain model robustness. For the task of English POS tagging, we find that the learned constraints can be directly incorporated into the Viterbi decoding algorithm, significantly improving its efficiency and accuracy. The application of learned constraints in a deterministic framework has the added benefit of inducing sparse models, which in turn speeds up inference and improves testing robustness. This demonstrates that deterministic constraints can effectively aid probabilistic modeling. Moving on to Chinese word segmentation, we observe that character-based tagging constraints can be learned using the same templates. However, for optimal performance, we find that these constraints are best applied to a word-based model. To incorporate these constraints, we develop an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation that strikes a balance between computational complexity and solution quality. Our empirical results show that the proposed ILP formulation achieves significant improvements over the baseline models, demonstrating the effectiveness of deterministic constraints in word segmentation.

Fine-grained opinion extraction, a crucial task in sentiment analysis, allows for a more nuanced understanding of opinions expressed in text data. In everyday life, opinions abound, and grappling with them has both intuitive and practical appeal. As a means of investigating user opinion, sentiment is a common evaluation metric in various reviews and product opinions on online forums. While group opinions in relation to online product reviews are of primary importance, the extraction of opinion has been approached using different views of meaning potentializing intermediate entity perception, combing the necessity of certain views to be drawn based on opinion discoveries [Kiela et al., 2015]. There are several types of opinions, such as expressing thoughts on product quality, personal opinion of an article or previous movie viewing, or firsthand review of a specific room found on hotel survey sites. However, an evaluation of these different types of opinions is not explicitly touched upon in this study. Fine-grained opinion extraction can be often framed as a Multi-Task Learning (MTL) problem, where we want to identify the opinion-related entities, including the opinion holder, the target, and the opinion expression, as well as their interrelations [Das et al., 2012]. Traditional pipeline-based approaches typically start by identifying opinion-related entities, such as opinion holders and targets, and then proceed to extract opinion expressions and their relations with these entities. However, such an approach suffers from the lack of interdependencies between the different extraction stages. In other words, identifying the opinion holder may require the knowledge of the opinion expression, but the pipeline-based approach does not capture such interdependencies effectively. Over the past decade, researchers have proposed various methods to address the challenge of fine-grained opinion extraction. For instance, [Hu and Liu, 2004] and [Tang et al., 2014] leverage various kinds of linguistic features, such as n-grams and Part-Of-Speech (POS) tags, to identify opinion expressions and their targets. [Min et al., 2010] employs a dictionary to identify opinion words. While these approaches have shown some level of success, they typically suffer from the limitation that the extraction stages are treated as isolated tasks. Ideally, we want to develop a joint inference approach that takes into account the interdependencies between the extraction stages. Recent advances in deep learning and sequence modeling have provided us with the tools to address this challenge effectively. Specifically, we can leverage the concept of graph convolutional networks [Kipf and Welling, 2016] to model the interdependencies between different extraction stages in a graph-based fashion.

The proliferation of digital information has been a defining characteristic of modern society, with millions of documents being generated every day. Under such an information overload condition, summarization technology has recently emerged as a crucial tool for assisting people in identifying and extracting the essential information from a large set of documents. Traditional summarization methods have primarily focused on generating static and plain-text summaries, where the produced summaries do not adapt to the diverse preferences and interests of individual users. Consequently, these summaries often fail to accurately capture the essence of what the users are interested in, leading to a mismatch between the generated summary and the actual need of the users. For instance, a user interested in the health benefits of a particular diet might find a summary that contains only information on the nutritional content of the diet, which is uninformative and uninteresting to the user. In other words, traditional summarization methods rely on a "one-size-fits-all" approach and generate the same summary for all users, regardless of their individual interests and preferences. This lack of personalization and adaptation in traditional summarization methods has led to a demand for the development of more advanced, Interactive Personalized Summarization (IPS) technologies. IPS technologies generate summaries that are tailored to the specific interests and preferences of individual users in an interactive and dynamic manner. This is achieved through a process of user elucidation and feedback, where users are enabled to interact with the summarization system by providing explicit feedback on their interests and preferences. This interactive feedback is then used by the IPS system to adjust and refine the generated summary, ensuring that it better captures the essence of what the user is looking for. Through IPS, users can therefore experience high-quality summaries that meet their specific needs and interests, which enables more productive and efficient information retrieval. As such, IPS technologies hold significant potential in various domains, including news summarization, digital Libraries, and life sciences documentation, where the efficient retrieval of relevant information can significantly impact decision-making and knowledge discovery. Several challenges must be overcome in the development of IPS technologies, however. Firstly, there is the need to develop more sophisticated algorithms that can effectively capture and incorporate user interests and preferences within the generated summaries. This includes the development of algorithms that can learn from user interactions and adapt to the evolving interests and preferences of the user.

The fair and efficient administration of justice demands that criminal cases be handled with the necessary skill and expertise required to ensure that the applicable laws are fully taken into account at all stages of the legal process. One important aspect of this involves determining the most suitable charges for a given case, taking into account the nuances of the underlying facts and any relevant laws that may be applicable. This charge prediction task is of particular importance for the development of legal assistant systems, where the user input is a description of the facts, and the system must then identify the most appropriate charges based on that input [Li et al., 2018;Xu et al., 2020]. However, this task poses significant challenges, particularly due to the complexity and variability of the facts and the corresponding depth and breadth of the applicable laws. Consequently, an effective charge prediction system would need to exhibit not only a sophisticated understanding of the underlying laws but also the ability to integrate this knowledge with the specifics of the case at hand. To this end, we propose a novel approach to the charge prediction task that leverages a key aspect of the legal system: the relevant law articles. Inspired by the conjecture that an accurate understanding of relevant law articles can provide a crucial foundation for making informed decisions about charges in a criminal case, we introduce an attention-based neural network framework that not only predicts charges but also identifies the pertinent law articles that support such charges. In this unified framework, two distinct components are fully integrated, with the attention mechanism playing a pivotal role in bridging the gap between the two tasks. Our hypothesis is that the exploitation of relevant law articles in the charge prediction task would not only supply the critical legal basis but also imbue the prediction process with a degree of robustness and accuracy. Furthermore, by incorporating the extraction of relevant law articles into the prediction model, we anticipate that our approach would enable the system to adapt to cases with different expression styles, thereby enhancing its applicability in real-world scenarios. To verify this hypothesis and evaluate the performance of our full model, we conduct thorough experiments on a diverse dataset of criminal cases. The experimental results attest to the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating that incorporating the relevant law articles indeed improves the charge prediction outcomes, and that our full model is capable of accurately predicting charges for cases of varyingexpression styles.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a central task in natural language processing, which aims to automatically translate sentences from one language to another based on statistical information of the given training data. Throughout the years, various statistical models have been proposed to improve the performance of SMT. One of the key factors in SMT is language modeling, which assigns a probability to a sequence of words, and is used to predict the next word given the context (Knesser, 1952;Rothenberg, 1973). There are different types of language models, such as n-gram language models and continuous-space language models (CSLMs). N-gram language models are widely used, but they suffer from the data sparsity problem, which can lead to poor performance when the number of n-grams is small (Brown et al., 1992). CSLMs, on the other hand, use neural networks and can capture the context of a word more effectively, but they require more computational resources and have difficulty in handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words (Mikolov et al., 2010). Researchers have employed CSLMs to rerank the candidates generated by n-gram language models during post-processing, thus achieving significant improvements in accuracy (e.g., (Ma and Chen, 2014)). However, these can be computation intensive. Since reranking involves computing probabilities for many candidates, employing CSLMs in reranking, although efficient, is not practical for real-time decoding. Specifically, this makes CSLMs challenging to use in the first-pass decoding phase of SMT, which was originally solved using back-off n-gram language models (BNLMs) (Knesser, 1952;Rothenberg, 1973). In this work, we focus on converting CSLMs into BNLMs, such that they can be easily used in the first-pass decoding phase of SMT. This is crucial for achieving high accuracy with lower computational complexity. The efficiency of the converted models will be demonstrated on a variety of language translation tasks. We will demonstrate that our converted CSLMs outperform traditional n-gram language models and are comparable to the traditional use of CSLMs for reranking. Thus, the contributions of this paper can be listed below. Firstly, we proposed a method for converting CSLMs to the prevalent back-off n-gram language models that can be used in the first pass decoding phase of SMT. Secondly, we show that the converted CSLMs have high predictive performance through a series of experiments. Our conversion approach, as shown below, contributes to accelerating large-scale machine translation tasks by combining the strengths of both CSLMs and n-gram models, both in terms of translation quality and low latency.

Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), focused on identifying the relationships between entities in unstructured text. Conventional relation extraction methods rely heavily on large-scale annotated datasets, which are not only time-consuming and expensive to produce, but also often difficult to obtain. Recently, distantly supervised relation extraction has emerged as an effective approach to scaling relation extraction up to large-scale corpora by leveraging existing knowledge graphs to automatically collect training data [Mintz et al., 2009;Saparov et al., 2019]. Although distantly supervised relation extraction has shown promising results in identifying valid relation instances, it inevitably suffers from the wrong labeling problem [Zeng et al., 2019]. In other words, noisy or incorrect supervision information can significantly affect the performance of distantly supervised relation extraction models, leading to the recognition of a large volume of false positive instances. Many efforts have been devoted to identifying valid instances from noisy data [Krishnamurthy and Finkel, 2018; Jia et al., 2019]. However, the existing methods often focus on refining individual relation instances, disregarding the rich semantic correlations that exist between relations in relevant relation hierarchies. These correlations can help alleviate the risk of obtaining noisy supervision information. By understanding the hierarchical structure of relations, it is possible to gain insight into the relationships between high-level abstract entities and discover long-tail relations composed of lesser-known expressions. Models that can capture such correlations would not only alleviate the noise effect of wrong labels but also yield better generalization ability. In this paper, we incorporate the hierarchical information of relations into distantly supervised relation extraction. Our proposed method employs a novel hierarchical attention scheme to capture the interrelation between relations across different levels in the hierarchy and between entities with specific semantics. Specifically, our model comprises multiple layers of coarse-to-fine attention mechanisms that provide a comprehensive understanding of relations, learning to weigh the importance of individual relation instances based on their relevance to latent high-level relation templates. By leveraging hierarchical attention, our models can effectively adapt to the given supervision information and minimize the noise effect. Moreover, this method allows our model to learn to extract long-tail relations more efficiently than existing approaches. We carry out comprehensive experiments on a large-scale benchmark dataset to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Our results show that the hierarchical relation extraction model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the importance of capturing hierarchical correlations in relation extraction tasks.

Dependency parsing is a critical component in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, particularly in supporting documentation of a language's syntax and semantics. In linguistics, the term 'syntax' refers to the rules and structures governing how words combine to form phrases and sentences, while 'semantics' pertains to the meaning of language constructs. Field linguistics, where researchers document and study a native speaker's linguistic abilities, involves annotating language samples using dependency parse trees, a way of representing syntactic structure as an unlabeled tree, where each node is a word and its dependencies are represented as edges. However, manually annotating data is an exhaustive, time-consuming, and often expensive process, particularly for languages that lack existing resources. Therefore, developing tools to aid in this process is highly beneficial. Traditional supervised parsing approaches rely heavily on large annotated datasets to learn a set of general rules to apply to new, unseen data. However, in the context of language documentation, it is often the case that the available data is limited and of varying quality. As a result, in this work, we are motivated to investigate incremental learning, an approach to learning that can utilize small amounts of training data to make predictions and continue to update the learned model as additional data becomes available. We propose a design to support field linguists in documenting languages using dependency parsing tools as part of the WordsEye Linguistics Tools (WELT) framework. The primary goal is to accelerate the syntactic annotation process for linguists by first introducing an incremental dependency parser to incrementally learn the syntactic structures from annotated data. In order to implement such a system, we have compiled a new parallel corpus of native speaker descriptions of spatial relations and motion events from pictures and video clips, collected from a diverse set of languages. Our corpus serves as a valuable resource in understanding both the syntax and semantics of language expressions. This new dataset offers the opportunity to compare various parsing algorithms with small amounts of training data. We turn our attention to comparing the performance of two dependency parsers, MSTParser (McDonald et al., 2006) and MaltParser (Nivre et al., 2006), using our compiled parallel corpus. These algorithms have gained widespread use in NLP applications but exhibit differences in how parsing functions are implemented. Our results reveal that the MaltParser achieves the best performance in predicting syntactic dependencies given several shallow and deep node representations.

Machine translation (MT) has been a key area of research in natural language processing (NLP), with advances in deep learning architectures leading to significant improvements in translation quality over the past decade. However, existing MT systems often struggle to effectively handle proper nouns, a critical component of any document. Proper nouns, such as names of people, organizations, locations, and other entities, carry important information that is essential for the overall understanding and accuracy of the translated text. The lack of proper handling of proper nouns leads to what we refer to as "name ambiguity" and "name alteration" in translated text. For instance, the Chinese name ""Yang You Jing" translates to "Qian Yang" in English but using only one of the names "You" or the last name "Jing" in the final translated text leads an incorrect identification of this individual. The conventional method of name processing consists of two stages: name detection and name translation. However, such a stage-wise approach can't ensure the successful handling of complex naming conventions and social norms inherent in different languages and cultures. Therefore, it is essential to revisit name processing, re-integrate it with the overall MT process, and generalize the handling of proper nouns to accommodate different linguistic, cultural, and linguistic complexities. With these considerations in view, we propose a Name-aware Machine Translation (NMT) approach to address the above issues. In contrast to the conventional pipeline approach, our NMT technique integrates name processing tightly and globally with the overall MT model by first annotating parallel corpora to obtain high-quality aligned name data, extracting name-aware translation grammar and rules, and adding name phrase table and name translation-driven decoding. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances the quality of overall translation, name translation, and word alignment over a high-quality MT baseline. Furthermore, we introduce a new name-aware evaluation metric to assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach, by assigning importance weights to different words according to their significance in the document. This name-aware evaluation metric enables us to accurately evaluate the quality of the informatic words for the first time. Overall, our work opens up new avenues for improving MT systems and sheds light on the future research directions of NMT. In this paper, we present the details of our NMT approach, evaluate its performance extensively and compare it with several state-of-the-art baselines.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which identifies the mentions of the same entity or group in a text. Consider the following sentence "John, along with his brother, visited the museum, and his wife joined them later." By analyzing this passage, a coreference resolution system should determine that "John", "his brother" and "his wife" are the same entities, while "them" refers to "his brother". The coreference resolution system has a significant impact on various downstream applications such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and entity disambiguation. However, the majority of existing coreference resolution methods rely heavily on supervised learning techniques where annotated datasets are required. Despite numerous datasets being released over the years, the supervision depth and breadth may still be limited in real-world scenarios. For instance, annotating coreference relationships can be very time-consuming and expensive due to the complexity of natural language. A convincing evidence of the need for unsupervised coreference resolution comes from the community of social network analysis where dataset curators often recycle short and noisy text. Our goal in this paper is to present an unsupervised coreference resolution approach for detecting entities relevant to various tasks, especially for scenarios with noisy and limited labeled training data. A major design challenge is determining which relations between mentions represent the coreference relation best as these may vary among different genres, styles, and registers. Traditional methods usually rely on heuristics, such as centering theory and discourse coherence, whereas sophisticated machine learning models exhibit poor generalization although successful on annotated benchmarks. To bridge the gap, we introduce the concept of informativeness in relation to improving the precision of coreference decisions by analyzing pairs of mention entities. Our hypothesis is that certain relations are more informative for coreference decisions than others and we latch onto these, both explicitly and implicitly, throughout this paper. This concept forms the core of the proposed unsupervised framework and it rests on several claims. Firstly, entities that frequently co-occur are likely to engender the same semantic entity for the coreference resolution task. Furthermore, linguistically grandfathered and co-referential qualities aid more than others in judging the strongest pair of entities for coreference resolution. Thus, the framework consists of two central components where the first one encourages informative relations between entities while the second deflects uninformative ones. Finally, we assure that the addition of non- informative pairs do not contribute in delocalizing the optimal inference location based on coreference resolution, refining the retrieval in this manner via permutations.

Phonological representations of language have been known to provide a more natural and linguistically-motivated representation of words and their underlying sounds, which in turn can be leveraged to improve performance in various NLP tasks. Traditionally, words are often represented as one-hot vectors, where each dimension represents the presence or absence of a particular token in a given vocabulary. However, this approach suffers from the curse-of-dimensionality and has been shown to be inferior to representations that capture intermediate linguistic representations, such as phonemes (Schultz, 2002;Yao et al., 2013;Kim et al., 2013). The key advantage of phonemes is that they can capture relational information between sounds (Karttunen and Beesley, 1992) which is often lost when working with tokens (Griffiths et al., 2008). In many languages, phonemes and acoustic features often correlate with one another (Meyer, 1902). For instance, sounds like 'p' and 't' (i.e. the IPA [p] and [t]) can be distinguished acoustically by their different formant structures (Fant, 1960). Recent work has shown that when coupled with suitable machine learning techniques, these phonological and phonetic representations can often outperform simple one-hot encodings of linguistic data in tasks such as morphological analysis (Yoo et al., 2014), part-of-speech tagging (Schmid, 2005), and named entity recognition (Turney, 2006). In this paper, we explore the use of sub-segmental articulatory features: a set of information-rich phonological representations that have been gaining popularity in speech processing research in recent years. Our key contribution is the PanPhon database, an open-access resource containing links between over five thousand phonetic segments to twenty-one sub-segmental articulatory features. This structured resource has an additional advantage that there's increased efficiency facilitating the incorporation of articulatory data into language processing for numerous languages. We trained various CRF models (Lafferty et al., 2001) on PanPhon features as native language embeddings for named entity recognition (NER) on monolingual and multilingual datasets. Our results show that phonologically aware models can attain equivalent or sometimes better performance compared to traditional character-based models that remain one-hot encodings (Maruf et al., 2017;Durrett and Sontag, 2015). However, existing approaches to transferring this same idea only achieved marginally comparable results to their state-of-the-art counterparts (Abboud et al., 2018). In following sections, we evaluate our alternative to strong learning based single language models that requires minimal supervision requiring finer resolution capture by 21-dimensional vector spaces that scale to tangible multilingual performance.
