Distributed word representations, a.k.a. embeddings, have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP) and have been successfully applied in a wide variety of tasks, including language modeling, syntactic parsing, named entity recognition, machine translation, and text classification, among others. These representations, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), and BERT (Devlin et al., 2018), capture various aspects of word semantics, including sensory-motor, syntactic, and semantic meaning, by encoding words as dense vectors in a high-dimensional space. These embeddings have shown to be extremely useful in leveraging the rich semantic structure of language to capture subtle relationships between words, and have achieved state-of-the-art performance in many downstream NLP tasks. However, developing effective distributed representations for many non-English languages, especially those with complex writing systems such as Chinese, presents unique challenges. One of the main difficulties lies in the fact that Chinese characters often serve as lexical-semantic units, and their internal compositions, such as phonetic radicals and semantic radicals, play an essential role in conveying meaning and relationships between words. In contrast, word embeddings based solely on the subword-level semantics (i.e., operating on morphemes or subword units) might overlook the complex interplay between the phonetic and semantic aspects of Chinese characters. Indeed, unlike English words, which often convey rich semantics by the concatenation of subwords (e.g., although), Chinese words are composed of individual characters that individually represent independent units of meaning. As a result, character-level representations are essential to fully capture the complexities of Chinese language modeling tasks, such as character similarity calculations, and applications like language generation and text classification. Therefore, in this work, we aim to develop two innovative Chinese character embedding models, the first of their kind, that take into account the inherent compositional structures of Chinese characters to better capture the nuances of semantic meaning in Chinese. Our character embeddings, denoted as CEnet, are enhanced by incorporating the predictions from a prediction network on the composition relationships between Chinese characters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these representations by comparing them with static character embeddings and other state-of-the-art embeddings through qualitative analysis of character similarity and a set of quantitative evaluations in text classification tasks. Finally, we conclude that the addition of compositional relationships between characters significantly improves the performance of the embeddings, especially in high-complexity Chinese language tasks. through qualitative analysis of character similarity and a set of quantitative evaluations in text classification tasks.

Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) is an essential task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications in education, linguistics, and language learning. Automated correction of grammatical errors is becoming increasingly important as the demand for written content in languages continues to grow. Traditional GEC systems relied heavily on rule-based approaches and machine learning techniques, with moderate success on correcting specific types of errors. However, recent advancements in deep learning have led to the development of sophisticated neural machine translation (NMT) models that can capture subtle patterns in language and achieve state-of-the-art performance in machine translation and related tasks. While NMT-based architectures have shown significant promise in GEC, there are still challenges to be addressed. For instance, many existing NMT-based GEC systems struggle to effectively capture and correct both global errors in word order and usage (e.g., subject-verb agreement, tense consistency) and local errors in spelling and inflection (e.g., single word correction, punctuation insertion). Moreover, the performance of NMT-based models often deteriorates for in-domain test data, suggesting the need for more robust, adaptive, and universal models that can generalize well across different linguistic domains. In this work, we propose a novel hybrid neural model, dubbed the nested attention neural hybrid model (NANHM), which addresses the above limitations through a combination of modular neural components and a specially designed attention mechanism. By incorporating word and character-level information, our proposed model can capture the complex interplay between grammatical and lexical features that underlie both global and local errors. Previous GEC systems typically rely on a single attention mechanism, which may not be sufficient to capture the richness of linguistic relationships and structural dependencies necessary for effective modeling of grammatical errors. Our NANHM model incorporates a nested attention mechanism that consists of two levels of attention: a word-level attention and a character-level attention. This two-stage attention framework enables our model to capture both local details of orthographic errors and global patterns of grammatical structure, facilitating accurate correction of errors in orthography, syntax, and semantics. The key novelties of our proposal are: (1) the nesting of attention layers to enhance the representation of both word and character-level information; (2) the combination of global and local attention to adapt to diverse linguistic structures and registers; (3) the use of hybrid information at different levels (character and word) to capture subtle relationships between the distribution of linguistic traits and grammatical errors.

Machine transliteration, often referred to as phonetic translation, has become an increasingly important task in multilingual text processing (Kondrak, 2002). There are numerous applications that benefit from transliteration, including information retrieval (Gao et al., 2008), question answering (Liu et al., 2009) and machine translation (Liu et al., 2006). A core assumption underlying such approaches is that transliterations capture more information from either the spelling or pronunciation of words (Grinyova and founding, 2013). However, many studies have found that transliterations in fact exploit both spelling and pronunciation of words (Al-Anzi et al., 2000). This is mainly because some pairs of characters from different scripts may be phonetically similar (e.g., , ) and perform similar functions in different languages (i.e., mark the same kind of prosody), notwithstanding their different spellings and phonetic values. These factors point to the intrinsic cross-modal nature of transliterations and become insurmountable challenges in developing transliteration systems that solely rely on either spelling or pronunciation based representations, and require the necessity for new-line approaches that consider both inputs. Quantifier Scope Disambiguation: A Fundamental Challenge In natural language processing, one of the most notoriously difficult challenges faced by state-of-the-art models is quantifier scope disambiguation. Quantifiers, such as "some" or "most", are fundamental elements of natural language that contribute significantly to the expressive power and complexity of language. However, their use in sentences can introduce uncertainty and ambiguity, making it challenging for machines to infer the intended meaning of a sentence. The scope of a quantifier refers to the portion of a sentence over which it holds. For example, in the sentence "Some students are graduating and some students are not, the first quantifier "some" can refer to students who are graduating, while the second "some" can refer to different students who are not graduating. The scope of "some" in this sentence can be interpreted in different ways, causing the meaning of the sentence to change. The challenge of disambiguating quantifier scope stems from its close relationship with pragmatics, the study of how context influences the interpretation of language. Pragmatic knowledge, such as shared background knowledge, speaker intentions, and context, is highly relevant to resolving the ambiguity introduced by quantifier scope. However, the current state of the art in natural language processing relies heavily on rule-based approaches, machine learning, and supervised learning methods, which fail to capture the subtleties of pragmatic knowledge. The use of pragmatic knowledge in quantifier scope disambiguation is essential, as it can significantly improve the accuracy and robustness of models. However, its incorporation has been historically limited due to the difficulty of acquiring and processing pragmatic knowledge automatically. Existing approaches rely heavily on hand-coded rules, which are time-consuming to develop and maintain, and often fail to capture the nuances of real-world language use. Additionally, most methods use task-specific knowledge sources, like knowledge bases, that are available for only a limited number of languages. In this paper, we present an innovative approach to incorporating pragmatic knowledge in quantifier scope disambiguation using an open information extraction (IE) technique. Our method automatically extracts pragmatic knowledge from text and integrates it into a Markov Logic Network (MLN) model. We leverage recent advances in open IE and use machine learning to build a model that can learn from large-scale linguistic resources and adapt to novel contexts. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on a range of quantifier scope disambiguation tasks, showcasing improvements in accuracy and robustness compared to state-of-the-art models that do not incorporate pragmatic knowledge.

Lexical cohesion is a fundamental concept in linguistics and NLP, referring to the relationships between different words or phrases within a text that convey meaning and create a coherent and cohesive discourse unit. One commonly used measure of lexical cohesion is word repetition, which captures the frequency with which identical words are used in the same document or passage. However, word repetition is not always a reliable indicator of topical cohesion, particularly in texts where authors employ stylistic variations or in domains where vocabulary is highly technical or dynamic. Moreover, research in topical segmentation, which involves identifying meaningful segments of a document based on its thematic content, has also highlighted the limitations of relying solely on word repetition. Traditional approaches to topical segmentation rely heavily on lexical features, such as word co-occurrence and word frequency, to detect topical shifts. While these features have proven effective in certain contexts, they may not be sufficient to capture the nuances of topical change, especially in genres where authors often exploit various linguistic devices to signal shifts in topic. For example, in literary narratives, authors frequently employ contradictory statements, ironic remarks, or non-literal language to convey complex themes, making it challenging for word repetition alone to identify topical shifts. This paper explores an alternative source of information for measuring topical cohesion, one that goes beyond the realm of word repetition. We propose that the type of referring expression used in a text can serve as a useful indicator of topical change. Specifically, we hypothesize that shorter and less informative referring expressions, such as pronouns or determiners, are more likely to be used when the topic under discussion has remained constant between two mentions. In contrast, more informative referring expressions, like noun phrases or proper nouns, are often employed when introducing a new topic or switching between topics. We argue that by incorporating this information into a topical segmenter, we can improve its ability to identify topical shifts and create more meaningful and coherent discourse units. To test our hypothesis, we conduct experiments on two types of data: literary narratives and lecture notes. Our results suggest that incorporating referring expression information into the topical segmenter can be beneficial, resulting in improved performance in certain settings. Furthermore, we observe that certain types of referring expressions are more informative than others, providing valuable insights for the development of more effective lexical cohesion metrics and topical segmentation algorithms.

Dependency parsing is a critical component in many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, particularly in tasks such as machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. Dependency parsers aim to identify the grammatical structure of a sentence by determining the relationships between words and their dependents. Despite the significant advances in parsing algorithms over the years, existing systems largely suffer from two issues: the first is that they are trained on a single objective function, which can be biased towards a specific set of linguistic phenomena or even just the in-domain training data, leading to poor performance on out-of-domain data; the second issue is that they do not capture the nuances of language well. Traditional parser training objectives such as the parser accuracy scores, (Klein and Manning, 2003), are often found to be not very informative about how an individual instance of parse is incorrect. Moreover, when evaluating the performance of the parser, using metrics such as unlabeled attachment score (Ballesteros, 2006) may not fully reflect the parser's ability to capture hypothetical relationships between words in a sentence. Another limitation of traditional parser training objectives is the lack of extrinsic evaluation metric. For instance, parser evaluation sometimes relies solely on parsing accuracy scores, (Klein and Manning, 2003), regardless of how well certain linguistic phenomena, such as coreference, pronoun resolution, coordination and subordination, are captured by the parser. In light of these considerations, training parsers by jointly optimizing multiple objectives would greatly aid the integration of intrinsic and extrinsic objectives that reflect different components of parser performance and provide a means to incorporate task-specific extrinsic measures. The goal of this paper is to present a novel algorithm for improving parser performance by supervised updates using combinations of the parser accuracy score, and intrinsic and extrinsic objective functions such as parsing accuracy, (Mai and van Halfteren, 2009), dependency path score, (Smith and Eisner, 2006), and extrinsic evaluation criteria from machine translation and parser adaptation. Broadly, to accomplish this, we turn to the field of multi-objective optimisation (Antczak, 2006). In a typical multi-objective optimisation framework, there is a conflict between two objective functions. In our case, we have to optimise two dominant objectives: parser accuracy (253) and dependency path score, (537). Our multi-objective optimisation algorithm modifies the existing parser training algorithm to first solve a Pareto optimal solution set based onparsers sourced from intrinsic and extrinsic sources, which includes permutations of loss functions, either based on dependency information or machine learning extrinsic evaluation metrics such as ones that tracks the parser's contribution to machine translation systems, (Riezler et al., 2002).

The analysis of semantic similarity in comparable text is a central task in natural language processing, particularly in the context of corpus-based analytics for linguistics and information retrieval applications. Comparable texts, such as texts on related topics written by different authors, contain instances of parallel language structures, including identical or highly similar syntactic and semantic components. Matching these parallel structures can be used to establish correspondences between semantically related entities or concepts, which is crucial for various tasks such as translation, terminology extraction, and text summarization. Despite the significance of this task, automatic analysis of semantic similarity in comparable text remains a challenging problem in the natural language processing community. Various methods have been developed to analyze semantic similarity in comparable text, including techniques that focus on lexical, semantic, or stylistic features of the text. However, these methods often rely on manual annotation or expensive computational resources. Moreover, they may not be able to capture the underlying semantic relationships and nuances in comparable text effectively. In this paper, we investigate a novel approach for analyzing semantic similarity in comparable text by matching syntactic trees and labeling the alignments according to one of five semantic similarity relations. Our approach is based on the conjecture that parallel syntactic structures in comparable text often contain semantically related entities or concepts. By identifying and aligning these parallel structures, we can establish correspondences between semantically related entities and measure the semantic similarity between them. We develop a framework that matches syntactic trees between two comparable texts and labels the alignments with one of five semantic similarity relations, which include synonymy, hyponymy, hypernymy, meronymy, and antonymy. Our framework combines the strengths of machine learning and combinatorial optimization to efficiently match the syntactic trees and optimize the alignments. To implement our framework, we design a Memory-based Graph Matcher (MBGM) that performs both tasks simultaneously. The MBGM first exhaustively classifies the paired nodes of the two trees into a set of predetermined classes using an accurate memory-based learner. The classification is followed by global optimization to find the optimal alignment for the entire pair of trees. This alignment is then used to establish correspondences between the semantically related entities and measure their semantic similarity. We evaluate our MBGM on a monolingual treebank consisting of comparable Dutch news texts. The results show that our method performs substantially above the baseline and close to the human reference, demonstrating its effectiveness in analyzing semantic similarity in comparable text.

Introduction   Synchronous Context-Free Grammars (SCFGs) are a formalism to define the semantics of formal languages in a compositional way. They are particularly well suited to formalize the syntax and semantics of programming languages, as well as aspects of natural language processing. A key feature of SCFGs is that they are expressive enough to encode the dependencies and interactions between two parallel string derivations, thereby providing a unified formal framework for both syntax and semantics. In order to fully utilize the potential of SCFGs, a central question is how to extract useful information from them, such as parse trees, semantic meanings and data types. The key to answering this question lies in being able to efficiently compute various probability distributions over derivations and their associated structures, which are crucial for language modeling and parsing tasks. In an SCFG, this probability distribution encodes the likelihood of a derivation, taking into account both the syntactic and semantic aspects of the input string. Prefix probabilities, a variant of the more commonly studied probabilistic context free grammar (PCFG) prefix probabilities, play a crucial role in this endeavor. They measure the probability of a given prefix of a parse tree, taking into account the probability of the other words in the derivation. In this paper, we study the computation of prefix probabilities for SCFGs. Our approach relies on a combination of a novel grammar transformation and standard techniques to bring SCFGs into normal forms. The former allows us to define a notion of SCFG prefix completion, while the latter enables us to compute the SCFG prefix completion probabilities efficiently. As a byproduct, our formalizations also naturally give rise to new results about prefix probabilities for SCFGs, including the ability to efficiently compute the prefix probabilities of PCFGs and CFGs by restricting the semantics of SCFGs in a specific way. We believe these results have the potential to be a useful tool for understanding various types of probabilistic models found in areas like natural language processing and programming languages. The efficiency of the SCFG prefix completion probability computation, achieved via restricting the semantics of SCFGs to those of PCFGs, has broad implications for parsing and formal language theory. The rest of this paper is organized as follows: In Section 2, we present the preliminary background of synchronous context-free grammar and its prefix completion. Section 3 introduces the definition of SCFG prefix completion and a uniform formal description of how existing methods for prefix completion in synchronous context-free grammars work.

Structured prediction deals with a broad class of machine learning problems, such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition and parsing, where we aim to predict a structured output, such as tags, where dependencies and relationships must be taken into consideration. One of the fundamental tools used in structured prediction is the structured perceptron (Collins, 2002), where a perceptron learning rule is applied to structured output space. This has been widely used in various structured learning tasks due to its simplicity, scalability and strong guarantees of convergence. However, in many real-world structured prediction problems, exact inference is often intractable. For instance, in speech recognition and machine translation tasks, calculating the best possible output using an exponential number of potential solutions is impractical and will incur extremely long training time and extremely large memory space usage. One common way to handle this limitation is to rely on approximate inference techniques, where the goal is to find an approximately optimal structured output. Among these methods, beam search (Viterbi, 1967) is one of the most popular techniques in speech recognition and machine translation. Despite its widespread use, the theoretical foundation behind the structured perceptron that is deployed with approximate inference is very sparse, especially for beam search. In other words, there is a major gap between theory and practice of structured prediction. In this paper, we fill this gap by proposing a novel, theoretical framework called structured perceptron with inexact search, which formalizes and justifies the use of approximate inference within a structured perceptron framework. Our framework provides a structured way to define and derive different update rules for the structured perceptron under conditions where exact inference is infeasible. This enables a principled treatment of popular approximate inference heuristics, and also opens the door to the design of more informed and advanced approximation techniques. We propose a general notion of "violation-fixing" perceptrons that can handle various types of inexact search problems, and establish strong convergence guarantees under relatively weak separability conditions. Moreover, we develop several efficient update methods within this framework, each of which can significantly reduce training time. Our results provide a solid theoretical foundation for using structured perceptron with inexact search in a wide range of structured prediction tasks, and suggest that more structured prediction tasks where inexact search can be offered can benefit from our proposed framework. In experiments, we show the effectiveness of our proposed methods by comparing with a widely used method - early-update (Collins and Roark, 2004) - in two tasks: part-of-speech tagging and incremental parsing, where the "max-violation" method outperformed the early-update method by achieving a 3-fold speedup.

Recent research in statistical machine translation (SMT) has focused on advancing the performance of phrase-based translation systems. A key component in state-of-the-art phrase-based systems is the use of translation grammars (Zens et al., 2004; Koehn et al., 2007). Current methods for constructing these grammars rely on group phrase extraction or use manually-crafted patterns (Chiang, 2005; Li et al., 2009). However, these methods are limited to discovering general phrase translations and typically do not handle more complex translation relationships, such as hierarchical phrases and idiomatic expressions. Statistical approaches have also been proposed, such as (Galley et al., 2006), where the authors use a parse-and-translate strategy, but translation grammar rules are still not extracted from alignments, an essential component of this technique. Extracting rules from alignments, on the other hand, has proven successful for rule-based machine translation systems (Och and Ney, 2002). However, the translations produced by rule-based models often lack flexibility and in ability to capture subtleties of natural language, such as nuances of word sense and semantics. Another major critique of rule-based systems is their limited ability to capture domain specificity and linguistic variation (Duh et al., 2004). Motivated by these caveats, our paper aims to address the issue of extracting hierarchical translation grammars automatically from alignment posterior probabilities. Unlike traditional methods, which extract rules from the Viterbi alignment alone, we aim to unlock these grammars based on posterior distributions over the alignments between the source and the target text. This allows us to uncover significantly more flexible translation relationships. To do this, we leverage the ability of the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) (Rabiner, 1989) to compute the alignment posterior probabilities given a set of discrete random variables representing the possible alignments. In the context of parallel text alignment, this model offers an effective probabilistic method to compute histogram distributions of alignment probabilities (Müller et al., 2006), which can then be used to extract translation grammars. This approach addresses a long-standing limitation of many translation systems, namely that they are only able to specify rigid, word- or phrase-level translations and cannot express more complex, hierarchical relationships between the source and target language. Additionally, the hierarchical nature of our grammar rule extraction method can uncover additional linguistic phenomena, such as idiomatic expressions, which may not be captured by simpler phrase-based systems or statistical machine translation systems lacking in sufficient training data.

Communication accommodation theory (CAT) (Giles et al., 1991) is a psycholinguistic phenomenon that examines how individuals adapt their communication styles to resemble or diverge from those of their interaction partners. This phenomenon plays a crucial role in determining the success and effectiveness of intergroup and interpersonal interactions. Existing research has widely applied CAT to various domains, including gift communication (Beebe et al., 1990), gestures (Mulac et al., 2013), backchannels (Fish et al., 1988), and social media (Garzone, 2013). While CAT has been extensively studied and applied in traditional communication contexts, the rise of online social media platforms has created new avenues for studying this phenomenon. Online debates, in particular, offer a unique opportunity for researchers to investigate how individuals accommodate their linguistic styles in the face of differing opinions and perspectives. In this study, we aim to analyze and understand the phenomenon of linguistic style accommodation in online debates. Our research is guided by a number of key questions: To what extent do individuals shift their linguistic styles to accommodate their debate partners in online debates? What specific features of language are most susceptible to accommodation in online debates? Do agreeing and disagreeing debating pairs exhibit different patterns of accommodation? To address these questions, we employ a novel approach that combines natural language processing (NLP) and topic modeling techniques to analyze a large dataset of debate posts. Firstly, we propose a Joint Topic Expression (JTE) model for modeling the content and style of debate posts. The JTE model is designed to capture the nuances of linguistic accommodation by integrating topic modeling and stylometric analysis. We use the JTE model to generate a unique dataset of debate posts, which we analyze to identify patterns of accommodation and distinguish between agreeing and disagreeing debating pairs. Our dataset is particularly well-suited for studying accommodation in debates, as it captures the dynamic and often intense nature of online discussions. Secondly, we introduce a formal framework for analyzing the linguistic phenomena of accommodation in online debates. Our framework, which we call the "Accommodation Framework," provides a systematic and theoretically-grounded approach for identifying and measuring accommodation in debates. The framework is comprised of three core components: 1) linguistic features, 2) accommodation metrics, and 3) effect analysis. Our Accommodation Framework offers a comprehensive and flexible tool for analyzing accommodation in a variety of linguistic and communication contexts. Through experiments on a large collection of real-life debate posts, we reveal striking insights about the complex phenomenon of psycholinguistic accommodation in online debates.

Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) has emerged as a comprehensive framework for representing the compositional semantics of natural language. Under this framework, individual sentences are annotated with graph-like meaning representations that capture both the syntactic and semantic structure of language. However, completing a comprehensive picture of document-level semantics requires moving beyond the confines of individual sentences. This is particularly important in contexts where texts convey complex, multi-part narratives or discourses. For instance, news articles typically do not convey a single proposition, but rather multiple claims that require drawing certain inferences or relationships between events. The demand for understanding these processes and relationships imposes the need for AMR semantics that operates beyond the single-sentence level. Typical approaches to document-level representation, such as document-level parse trees or the discourse structure of certain theories, lack the depth of representation inherent in AMR graphs. We present the Multi-sentence AMR corpus (MS-AMR), a collection of annotated documents that cohesively represent the meaning associated with text beyond the confines of the individual sentence. Unlike traditional AMR, our MS-AMR model not only extends to more than one sentence, but does so in a consistent and theoretically motivated manner. As relevant elements from different sentences become integral to meaning, we characterize this as a process of multi-sentence meaning chunking. Examples of such meaning chunks comprise: sentences describing related events, bridging relations, entities that maintain continuity over time and recipients of implicit communications such as coreference, dialogue and prerequisite-descriptor relationships. Our annotations of coreference and coreferential pronominals demonstrate the disruptive function they exert when situated in such a multi-sentence context. For example, the pronoun "it" is typically not coreferential with the final element of its current sentence in the multi-sentence text. Furthermore, multi-sentence representations allow statements of metacoreference: expressions that manifest the analyst's knowledge that the text comprises meaning-comparable elements but which currently does not reveal an explicit coreference. To automate the process of generating multi-sentence meaning representations, one would need not only more trained annotators and linguists but more sophisticated language technology to mine the connections between documents at the semantic level. Throughout this paper, we outline the MS-AMR framework as an alternative approach to capturing the complete meaning of documents, view the course and quantity of data developed here, the statistical characteristics of multi-sentence AMR annotations and evaluate a baseline distribution of existing AMR-based models for use in evaluating high-complexity query environments.

Understanding the dynamics of fictional relationships within a novel is an essential aspect of digital humanities scholarship. Analyzing how these relationships evolve over time can reveal deeper insights into character development and the author's narrative strategy. Researchers have employed various methods to study literary relationships, including manual annotation, topic modeling, and deep learning (cf. Bamman et al. 2014; Hardt & Roth 2018). However, most approaches rely on pre-defined labels or binary annotations of relationships. A glaring gap in this scholarship is the lack of models that can capture the nuanced and non-linear progression of relationships over time. By employing the lens of dynamic data analysis, this study proposes an unsupervised learning model that can discover new patterns and insights into fictional relationships by extracting meaningful and interpretable relationships from unannotated text data. Our key hypothesis is that these models with general capabilities should be able to identify the key dynamics and patterns that are of importance to linguists and literary scholars. Inspired by the temporal grids and matrices used in weekly, monthly and yearly analysis of websites, by time series in short periodic profiling, we propose an extension of dictionary learning to discovery of the relationships timelines. Dictionary learning provides a convenient framework for this problem, as it learns a set of bases that describes the data well while interpreting these bases. Our goal is to represent the time evolution of a relationship with a compact set of bases, potentially including despair or romantic endings. This way of presentation looks helpful, and should allow for the estimation of trends as changes of the bases through time by adding time although space changes by the bases dimension extension. To incorporate time and dimension in a low-dimension way, our novel approach: Dynamical Dictionary Relationship Model (DDRM), updates dictionary learning to generate trajectories rather than just static vectors. Our key idea is to learn both a set of global relationship descriptors and a trajectory over these descriptors for each relationship. This consists of two main learning steps. First, we train a dictionary learning model to extract descriptors that capture the essence of each relationship. Second, we define a new loss function that encourages the trained descriptors to occupy positions along a trajectory. By learning positional embeddings of these relationships, our DDRM can capture the non-linear progression of relationships over time. Moreover, to ensure these descriptors are interpretable, we incorporate meaningful names from a given course list of relations to the model during the training.

Recommender systems have been widely used in content-based recommendation, allows platforms to recommend products to users based on their preferences and behavior (Jannach et al., 2010; Koren et al., 2009). Traditional content-based methods typically rely on users' past behaviors to recommend similar items and achieve better performance on rating prediction tasks (Wu et al., 2016). However, most existing methods fail to tackle one of the most significant challenges in real-world recommender systems, i.e., the problem of missing or incomplete modalities. The modality issue can arise due to various factors, including the presence of multiple representations of users' or items' information, such as text, images, or reviews, and the possibility that some of these representations are missing or corrupted (Weldrafty et al., 2019). For instance, some item information, such as the product description or the item image, might be missing or of low quality in the case of older items. Similarly, some users may provide more abundant text-based information but lack in providing enough image reviews. Our goal in this paper is to design a robust framework that not only addresses the problem of missing modalities but also alleviates the cold-start problem of recommender systems in a more general sense. Cold-start problem is considered as one of the most challenging problems in recommendation systems as it is difficult for the systems to make recommendations for new users or items with little training data (Li et al., 2010). To tackle the aforementioned issues, state-of-the-art recommendation methods have been proposed in recent years (Weldrafty et al., 2019;Singh et al., 2018). For instance, Weldrafty et al. (2019) proposed a multimodal cooperative neural network (MCNN) that can handle missing modalities by learning to complement missing modality information with well-represented information from other modalities. Although MCNN has shown great potential in handling the problem of incomplete modalities, it still relies on a hand-design knowledge graph to inform the model about the relationships between different modalities. In contrast, our proposed framework, named LRMM, aims to learn multimodal representations in a more implicit way. By leveraging a sequential autoencoder to learn a hierarchical multimodal representation of users and items, this framework can complement and impute missing modality information that would otherwise be discarded. Moreover, the proposed framework achieves robustness on alleviate data-sparsity based on diverse sourced of information. LRMM is designed upon a complete multimodal framework, where the user and item modalities are both allowed to be missing.

Text similarity measures are a crucial component of various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, such as plagiarism detection, information retrieval, and text recognition. These measures are used to evaluate the similarity between two text sequences and can be employed in numerous applications, including question answering, text classification, and information extraction (Lebret et al., 2011). As deep learning techniques have gained increasing attention in the field of NLP, sequential models have emerged as powerful tools for a range of text-related tasks. However, traditional similarity measures, such as n-grams and skip-grams overlap (Manning and Schütze, 1999), fail to exploit the sequential nature of language effectively. These measures rely on distinct slices of the input texts, which can capture only specific aspects of language and often neglect the nuances of context and semantics (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005). In many cases, semantic similarity and related concepts often appear in text in an entangled way, and it is difficult to identify which specific words or parts of words play a role in similarity and which not. Our goal in this paper is to present a novel text similarity metric, referred to as TextFlow, inspired from a representation commonly employed in DNA sequence alignment algorithms. This method represents input text pairs as continuous curves and effectively takes into account both the actual position of the words and sequence matching to determine the similarity value. Specifically, we modify the way two input sequences are shown and define our similarity measure using the continuity of sequences while skipping unrelated pieces to obtain much more compact space of sequences. By introducing a similarity measure that combines both the spatial and sequential relationships in text, we show that TextFlow can achieve state-of-the-art results on paraphrase detection, textual entailment recognition, and ranking relevance. Our contributions can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we present a new text similarity measure called TextFlow that incorporates the sequential and spatial aspects of text. This represents input text pairs as continuous curves and uses both the actual position of the words and sequence matching to compute the similarity value. Unlike previous approaches, TextFlow allows for the discovery of more nuanced relationships between words within a text and enables the identification of complex patterns and structures that are not apparent through discrete measures like n-grams and skip-grams overlap. Our second contribution is the application of TextFlow to various problems in NLP, demonstrating its effectiveness in tasks that require a deep understanding of semantic similarity and language relationships.

Unlike their explicit counterparts, they are not directly connected to their respective predicates, and as such are hard to locate and disambiguate. Traditional approaches to identifying implicit arguments rely heavily on hand-crafted feature extraction (e.g., Lample et al., 2016;Gardent et al., 2017) and often employ rule-based mechanisms (e.g., Zettlemoyer and Collins, 2007). Medical named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial problem for medical text mining, which plays a vital role in clinical decision support, disease surveillance, and personalized medicine. Electronic medical records are rich sources of unstructured text that require NER for effective analysis and storage. However, annotating medical records is labor-intensive and requires domain expertise, particularly in different specialties. For instance, radiation oncology and pediatrics use distinct jargon and medical terminologies that vary significantly from those used in cardiology or orthopedic surgery. Moreover, even within a single specialty, different physicians may employ unique language and notation styles. As a result, data shortage and the specialist gap present significant challenges to training a broadly applicable medical NER model. Recent advances in deep learning have improved the performance of various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including NER. However, training a high-quality NER model for one specialty does not automatically generalize well to other domains or specialties. In this work, we investigate the problem of cross-specialty medical NER and propose a novel transfer learning framework to alleviate the discrepancy between NER tasks from different domains, including specialty-driven terminological differences. The goal is to design an NER system that, with minimal additional annotations, can be applied across multiple specialties. Our approach to this multi-specialty transfer problem is based on a simple yet effective paradigm: double transfer learning. Concretely, we propose label-aware double transfer learning (La-DTL), which consists of two primary components. Firstly, we devise label-aware maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) for feature representation transfer. In traditional MMD-based feature transfer, the discrepancy metric does not take into account label information, which is crucial for evaluating NER modeling performance. To address this limitation, we propose to incorporate label information into MMD metrics through a form of "semi-supervised" learning. Our formulation leverages low- to high-frequency information to capture both label-aware and label-invariant patterns in an NER model. Secondly, we perform parameter transfer with an established theoretical upper bound that inherits the label-aware property. The theoretical bound quantifies the upper limit of the transfer loss contributed by differing specialty data, allowing the model to differentiate between fruitful adaptation and unrealistic leveraging. By leveraging this double transfer mechanism, we aim to enable cross-specialty NER with a transfer learning framework where the model not only learns which features are transferable but also which non-transferrable knowledge to prune.

The evaluation of summarization systems is a crucial task in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Automatic summarization systems have the potential to revolutionize information retrieval and communication, however their performance is heavily dependent on effective evaluation metrics (Nenkova and McKeown, 2011). In order to better understand the strengths and weaknesses of summarization systems and to improve their performance, researchers have been developing and refining evaluation metrics (Denkowski and Lavie, 2014;Rothe et al., 2014). The Text Analysis Conference (TAC) has been a leading forum for the evaluation of summarization systems since its inception, and the document summarization track has played an integral role in this effort (Durrett, 2012). In the document summarization track of the TAC, evaluation is framed as a ranking problem, where the goal is to rank systems by their ability to select and arrange the most informative content of a set of documents (Dang et al., 2008). One key challenge in this ranking task is in determining a suitable metric for comparison of systems (Fritzinger et al., 2012). To address this challenge, TAC uses a ranking system based on scores from human annotators (Durrett, 2012). This ranking system scores summary systems based on their average score over a collection of document sets, with the top-scoring system declared the winner (Durrett, 2012). However, this approach has some limitations. First, it treats the quality of a summarization system as a single number, which is the average score. This approach does not capture the variability of a system's performance over different document sets. In addition, it does not effectively distinguish between human and machine summarization systems. A human summarizer is expected to produce high-quality summaries regardless of the document set, whereas a machine summarizer may perform well on specific document sets but poorly on others (Kopp and Schwartz, 2012). Moreover, the average score does not provide information on the relative ranking of runs with different average scores (Paass and Eggo, 2013). In this paper, we investigate the statistical appropriateness of the current evaluation metric used by TAC. Specifically, we examine whether the ranking of human and machine summarization systems based on their average score is accurate and reliable. Building on this understanding, we propose an alternative evaluation metric that better captures the variability of a summarization system's performance over different document sets and distinguishes between human and machine summarization systems. Our proposed metric is a Bayesian ranking statistic that takes into account both the average score and the variability of a system's performance, allowing for a more nuanced evaluation of summarization systems.

The convergence of computer vision and natural language processing has been a fundamental goal in the field of artificial intelligence for several decades. Research in this area has garnered significant attention in recent years, driven by the increasing availability of large datasets, advances in deep learning, and the ever-growing demand for more sophisticated and human-like AI systems. The integration of vision and language enables systems to interpret, understand, and interact with the visual world in a more human-like way, unlocking exciting possibilities for a range of applications, including image and video analysis, multi-modal dialogue systems, and multimedia indexing and retrieval. A key factor driving progress in this area has been the availability of high-quality datasets, which serve as the backbone of deep learning-based approaches. These datasets provide the necessary training data to learn complex relationships between visual and linguistic features, allowing researchers to develop and test novel models and algorithms. In recent years, we have witnessed an explosion of new datasets, which not only provide larger and more diverse collections of images, videos, and audio, but also tap into more complex language and abstract concepts. However, with the increasing proliferation of datasets, there is a growing need for systematic evaluation and categorization to help researchers navigate the vast array of options and make informed decisions about which datasets to use for their research. A major challenge in this endeavor is the intrinsic subjectivity of evaluating datasets, as different researchers may have diverse opinions on what constitutes a high-quality dataset. To address this issue, we propose a set of quality metrics that can be used to evaluate and compare vision & language datasets. These quality metrics are categorized into three broad categories: (1) data quality, (2) diversity and complexity, and (3) annotation quality. Data quality metrics include measures of dataset size, diversity, and completeness, while diversity and complexity metrics assess the range of tasks, subjects, and scenarios covered in the dataset. Annotation quality metrics evaluate the accuracy, consistency, and transparency of the annotations provided. Our analysis of the surveyed datasets reveals that the most recent ones have been using more complex language and more abstract concepts, indicating a shift towards more challenging and sophisticated tasks. However, we also observe that each dataset has its own strengths and weaknesses, and that there is no single "best" dataset that suits all research needs. By providing a comprehensive survey of current datasets and proposing a set of quality metrics, we aim to facilitate the development of more effective and efficient vision & language models, and ultimately, to advance the state of the art in this exciting and rapidly evolving

Dependency parsing is a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications in summarization, question answering, machine translation, sentiment analysis, and more. There are two primary approaches to parsing: Constituent- Dependent (CFG) parsing and Dependency parsing. Constituent-Dependent parsing represents the structure of a sentence as a nested collection of phrase structures where a non-terminal can be replaced by a phrase that consists of a combination of non-terminals and terminals. Dependency parsing represents the structure of a sentence as a set of directed relations between words, known as dependencies, where each word is a head and its dependent(s) are the words it depends on. Tree Substitution Grammar (TSG) is an extension of constituent-based grammar, where phrase structures are represented as labeled trees, and non-terminal nodes represent a type of phrase (e.g. noun phrase, verb phrase, etc.). In contrast, dependency parsing is focused on capturing the relational structure of language directly in terms of the dependencies between constituents. For dependency parsing, commonly used models are Transition-based Dependency Parsing and Graph-based Dependency Parsing. However, while syntactic parsing models can achieve high accuracy when trained on large parallel training data, relevant training data often must be heavy labor-intensive to annotate and may not be available for a given domain. For certain languages or domains where parallel training data is scarce, inducing a grammar directly from text becomes a more feasible approach. Inducing a grammar directly from text, or unsupervised grammar induction, is one of the oldest and most challenging tasks in Computational Linguistics. Despite the challenges, researchers have made significant progress in recent years in inducing dependency grammars. Nonetheless, the induced dependency grammars produced by these models are still overly simplistic, particularly in comparison to supervised parsing models. One of the key reasons is that these models tend to either ignore contextual information or use hand-crafted features to capture complex patterns, both of which can result in poor modeling of complex linguistic phenomena. In an attempt to address this limitation, several researchers have explored unsupervised learning of complex dependencies for dependency parsing. Some researchers have applied non-parametric Bayesian models and dependency-based grammar learning. In a typical unsupervised grammatical framework, a grammar is typically represented as a set of trees, and the goal is to induce a grammatical model that can generate a set of trees from the given unannotated texts. This is a classic example of non-parametric Bayesian distribution modelling which enables the direct induction of a large set of dependencies.

Introduction   Language models are a crucial component of natural language processing (NLP), particularly in tasks such as machine translation, text summarization, and speech recognition. Traditional n-gram language models, where words are modeled as a consecutive sequence of n items, have been widely used for many years. However, they have several limitations, including the failure to capture long-range dependencies and the inability to generalize to unseen contexts. Recently, there has been a surge of interest in exploring novel approaches to language modeling that can better capture the structure and semantics of language. Given that human languages exhibit a hierarchical and compositional structure, it is natural to ask whether language models can benefit from incorporating this structure into the modeling process. This question is central to the field of syntax and semantics, which aims to assign meaning to words and phrases within an utterance. Recent work in linguistics has shown that the study of syntax and semantics is closely tied to the study of the co-occurrence of words, with syntax and semantics influencing each other in a complex and dynamic way. For example, in English, the verb phrase "cook a fish" conveys a different meaning from the individual words that comprise it, "cook" and "a fish". This meaning is achieved through the arrangement of these words into a specific structure, which reflects their roles in the sentence. In this paper, we introduce Latent Tree Language Model (LTLM), a novel approach to language modeling that encodes syntax and semantics of a given sentence as a tree of word roles. We propose that the nodes in the tree represent specific roles, such as the agent or the patient, while the edges represent the relationships between these roles. We argue that this representation is well-suited to capture the compositional structure of language and to represent long-range dependencies between words. Our proposed model, LTLM, has two key innovations: (a) it incorporates the structure of language into the modeling process through a tree-based representation, and (b) it learns the structure of the tree from the data using a probabilistic framework. The key challenge in developing LTLM is learning a good representation of the tree structure. We address this challenge by proposing two algorithms to infer a tree for a given sentence: a Gibbs sampling algorithm that is fast but may not find the most probable tree, and a dynamic programming algorithm that guarantees to find the most probable tree but is slower.

Parsing plays a central role in NLP applications where unanalyzed input strings are used as input, such as machine translation, question-answering and information retrieval. The input string is typically analyzed into a hierarchical representation, which we will refer to as a syntactic tree. A syntactic tree consists of a set of nodes, where each group of nodes represents a sub-string of the input and the structure that connects them represents the grammatical dependency between the constituent sub-strings. A syntactic parser is an algorithm that determines a syntactic tree from a given input string, given a set of grammar rules that specify the syntactic structure of the language. These rules are often organized as a phrase structure grammar. The locality-based LR parsers, whose theory and operation are thoroughly studied in compiler construction (Aho, 1968; Hopkins, 1972), are based on the notion that the parser can only look ahead and not insert anything before it. In this approach, syntactic structure is represented as a sequence of primitives related by certain rules. For a long time, non-lexicalized parsing techniques such as stochastic LR parsers (Johnson, 1998) have been highly successful in parsing English and other heavily inflectional languages notwithstanding their simplified rule based method. A major design option is whether certain features of words are allowed to influence parsing decisions as they may represent genuine features of syntactic structure. Collins (2003) proposed lexicalized parsing, which explicitly distinguishes the processes of lexicalization (word-level annotation of part of speech and syntactic function) and parsing, and permits the application of special lexicalization rules at parsing time. This new approach has been highly successful in a number of areas, achieving a modeling power that almost reaches the current theoretical bound and applications where practical use is maintained. Despite its success in achieving both highly accurate and efficient parsing results, lexicalized parsers are restricted to the notion that words have a simple bundle of attributes that determine their function within the sentence. However, highly morphologically inflected languages like French, unlike English, possess numerous word banks given their prolific succession of suffixes. A problem that has been the subject of study is why many word forms exist, which can have free selections of auxiliary arguments that carry nothing essential but whose functions participate to build a grammatical structure that contains more course and quantity relations inside the word forms compared with the several more English word forms.

Harvesting knowledge from textbooks is a key challenge in many educational applications. Textbooks are rich sources of knowledge that contain valuable information in various formats, including axiomatic knowledge that are essential for learning and problem-solving. Math textbooks, in particular, are a treasure trove of axiomatic knowledge, which if extracted and utilized effectively, can facilitate intelligent systems that solve math problems. Geometry, as a branch of math, is one such area that consists of well-structured axiomatic knowledge, which can provide a solid foundation for intelligent math problem-solving systems. However, extracting axiomatic knowledge from textbooks is a daunting task that requires advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques as well as an in-depth understanding of the subject matter. Existing approaches to extracting knowledge from textbooks largely rely on shallow parsing techniques, which fail to capture the complex relationships between concepts and are often prone to errors due to the diversity of writing styles and notations used in textbooks. In this paper, we present an approach to obtain axiomatic knowledge of geometry in the form of horn-clause rules from math textbooks. Our approach uses a combination of contextual and typographical features extracted from the textbooks, including linguistic features relevant to math, such as equation, formula, and theorem identification. Moreover, we leverage the redundancy and shared ordering of axioms across multiple textbooks to accurately harvest axioms, thereby reducing errors and improving the accuracy of extracted knowledge. The extracted axioms are then parsed into horn-clause rules that can be seamlessly integrated into existing math problem-solving frameworks to improve their performance. This paper presents a comprehensive study on harvesting axiomatic knowledge from math textbooks and solving geometry problems using the extracted knowledge. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing it with state-of-the-art systems in solving geometry problems and highlighting its strengths and limitations through a series of experiments and analysis. Our findings indicate that the proposed approach significantly improves the performance of geometry problem-solving systems and has promising applications in areas such as math education and intelligent tutoring systems. Furthermore, we provide insights into the potential of using textbook data for knowledge extraction and highlight future research directions that can further enhance the effectiveness of our approach. In the remainder of this paper, we discuss the background and related work on knowledge extraction from textbooks, our approach and system design, the experiments and results, and finally, we conclude with a discussion on the implications and future work.

The importance of high-quality parallel corpora is well acknowledged in the natural language processing (NLP) community. They serve as the foundation for building effective statistical machine translation (SMT) systems. Among various sources of parallel data, including manually aligned databases, flameo songs lyrics, and parliamentary debates, the quality and quantity of available corpora vary significantly (Koehn and Knight, 2003;Zapirain et al., 2012). As a result, researchers have turned to mining parallel data from various Web resources, such as Wikipedia, copy-paste Websites, and online forums. Specifically, Web mining data relies on the idea of translating document pairs from corresponding non-parallel but comparable corpora (Koehn, 2005;Lavie et al., 2007). However, this line of work is generally restricted to pre-existing, comparable collections, where the documents are either roughly translated or often similar in content. Thus, several critical issues limit its applicability. First, the quality and efficiency of hypothetical machine translation (HMT) automatically extracting parallel data is typically unknown, since mainstream SMT approaches perform poorly on low-quality parallel training examples (Lavie et al., 2007). Second, current approaches neglect the truth that comparable documents do not always have intrinsic cross-document parallelism (Lavie et al., 2007), potentially resulting in noisy matches and wasted computational resources. In contrast, automatically finding high-quality sentence pairs from the Web would be capable of creating quickly and constantly updated large-scale translation resources by taking advantage of its abundance and rapidly changing landscape. Moreover, tackling the problem in this direction would push the field towards a new platform for processing large-scale updates and real-time parallel data rather than just focusing on offline problems such as inducing parallel pairs from comparable corpora or tuning mono lingual task parameters (Popovic-Sijliaški et al., 2012). In recent years, researchers have made significant strides in developing highly effective techniques for searching for similar subsets of documents, thereby forming the core component of Web mining approaches. Event extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP) with a wide range of applications in text analysis, information retrieval, and knowledge representation. It involves the extraction of structured information about events from unstructured texts, which enables the construction of a comprehensive and accurate event database. Recently, with the rapid growth of social media, extracting events from social media has become an increasingly important task, as it allows for the analysis of current events, trending topics, and public sentiment. However, existing event extractors for social media suffer from several limitations. Firstly, social media messages often lack context due to the informality of the language used. For instance, a tweet like "just got a new job" does not provide sufficient information about the type of job, the company name, or the location of the job. Secondly, the informal nature of social media language often contains jargon, abbreviations, and slang that are difficult for event extractors to comprehend. As a result, existing event extractors may struggle to identify the key elements of an event, such as the participant, location, and time. To address these limitations, mainstream approach for event extraction in social media is to rely solely on relevant features from the social media text, such as named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech (POS) tagging. However, these feature-based approaches can be vulnerable to noise and variability in the social media text. Moreover, they may not capture the deeper, contextual relationships between events that are critical for accurate event understanding. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to event extraction in social media that leverages cross-genre knowledge enrichment to improve the performance of event extraction. By incorporating knowledge from outside the social media text, such as Wikipedia, knowledge graphs, and web pages, we aim to provide a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of events. Our approach is based on the assumption that cross-genre knowledge can provide valuable context and depth to social media text, enabling event extractors to better identify the key elements of an event. To achieve this, we adopt a knowledge graph-based framework that integrates social media text with cross-genre knowledge. We create a graph that represents the events, entities, and relationships between them, and then use link prediction and entity disambiguation to enrich the event representation. By incorporating cross-genre knowledge, we enhance the event extraction capabilities of our system and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of F-score improvement.

Part-of-speech (POS) tagging is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which consists of identifying the grammatical category of each word in a given text, such as noun, verb, adjective, etc. Traditional POS tagging methods have been developed for single-language texts, and they generally take advantage of a language's intrinsic properties to improve their performance. With the increasing globalization of information exchange, texts in multilingual languages have become increasingly popular, particularly on the internet. A common type of multilingual text is the Chinese-English mixed text, where a few English words are embedded in a predominantly Chinese text. Examples of Chinese-English mixed texts can be found in modern Chinese articles, conversations, emails, and internet literature. However, part-of-speech tagging for such texts presents a significant challenge due to the difference in writing systems between Chinese and English. Chinese is a logograph-based language, where each character represents a word, while English is an alphabetic language, with each word represented by a sequence of alphabetic characters. As a result, existing POS tagging methods for Chinese are often inadequate for Chinese-English mixed texts. In the absence of a well-annotated corpus for Chinese-English mixed texts, most English words are simplified as "foreign words" (and treated as a certain type of "NOUN"), which loses important information about the word's POS and functionality within the sentence. In recent years, dealing with Chinese-English mixed texts has become an essential task in NLP, and there is growing interest in developing methods specifically for POS tagging in multilingual texts. Traditional POS tagging methods for single-language texts rely heavily on static features, including: character-based features, word shape-based features, and context-based features, which are not sufficient to distinguish the POS of English words in Chinese-English mixed texts. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach to POS tagging for Chinese-English mixed texts by incorporating dynamic features that take into account the spatial relationships between the Chinese and English words. In this paper, we explore the applicability of using dynamic features to enhance the accuracy of POS tagging for Chinese-English mixed texts. We contributed by extracting and evaluating the effects of five types of dynamic features on the POS tagging performance of the Chinese-English mixed texts. Our results show that our method outperforms traditional sequence labeling methods and boosts the performance of POS tagging for pure Chinese texts.

Enabling a computer to understand a document so that it can answer comprehension questions is a central goal of NLP. Achieving this goal, however, has proven to be a challenging task due to the complexity of text comprehension and the limited availability of high-quality human-annotated data. For this reason, most current NLP systems are limited in their ability to understand and interpret the meaning of text, relying instead on rules and heuristics that are not robust or transferable. In order to address this challenge, Hermann et al. (2015) have attempted to create a large-scale dataset of reading comprehension tasks. This data is based on summarised bullet points that have been paired with CNN and Daily Mail news articles, resulting in a corpus of over a million training examples. The creation of this dataset was a significant step forwards for the field of NLP, and marks an important point in the development of computer systems that can understand and interpret text. One of the key features of this dataset is that it is designed to assess the ability of a machine learning system to understand and comprehend the meaning of a passage of text, rather than simply relying on patterns and associations that may not be relevant to the task at hand. This is in contrast to many current NLP systems, which are often trained on datasets that are focused on very specific tasks, such as sentiment analysis or named entity recognition, rather than more general language understanding tasks like reading comprehension. However, despite the potential of the dataset created by Hermann et al., there remains a need for a deeper understanding of the linguistic features and cognitive processes that are required in order to perform well on this task. In order to gain a better understanding of these factors, we conducted a thorough examination of the CNN/Daily Mail Reading Comprehension Task. Our primary aim was to understand what depth of language understanding is required in order to do well on this task. In order to address this question, we took a two-pronged approach. On the one hand, we conducted a careful hand-analysis of a small subset of the problems in the dataset. This involved manually reviewing the passage and question for each problem, in order to identify the key linguistic features and cognitive processes that are required in order to answer the question successfully. This analysis was useful in providing insight into the types of language understanding and cognitive processes that are required in order to perform well on this task.

Distributed Representations for Building Profiles of Users and Items from Text Reviews Recommendation systems have become increasingly important nowadays as they have the ability to revolutionize the way we discover new information, products, and services. With the rapid growth of e-commerce, blogs, social networks, and other online platforms, the sheer volume of available information makes it extremely difficult for users to find the most relevant and useful items or services without personalized guidance. This is where recommendation systems come into play. Traditional recommendation algorithms, such as collaborative filtering (CF) and matrix completion, rely heavily on user-item interaction data. While CF and its variants are particularly effective in exploiting the relationships between users who share similar behavior, they suffer from several limitations, including data sparsity, scalability, and cold start problems. These algorithms lack the ability to exploit key information hidden in text comments and opinions. On the other hand, opinion mining methods provide valuable information, such as sentiment analysis results and co-occurrence of words associated with users and items. However, these methods do not provide direct support to recommendation systems in terms of profiling users and items. To bridge this gap, various methods have been proposed in recent years, including hybrid models that combine CF with content-based methods, and autoencoders based approaches that learn dense representations from text data. However, these models either lack the ability to provide explicit insights into user and item profiles, or require complex architecture designs and large amounts of training data. In this paper, we attempt to address these challenges by introducing a novel approach for constructing vector representations of users and items from text comments. Our proposed approach learns a unified framework for distributed representations of users and items, where each user or item is represented as a vector that captures its inherent characteristics and attributes. By maximizing the likelihood of word appearances, we can effectively learn the underlying patterns and relationships in text comments, and utilize this knowledge to improve the accuracy of recommendation systems. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on real-world datasets and compare our results with state-of-the-art baseline systems. This work focuses on addressing the key challenges in building profiles of users and items from text comments within a unified framework. We explore the strengths of incorporating text data into recommendation systems and leverage the power of distributed representations to unlock valuable insights into user and item behaviors.

Structured learning approaches have been widely used in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks to model complex relationships between entities and predict structured outputs such as dependency parses, semantic role labels, and part-of-speech tags. One of the key challenges in these tasks is to induce the underlying structure of the output, which requires modeling the relationships between the group of entities that share a specific property, rather than predicting them independently. Taxonomy induction, which aims to derive hierarchical relations between concepts or entity types, is one such complex task. Taxonomies or ontologies, such as WordNet, play a crucial role in many natural language and data mining applications, serving as the backbone for knowledge representation and derivation of relational information. However, current hypernymy-taxonomy induction methods, such as father-son algorithms and path-based approaches, face significant limitations. These approaches generally suffer from high error rates due to the lack of robust semantic evidence and the intractability of learning complex taxonomy structures, which leads to either missing many weekly validated relations or permissive admission of hypothetical unrelated pairs (Budanitsky, 1999').' Many mainstream methods for taxonomy induction focus on graph-based distance metrics, which sometimes result in blindness to other heavy linguistic patterns notwithstanding theoretically powerful information (Morin & Rappoport, 2002, Budanitsky, 1999). Most approaches currently in place basically trade one critique for another. This challenge further underscores the necessity of finding ways to effectively combine high-level relational insights and noise-tolerant solutions to learn the actual taxonomy structure from the available data. In this paper, we propose a structured learning approach using Probability Graphical Models (PGMs) for inducing hypernym taxonomies from heterogeneous relational evidence. We integrate a family of factors into the model, including ontological features, siblinghood, both of which gathered from statistical patterns over Wikipedia articles and low-level patterns from the available Web n-grams. In particular, we introduce an extension to belief propagation which combines loopy belief propagation for incorporation to the siblinghood factor for restricting the factor space runs. Furthermore, we factor grandfather-child patterns that are positional within the graph using an approximate algorithm that combines an explicit spanning tree constraint with belief propagation. In our architecture, our goal is to reproduce sub-trees of WordNet using discriminatively trained adaptive subgradient-stochastic optimisation. We initially test our architecture that gets a chance based error rate of 49%, compared to 51% error rate with no subparsers or siblinghood involved.
