Temporal relation classification (TRC) is a task central to a wide variety of natural language processing (NLP) applications, including information extraction, question answering, and narrative understanding (Chen et al., 2017;Verhagen et al., 2018). The aim of TRC is to identify and classify temporal relationships between events mentioned in text. This task is critical in applications related to healthcare, finance, and social sciences, where understanding the temporal context is vital. A key challenge in TRC is the fact that events can exhibit a rich variety of temporal dependencies, including containment and spatial relationships (Chen et al., 2016). These relationships are often implicit and can be difficult to identify, even for humans. Narratives in the clinical domain are no exception; they often involve complex temporal relationships that must be identified accurately to inform treatment decisions. Incorporatingauxiliary tasks or loss functions that leverage the temporal dependencies in the data is one effective way of addressing this challenge. Deep learning methods have become increasingly popular for TRC, thanks to their ability to learn complex, hierarchical representations of text (Mikolov et al., 2013). These models often rely on pre-trained word embeddings as feature representations (Wang et al., 2020;Chen and Cardie, 2014). These pre-trained embeddings can provide strong, general-purpose representations that are often effective in many NLP tasks. However,pretrained-word embeddings, even those that have been task-adapted through continued training, are often limited by their fixed assignment to specific word types (Vilnis and McCallum, 2015). In this paper, we investigate a new extension to the popular supervised loss function that is traditionally employed for TRC and demonstrate its practical benefits in inducing word-embeddings that represent both the general and task-specific properties of words This new extension incorporates the well-known pre-trained word representations as features but also introduces an auxiliary loss term designed specifically to histogram the representations into angles relative to the task space. The resulting embeddings retain the generalizability afforded by pre-trained embeddings, while also adapt to the task-specific requirements unique to TRC. We demonstrate its effectiveness in narrative containment relation extraction from clinical records on the widely used THYME dataset where the pre-trained word representations offered a more course and surface meaning while the auxiliary histograming loss retrieved several more general word properties left untapped by the pre-trained vector space. During the evaluations, pre-trained based word-level loss model TRC performance through the supervised loss, auxiliary loss and the combination of the two loss type models demonstrated large improvements in overall accuracy, ROUGE score and more noticeable statistically significant performance gains following the application of the histograming word-level loss

Sentence similarity (SS) tasks have received significant attention in the field of natural language processing in recent years, with the primary goal of automatically computing a similarity score between two sentences. SS tasks are distinct from document-level semantics tasks, which typically feature a high degree of word co-occurrence within a document (i.e., a dense representation). Conversely, SS tasks often involve sparse and heterogeneous word distribution within a sentence, leading to a greater challenge in capturing the underlying semantic meaning. A robust model of lexical semantics is, therefore, essential to accurately represent the complete semantic picture of a sentence. This assertion is supported by the fact that even small changes in the word choices within a sentence can significantly impact the overall meaning of the sentence (Kintsch, 1974). Previous approaches to SS tasks have primarily focused on recognizing key aspects of sentential semantics, including contextual relationships, compositionality, and lexical nuances (Li et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2014). However, these methods have typically overlooked the importance of incorporating robust lexical semantics, which is inextricably linked to the meaning of individual words within a sentence. Inspired by the conjecture that better modeling of lexical semantics can lead to improved sentential semantics (Harris, 1954; Firth, 1957), we propose an enhanced latent variable model that converges both corpus-based and knowledge-based aspects of lexical semantics. In this work, we focus on developing a novel approach that incorporates selectional preference information from the corpus and similar words extracted from a dictionary into the model. We contend that this method will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the semantic relationships between words, ultimately yielding higher-quality sentential representations. Our investigations aim to demonstrate the efficacy of incorporating robust lexical semantics by comparing the performance of our proposed model to existing state-of-the-art models in the SS domain. We will evaluate our approach on two benchmark SS datasets, with the objective of showcasing its capacity to deliver superior performance among unsupervised models. Our research provides new insight into the significance of lexical semantics in determining sentential semantics and emphasizes the value of robust lexical modeling in improving the effectiveness of sentence similarity tasks. By tightly integrating the strength of lexical knowledge within a latent variable framework, we may unlock the full potential of sentential semantics and offer a qualitative leap in the representation of meaning in natural language data. Our results suggest that the introduced model is a promising addition to the growing field of distributional semantic models and may offer new avenues for SS research.

Electronic Health Record (EHR) systems are abundant sources of data containing valuable insights into patients' medical histories. A remarkable challenge in the field of Health Informatics is the automation of information extraction from the unstructured text in EHR notes. The mentioned text comprises mixed signals including past medical events and patient interactions with the healthcare system. These systems can group together competent medical professionals, and can assist them in compiling necessary patient data at the convenient time. With the help of sophisticated Information Extraction (IE) algorithms, they provide healthcare professionals with a formatted report of valuable patient information. Entity linking is a challenging task in natural language processing (NLP), as it requires a deep understanding of various aspects of entities, including their descriptions in knowledge bases (KBs), contexts in which they are mentioned, and structured knowledge. Traditional entity linking models often rely on hand-engineered features and domain-specific training data, which can limit their applicability to new domains and texts. However, the widespread availability of texts and knowledge bases has made it increasingly necessary to develop sophisticated models that can entity linking across multiple domains without relying on domain-specific resources or features. The success of entity linking heavily depends on its understanding of the entity. Current traditional methods for entity linking only consider part of information of entities, such as descriptions in knowledge bases, contexts around mentions, or the structured knowledge about certain aspects of the described phenomena. However, an entity is more complex than that. Entity descriptions, contexts, and types contain many aspects that are useful for entity understanding. For example, an entity description can give a general idea about what an entity is like, and structured knowledge about some aspects of the described phenomenon can provide valuable insights into more specific information, such as birth and death dates. The issue is that these different relevant sources of information must be combined in a meaningful way. By requiring multiple sources of information, current traditional methods for entity linking become cumbersome. A well-designed entity linking system should incorporate diverse features of entities mentioned in texts. However, the entity linking problem is inherently related to information retrieval, hence it would be nice if entity linking systems can quickly and efficiently retrieve the relevant information from the knowledge base without having to perform multiple, time-consuming database queries. The goal of this paper is to present a neural, modular entity linking system that learns a unified dense representation for each entity by jointly encoding multiple sources of information, including entity descriptions, contexts in which entities are mentioned, and fine-grained types. Unlike previous methods, our approach is able to effectively combine these diverse sources of information without relying on hand-engineered features or domain-specific training data, thus reducing the data preparation, engineering effort required. By learning a unified dense representation for each entity, our model can effectively "embed" entities that are new to the knowledge base, enabling it to link their mentions accurately across different domains and texts.

These DLMT systems postulate a set of precursor sentences or contexts from an MT database and then postulate perplexity scores for each [Tierney et al., 2005]. They therefore, the flexibility to learn from unannotated text and the ability handle an arbitrary number of context with ease. Recent advances in deep learning have proposed the use of neural networks for handling document-level context [Luong et al., 2015; Sutskever et al., 2014; Vaswani et al., 2017]. This approach, known as Neural Machine Translation (NMT), has achieved highly competitive results in machine translation tasks, especially for languages pairs with limited training resources [Dong et al., 2015]. However, NMT often relies on surface-level context, neglecting the underlying semantic relationships within the document. Sentence compression is a natural language processing (NLP) task that allows for the simplification of sentences, with the goal of preserving their essential meaning while reducing their length and complexity Dershowitz et al. (1995); Knight and Marcu(2000). Sentence compression is an important task in the context of text simplification, as it can improve the readability and comprehensibility of sentences, particularly for non-native speakers and people with dyslexia or other reading disabilities. Traditionally, sentence compression has been applied in a monolingual setting, where the goal is to compress sentences in a single language, such as English. However, with the advent of multilingual NLP, there is an increasing interest in extending sentence compression to a bilingual or multilingual context, where the goal is to obtain parallel compressions of parallel sentences Cettolo et al. (2012). In this context, if we have a parallel corpus of English and French text, where each sentence in the English text has a corresponding parallel sentence in French, we would like to obtain compressed sentences that are parallel, i.e., while preserving the translation relationship between the original sentences. This can be beneficial for a series of multilingual NLP tasks, such as machine translation, text summarization, and question answering. For instance, having compressed parallel sentences can facilitate the generation of summaries for parallel texts, or enable the development of parallel question answering systems. Several approaches have been proposed to perform sentence compression in a bilingual context, including the use of machine translation followed by sentence compression in the target language, or the use of bilingual models that jointly perform sentence compression and machine translation. However, these approaches have some limitations, as they may not preserve the translation relationship between the original sentences, or may introduce errors in the translation process. In this paper, we study ways to extend sentence compression in a bilingual context, where the goal is to obtain parallel compressions of parallel sentences. We propose two approaches to taking bilingual information into account when compressing parallel sentences: a bilingual compression approach, and a bilingual ranking approach. The bilingual compression approach involves training a bilingual sentence compression model that jointly considers the two languages and preserves the translation relationship between the original sentences. In contrast, the bilingual ranking approach involves ranking alternative compressed sentences in both languages, based on their likelihood of preserving the translation relationship. We assess the efficiency of the two approaches on a parallel corpus of News articles, and compare the results to a monolingual compression approach.

Ontology matching is a crucial process that enables the unification, extension, and interoperability of different ontologies. That is, multiple ontologies describing the same domain and sharing common entities are merged into a single and comprehensive knowledge graph, thereby providing a more robust and accurate representation of reality. However, the manual alignment process of matching entities across ontologies is time-consuming and laborious, even for related ontologies that were developed independently. This process can be further complicated when a large number of ontologies are available, such as those dealing with different application domains, such as life sciences, engineering, and business. To address the data integration problem in many knowledge-intensive applications, ontology matching has attracted significant attention in recent years (Kalfoglou & Schorlemmer, 2003; Euzenat & Shvaiko, 2007; Shvaiko & Euzenat, 2012). Ontology matching often relies on a feature-based approach, where a set of attributes (features, or primitives) is extracted from entities to describe their properties, and a matching function is then applied to compute similarity scores between features. The features may be chosen by manual design or sometimes generated from the ontology's structure, such as by exploiting synonyms or hyponyms. A crucial challenge in ontology matching is capturing the semantic similarity between different entities as described by their features. Many state-of-the-art methods rely on the Vector Space Model (VSM), which represents entities as vectors in a high-dimensional space and relies on Euclidean distance measures for determining similarities. However, features generated through the traditional VSM fall short in terms of capturing fine-grained semantic relations between entities. Word embeddings, also known as word vectors, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) or GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), have become a popular tool for capturing subtle meaning representations. These models have been trained on large text corpora to learn the representations of words relative to their context to produce dense, distributed vector representations of words which capture much of the linguistic structure present in the language (Finin & Mika, 2003). These learned vectors can provide a richer representation of word meanings. Recent studies have demonstrated their benefits in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks and even extended to the field of ontology matching (Troncy, 2013). However, the distribution of existing word vectors is inherently biased toward capturing general linguistic patterns, and not inherently specialized towards the task of matching entities within a domain-specific ontology. Using general word vectors falls short of fulfilling our need for sufficiently accurate and efficient matching, especially when semantics are nuanced due to domain-specific concepts as seen in many ontologies.

Clinical notes are text documents that are created by clinicians for each patient encounter. They are typically accompanied by medical codes, which describe the diagnosis and treatment. These codes are assigned by extracting information from the text and provide critical information regarding a patient's medical condition, procedure and billing purposes. Despite the critical role these codes play in managing patient records, assigning groupers for billing and medical research study, the task of assigning the relevant codes is labor intensive and inherently prone to human error. Manual annotation of these codes is also an expensive and time-consuming process. Moreover, not only the codes, but also the reasons and details behind the specific diagnoses and treatments are obscured when only the codes are annotated without being shown to correspond to any specific locality in the text. Overcoming the gap between the description found within the clinical text and the diagnosis provided by the code classification with the aid of automatic methods marks an important point for many if not most of natural language processing (NLP) applications in healthcare, as does identifying the reasons for each code being chosen from clinical text in order to make the inferences and decisions exhibited by the computer more transparent, thereby to improve trust and reliability in the results that come out of these NLP-based health applications. Deep learning approaches, especially the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been successful in various NLP tasks, such as text classification (Kim, 2014;Kim, 2014), semantic role labeling (Yao et al., 2009), and named entity recognition (Collobert et al., 2011). However, these models are typically trained using classification loss and outputs high logits but do not provide explanations for the code assignments. Few works have integrated explanations into deep learning models for medical coding tasks. These are limited to describing the models or simply outputting measures of similarity (towards the gold standard codes) rather than exposing explanations for specific code assignments. Given the critical role of clinical text and the highly hierarchical nature of medical code classification, we introduce an attentional convolutional network trained with classification loss plus an additional loss requiring that the network output the top-ranked documents where each word ranked as high within those documents for each medical code. This architecture enables our network to not only predict the medical codes accurately but also select the relevant segments of the patient's clinical documents that support the assigned codes, that is, provide explanations for why the specific codes were chosen.

Linguistic alignment between dialogue partners has long been an intriguing phenomenon in the field of language and social interaction. A wealth of research has demonstrated that participants engage in various linguistic adaptations, such as adjustments in speech rate, pronunciation, and syntactic complexity, to negotiate and maintain social relationships (Brenneis and Macaulay, 1996; Erickson and Shulha, 2002). Recent studies have also contended that the power dynamics between interlocutors play a vital role in shaping linguistic alignment (Wolfram, 2006; Romero-Rodriguez et al., 2014). For instance, individuals in positions of higher power (e.g., employers, professionals) have been shown to exhibit more linguistic alignment with their counterparts, who are often found to be less assertive and less similar in terms of linguistic characteristics (Johnson, 2006). While this body of work has garnered significant attention, it often overlooks a critical aspect of language use: the pervasiveness of low-level linguistic features that can equally influence alignment. Variously known as low-level, high-frequency, or micro-features, these linguistic markers can comprise elementary building blocks such as word length, utterance duration, prosody, and phonological characteristics (Daly et al., 2004). Although some research has highlighted their importance in conversations (Hay ard, 2011), the majority of studies focused on the impact of social power have only subtly acknowledged, if not entirely disregarded, the potential effect of these low-level features (McGrath, 2013). This oversight might be attributed to the complexity of isolating the influence of individual low-level features, coupled with the pursuit of attributing the phenomenon to more higher-level constructs, such as social power and social status. In this paper, we revisit the assumption that interlocutors' social power is a primary determinant of the linguistic alignment between dialogue partners. To examine this issue, we employ logistic regression models to analyze two datasets and tease apart the unique contributions of both low-level linguistic features and social power to the observed alignment patterns. The first dataset includes conversations between speakers with varied levels of linguistic and social status, while the second dataset consists of free conversation data collected from a broader population. By carefully controlling for low-level features such as utterance length, syntactic complexity, and word order, we investigate whether the association between power and alignment diminishes, vanishes, or even inverts after accounting for these micro-structures. Our aim is not to completely dismiss the role of social power or even the idea that power differentially contributes to alignment under specific interactional conditions.

Open Information Extraction (IE) has emerged as a powerful technology for extracting assertions from large corpora without requiring a pre-specified vocabulary (Riedel et al., 2010;Fader et al., 2011). Traditional closed-domain extraction systems, relying on pre-defined entities, templates and lexicons, have limited applicability due to their reliance on predefined knowledge (Banko et al., 2007). However, the open nature of IE systems like REVERB (Gupta et al., 2014), TEXTRUNNER (Yosef et al., 2013), and WOE (Liu et al., 2015) allows them to operate without prior knowledge of entities or domains. They parse large corpora to extract relationships between entities using machine learning and statistical models, similar to those employed in standard information extraction systems. These systems, however, typically lack the robustness and precision required in practical applications such as question-answering, text summarization, and knowledge graph construction. After reviewing the extractions produced by recent state-of-the-art Open IE systems such as REVERB, TEXTRUNNER, and WOE, we found that the output often consists of numerous extraneous and theoretically useless information (Durrett and Klein, 2013). Examples include extraction of facts like: sentences can have paragraphs, exits can have doors, dogs can bark. Such uninformative extractions make it difficult and sometimes even pointless to relate the extracted facts to real-world knowledge graphs (Kotis and Stephanides, 2008). Furthermore, the output is often incoherent as in: [Prince William’s parents are Diana and clan] (Song et al., 2014). Despite the limitations of the current state-of-the-art Open IE systems, we believe that Open IE has great potential for advancing information extraction and the ability to draw inferences from large collections of text. To address the issues mentioned above, we present two novel syntactic and lexical constraints on binary relations to the traditional techniques utilized for restricting the extraction space within Open IE. The first constraint necessitates that the subject within the relation extracted is a person, animate object, institution, etc. The second constraint implies that the property expressed within the extracted relation should be a qualitative or quantifiable attribute of a noun. We assess the impact of the proposed constraints by integrating them into the REVERB system (Gupta et al., 2014), which is based on a BiLSTM-CRF framework with sentiment sensitive training permutations. Our results, as shown in subsequent sections, demonstrated that both our syntactic and lexical-based constraints improve the precision of Open IE significantly over the results obtained with prior extractions by TEXTRUNNER and WOE pos.

Word Embeddings: The Backbone of Modern Natural Language Processing In recent years, word embeddings have become a cornerstone of the natural language processing (NLP) toolkit, and a ubiquitous component of many NLP applications. These continuous vector representations of words have proven to capture semantic relationships between words, and have been instrumental in achieving state-of-the-art results in a wide range of NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, topic modeling, and language translation. Popular methods for learning word embeddings include Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014), which have been extensively used in both research and industry. While these methods have been successful in capturing word semantic relationships, they suffer from the drawback of being fixed-dimensional representations. This means that each word is mapped to a unique vector that captures a fixed range of contextual information. In many applications, however, it would be beneficial to have a representation that is adaptable to the specific requirements of the task, rather than a fixed one-size-fits-all representation. Consider, for instance, the task of language modeling, where the context is often a limited window of surrounding words, and a lower-dimensional representation may be sufficient. In contrast, other applications such as text classification may require higher-dimensional representations to capture more nuanced semantic relationships. Existing word embeddings can exacerbate this issue, as they often require retraining from scratch for each new application, or require manual feature engineering to downscale high-dimensional representations. This is not only computationally expensive but also increases the risk of overfitting, which can lead to poor generalization performance. To address this problem, researchers have proposed a range of techniques, including vector reduction (Lebret and Collobert, 2014) and dimensionality amplification (Goyal et al., 2017). However, these methods either rely on computationally expensive linear transformations, or can suffer from a loss of semantic information. This paper proposes an alternative strategy for learning neural word embeddings, one that leverages an incremental learning paradigm to generate right-truncatable vectors. By building on the principles of neural word embedding methods such as SkipGrams and Global Vectors, we show that our approach can efficiently generate vectors that inherit the semantic properties of their higher-dimensional counterparts. The resulting representation has the unique property of being right-truncatable, meaning that any right-truncated vector matches the solution of the corresponding lower-dimensional embedding. This allows a single embedding vector to manage a wide range of dimensional requirements imposed by many different uses and applications.

Nested mention recognition is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), which identifies entity mentions in text. A common challenge in this task is that an entity mention can contain other mentions recursively. Consider the following example: "George W. Bush mentioned John Kerry and John's family members during his presidential campaign." In this case, the nested mention group consists of John and John's family members, which are contained within the larger mention of John Kerry. Current approaches to nested mention recognition often rely on heuristic rules and hand-crafted models, which can be brittle and prone to errors. For instance, many approaches adopt the strategy of first labeling the individual mentions, and then iteratively merging the overlapping mentions to form new spans. However, these solutions are often computationally expensive, and may struggle to capture complex nested mention patterns. To address these limitations, we propose a novel transition-based method for nested mention recognition. The key idea is to model the nested structure of mentions as a forest, where each mention corresponds to a constituent of the forest. Our approach learns to construct the forest structure in a bottom-up manner through an action sequence, which can be viewed as a sequence of graph operations. Our transition-based system is inspired by the shift-reduce parser, which is widely used in dependency parsing and constituency parsing. In our context, the system maintains a queue of sentences with nested mentions, and iteratively dequeues each sentence to construct its forest structure. The system performs a sequence of operations, including SHIFT, REDUCE, and ADJUST, to manipulate the forest and generate the output. To efficiently and effectively represent the states of the system in a continuous space, we employ a Stack-LSTM architecture. The Stack-LSTM is a type of recurrent neural network (RNN) that can maintain a stack of hidden states, which enables it to represent the hierarchical structure of the forest. Our system further incorporates a character-based component to capture letter-level patterns in the mentions. This is achieved through an additional neural network that processes the character sequence of each mention. We evaluate our model on the ACE (Automatic Content Extraction) datasets, which provide a challenging benchmark for nested mention recognition. Our experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on these datasets, with significant improvements over the existing state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our transition-based method in detecting nested mentions, which can be used as a building block for various NLP applications, including information extraction, question answering, and text classification.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a central task in natural language processing, which aims at translating text from a source language to a target language. Recently, the performance of SMT models has improved significantly with the advent of novel feature extraction methods, large-scale training data, and sophisticated optimization techniques (Och, 2003; Koehn et al., 2007). Nonetheless, the key to the success of SMT models lies in the quality of the features used to represent source and target sentences. Traditional feature extraction approaches rely heavily on handcrafted features, such as language models and parse tree based features (Chen et al., 2010), which often limit the ability to generalize to unseen data. Recent advances have led to the development of semi-supervised and unsupervised feature learning approaches, which aim to learn task-specific features from small amounts of labeled data and large amounts of unlabeled data, respectively. The deep auto-encoder (DAE) paradigm is one of the promising approaches, which has achieved state-of-the-art performance in various machine learning and natural language processing tasks (Bengio, 2013). DAE learns to reconstruct the input data by compressing it into a lower-dimensional representation and then decompressing it back into the original data. This process is inherently capable of learning task-specific features from unlabeled data, as demonstrated by numerous studies (Vincent et al., 2010; Shahreza, 2012). Furthermore, by using the pre-trained deep belief net (DBN) to initialize DAE's parameters and the original input features as a teacher for semi-supervised fine-tuning, DAE can learn effective and stable features from both labeled and unlabeled data. However, current DAE feature learning methods often rely on a single hidden layer to represent the input data, which may limit the ability to capture the complex patterns and relationships between words (Radford et al., 2015). In an attempt to address this limitation, several researchers have explored the incorporation of multiple hidden layers or stacked auto-encoders (SAE) (Hinton et al., 2006). In SAE, each hidden layer serves as a bottleneck, which acts as a feature extractor. By stacking multiple SAEs together, it is possible to learn high-dimensional feature representations that capture the complex patterns and relationships between words. In this paper, we focus on the development of a novel semi-supervised DAE feature learning approach for phrase-based translation models. By using the pre-trained DBN to initialize DAE's parameters and the original input features as a teacher for semi-supervised fine-tuning, we learn new semi-supervised DAE features, which are more effective and stable than the unsupervised DBN features.

Generating high-quality and informative responses in a conversation is a challenging task in natural language processing. Although neural response generation has made significant progress in recent years, most existing approaches still suffer from several drawbacks. One major issue is that they often produce non-informative or "safe responses", which are uninteresting, unengaging, and do not contribute to the conversation in a meaningful way. This is mainly caused by the oversimplification of the response generation process, where the potential responses are limited to a small set of possible outputs. Another issue is the lack of diversity in the generated responses, which makes it hard to evaluate the performance of the response generator. To address these problems, researchers have proposed various techniques, such as incorporating external knowledge sources, using reinforcement learning, and designing more sophisticated language models. However, most of these methods tend to add complexity to the response generation process, making it harder to train the model and increasing the risk of producing low-quality responses. In this paper, we propose a novel Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture for neural response generation, which combines the strengths of sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) networks and discriminative classifiers to produce high-quality and informative responses. A key feature of our approach is the introduction of an approximate embedding layer, which is designed to handle the non-differentiable problem caused by the sampling-based output decoding procedure in the Seq2Seq generative model. This layer enables the model to learn a more accurate representation of the input context and produce responses that are more diverse and informative. Our proposed method is evaluated on two different corpora, a Mandarin corpus and an English corpus, and is compared to several existing neural response generation models. The experimental results show that our approach significantly outperforms these models in terms of diversity metrics, with slight increases in relevance scores, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed method in generating high-quality and informative responses in a conversation. The proposed architecture has a wide range of applications in various areas, from customer service and dialogue systems to language translation and text summarization, where generating high-quality responses is critical. Furthermore, our approach can be easily extended to other language processing tasks that require generating diverse and informative output, such as text summarization and language translation. In the following sections, we will introduce the proposed methodology, provide the experimental results, and discuss the implications and limitations of our approach.

Argumentation and persuasion have been essential skills in human communication throughout history. Effective argumentation relies heavily on the ability to express opinions or make assertions supported by strong evidence. In recent years, argumentative writing has become increasingly important in various fields such as academic writing, politics, law, and business. Given the complexity and subjectivity of argumentative writing, finding competent and relevant supporting evidence can be challenging. One valuable source of supporting evidence is anecdotal information, which often provides a vivid and compelling narrative that helps to solidify a writer’s point or argument. Anecdotes, in this context, refer to brief, revealing stories or accounts that are often narratives of an individual person. While anecdotal information is widely used in various domains, there is a pressing need to develop systematic methods for identifying and recommending relevant anecdotes to support an argument or writing task. There are a few reasons why anecdote recognition and recommendation are important and timely. Firstly, the Internet and digital libraries have created vast repositories of text data containing anecdotes. However, manually sifting through this vast amount of text data to find relevant anecdotes can be very time-consuming, making it difficult for writers to find the evidence they need. Secondly, the unstructured and variable nature of anecdotal information makes it challenging to identify and find relevant anecdotes using traditional search methodologies. This is often compounded by the fact that many anecdotal accounts are buried in lengthy documents or buried in highly specific domains. Even with the rise of information retrieval systems such as search engines, the majority of anecdotal information remains archived and unaccessible. In this context, the development of systems that can automatically identify, understand, and recommend relevant anecdotes can greatly alleviate this challenge. This is precisely the motivation behind our work on Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation. We define the task of Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation as a novel problem that involves identifying and extracting structured anecdotes from archived argumentative essays and recommending them to users based on their interests and topics of interest. Our method is centered on the structured representation of anecdotes, which we denote as -< person, story, implication >. Here, person refers to the individual who is the subject or author of the anecdote. story refers to the actual narrative or account that is provided to illustrate a point. Implication represents the meaning or the topic of the anecdote, which often reveals the argumentative relevance of the anecdotal information.

Sequence labeling is a prominent task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, among others. However, annotating large datasets with sequence labels is time-consuming and expensive, which motivates the development of semi-supervised methods that can leverage unlabelled data to improve model performance. Traditional semi-supervised learning approaches use unlabeled data to augment the training process for a fixed model architecture (Joachims, 1999) or to create pseudo-labels that can be used to augment or correct the labelled data (Chapelle et al., 2009). However, traditional sequence labeling models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) (Lafferty et al., 2001) and long short-term memory (LSTM) recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), are primarily discriminative in nature and do not naturally incorporate inductive biases that can be leveraged when working with unlabelled data. In this paper, we introduce a family of multitask variational methods, called Variational Sequential Labelers (VSL), for semi-supervised sequence labeling. Building on the recent advances in variational methods for learning word embeddings (e.g., Vinyals et al., 2015), our models can incorporate the inductive biases of generative models, which provide a more principled way to model sequence dependencies and define the conditional probability of a word given its context. In this way, our models draw inspiration from the objectives used in learning word embeddings, which are known to capture useful information in the latent space. Our labeler component injects discriminative information into the latent space, allowing the model to capture the relationships between word and label representations that are inherent in sequence labelling tasks. To further enrich the latent space and capture the complex patterns that arise in sequence labelling, we experiment with several latent variable configurations, including ones with hierarchical structure. The hierarchical latent space architecture naturally enables the model to account for both label-specific and word-specific information (Bengio et al., 2006). Our aim is to design a model that can leverage the power of both generative models and sequential architecture to learn from unlabelled data. The dominant architecture for sequence labeling models has shifted from CRFs to seq2seq (Sutskever et al., 2014) and BERT-based models (Devlin et al., 2019). Interpreting anaphoric shell nouns (ASNs) such as this issue and this fact is a notoriously difficult task in natural language processing. ASNs are crucial to understanding virtually any substantial natural language text, and yet, their interpretation remains a largely unsolved problem. One of the primary obstacles in developing methods for automatically interpreting ASNs is the lack of annotated data. This is because annotating ASN interpretations requires manual expert knowledge and review, which can be time-consuming and expensive. We posit that ASNs can provide valuable insights and meaning to a sentence, but identifying this meaning is often arduous due to the absence of explicit data that demonstrates the relationship between the shell noun and its antecedent. As an example, consider the statement "I was aware of this fact." While "this fact" functions as a type of shell noun, with the noun "fact" playing the role of the antecedent, the content of "this fact" is not directly indicated in the sentence. Therefore, automatic methods have difficulty in determining the specific content of "this fact." Therefore, developing an accurate and efficient method to interpret ASNs is essential. The primary conjecture that underlies our approach is that the antecedents of cataphoric shell nouns (CSNs) can provide a rich and diverse dataset that can be exploited to improve the performance of ASN interpretation methods. CSNs have a clear construction that is structured around the antecedent, such that, in the example sentence "the reason that the engineer was fired was this issue," "this issue" is the antecedent, but its content, such as 'unfairness in the company's procedure,' can be identified through the antecedent ("the reason"). This structured construction is a key property of CSNs and is distinct from ASNs, which form a closed category and do not have an explicit form related to an antecedent. Based on this characteristic, we argue that the antecedents of CSNs can be used as training data to enhance the performance of ASN interpretation. This paper focuses on addressing the challenge of ASN interpretation by capitalizing on the exploitation of CSN antecedents. We explore the use of labeled CSN antecedents as a means to develop an alternative approach to interpret ASNs. Our proposed method leverages this resource-rich and well-structured dataset to improve the accuracy and efficiency of ASN interpretation. Specifically, we evaluate the hypothesis that the collection of CSN antecedents can serve as a diverse and representative dataset that can be exploited to augment the desciption of ASNs.

Introduction Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) is a formalism that uses a logic-based syntax to generate tree structures, which makes it a powerful and expressive tool for modeling linguistic structure (Steedman, 2000). CCG has been successful in various NLP tasks, such as parsing, generation, and semantics (Clark and Curran, 2004; Clark et al., 2005; Bos, 2008). However, a major limitation of CCG is that it relies heavily on annotated resources, specifically treebanks, to train models. Creating and annotating large and wide-coverage treebanks for CCG is an expensive and time-consuming task, which hampers its applicability and adoption by the broader NLP community. In recent years, unsupervised parsing and grammar induction have emerged as promising alternatives to conventional supervised learning approaches, leveraging the abundance of plain texts available online and the advances in machine learning (Oepen, 2008; McDonald and Cram, 2012). Among various unsupervised parsing frameworks, Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) induction is a particular attractive option, as it leverages the strengths of CCG's expressiveness and logic-based syntax. Yet, despite these advances, current CCG induction methodologies still face several challenges. Firstly, most existing CCG induction approaches rely on surface-level linguistic features or statistical patterns, which may not capture the deeper, underlying semantic and syntactic structures of language. Secondly, the resulting induced grammars are often over-specified and lack generalizability across different domains, such as in terms of shared linguistic patterns and structures. Finally, the current lack of effective evaluation metrics and supervised modeling architectures limits the overall performance and interpretability of induced CCG models. In this paper, we address these limitations by proposing a novel unsupervised CCG induction approach, which consists of two main innovations. Firstly, we incorporate boundary part-of-speech (POS) tags into the model, recognizing that lexical information plays a crucial role in forming the structural relationships between words. By utilizing boundary POS tags, our model can effectively capture the unique properties of individual words and grammatical patterns within a sentence. Secondly, we implement a nonparametric Bayesian inference framework using the Pitman-Yor process, which enables the model to learn compact and generalized grammars. This Bayesian approach allows our model to capture the variability and uncertainty inherent in linguistic data, leading to more robust and accurate CCG induction. We conduct experiments on the English Penn treebank to evaluate the effectiveness of our innovations, demonstrating that incorporating boundary POS tags and using Bayesian learning significantly improves the grammatical structure and semantics of the induced CCG models.

Sentiment analysis has been a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with numerous applications in product review analysis, opinion mining, and sentiment classification. However, the task becomes increasingly challenging when faced with dynamic sentiment ambiguous adjectives (DSAAs) - a set of adjectives whose meaning and sentiment orientation change dynamically depending on the context. Examples of DSAAs include "large," "small," "high," and "low," which can both be positive or negative depending on the situation (e.g., "large" is typically positive when describing a house, but negative when describing a financial loss). Given the complexities involved, traditional sentiment analysis methods, which often rely on pre-trained models or hand-crafted rules, may struggle to accurately capture the nuances of DSAAs. A more promising approach is to revisit the problem from a knowledge-based perspective. Rather than relying on general-purpose sentiment lexicons or machine learning models, our approach focuses on the co-occurrence of adjectives with target nouns to infer their sentiment expectation. We propose to frame this as a sentiment classification task, where the goal is to predict the sentiment of target nouns rather than the adjectives themselves. This shift in focus allows us to leverage the power of linguistic patterns and word senses, avoiding the noisy and often ambiguous semantics associated with certain sentiment lexicons. Our approach is grounded in the insights from linguistic theory, which suggests that the meaning of words is composed of multiple components, such as their lexical, grammatical, and pragmatic aspects. By analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of adjectives and target nouns, we can infer the sentiment expectation associated with these nouns. To this end, we design a framework that leverages the following key components: First, we employ a lexico-syntactic pattern mining technique to extract sentiment expectation features from a large corpus of text. This involves identifying relevant patterns and associations between adjectives, target nouns, and sentiment-bearing words. By analyzing these patterns, we can infer the sentiment expectations associated with target nouns, which serve as crucial features for our sentiment classification task. Second, we develop a character-sentiment model to reduce noise and ambiguity contributed by web data. This model is designed to differentiate between sentiment-oriented and non-sentimentoriented character features, allowing us to filter out irrelevant information and focus on sentiment-relevant characteristics. Third, we propose a multi-stage framework for integrating knowledge-based features with deep learning-based models. This allows us to leverage the strengths of both approaches and produce state-of-the-art results.

Event detection is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in summarization, question answering, and information extraction (IE). In most applications, the term 'event' refers to a specific occurrence or action that has impact on some aspects of the world. For instance, news events, such as "Apple acquires Beats Electronics group for $3 billion", can be regarded as related to corporate finance or electronic product releases. Events can be described using a variety of linguistic structures, ranging from short phrases such as "Bill Gates retires" to lengthy articles describing entire incidents. Word-wise classification models based on neural networks (Yang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2016), have become the dominant approach to event detection. In this approach, event detection is framed as the classification problem of identifying event types given individual word tokens in the input text, without attempting to identify the underlying semantic structures and entities in the event description. However, it is well-known that words may not directly match event triggers, and this word-trigger mismatch problem (Wang et al., 2012) is especially severe in languages without word delimiters, such as Chinese. To address this challenge, several studies have proposed solutions by incorporating word-centric information or incorporating multiple subtasks in the pipeline (Revow et al., 2000). However, these approaches overlook the intricate syntax and compositionality of Chinese language, where event triggers can comprise entire words, and sometimes even comprise multiple adjacent words. Given that event triggers in Chinese exhibit such rich and complex compositional structures, merely relying on word-centric representations may fall short in terms of precision. For instance, the event description "Bill Gates resigns" is characterized by the quit action he performs, rather than the individual words "Bill", "Gates" or "resigne". In contrast, we propose Nugget Proposal Networks (NPNs) for Chinese event detection, capable of addressing the word-trigger mismatch problem by directly proposing entire trigger nuggets centered at each character, regardless of the word boundaries. NPNs can more effectively model complex event triggers in Chinese language and provide more accurate events. In our work, each character is first learned to capture both structural and semantic information from both the character alone and the word where the character appears. Then, the hybrid representation of the character is used to propose and categorize trigger nuggets, that are modeled as being composed of the distribution of characters in the input sequence. Specifically, NPNs adopt a two-step paradigm, through which, events can be accurately detected in a character-wise fashion.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), involving identifying the mentions of the same entity within a text (Hirschman and Liu, 2000). Throughout the years, various approaches have been proposed to tackle this complex problem, with pairwise models representing the predominant paradigm (Bansal et al., 2014;Lee et al., 2017). However, these methods have drawn significant criticism (Lee et al., 2017) due to their inability to scale to large datasets and their limited representational power. The primary issue resides in the pairwise architecture, which relies heavily on independently computing the compatibility of each pair of mentions. Consequently, as the number of mentions increases, so does the computational complexity, making the approach infeasible for large-scale applications. Furthermore, pairwise models operate on flat spaces with predefined features, thus failing to capture the inherent hierarchical nature of entities, where multiple entities can often be co-referent in a nested relationship (Pradhan et al., 2014). To overcome these limitations and satisfy the growing demand for scalable and highly expressive coreference resolution models, we propose a discriminative hierarchical model, dubbed HierarchicalCoref, that addresses these concerns by incorporating a latent hierarchical structure into the coreference modeling process. Within this frame- work, we introduce a novel approach to recursively partition entities into trees of latent sub-entities. This hierarchical representation provides a concise yet potent summary of the relevant mentions, markedly enhancing the ability to reason about entity interdependence and coreference uncertainty at massive scales. We demonstrate that HierarchicalCoref offers a substantial improvement in terms of scalability, significantly outperforming pairwise models by several orders of magnitude. This ability to efficiently process large numbers of mentions makes our proposed framework ripe for practical deployment in scenarios such as author coreference, where identifying entities across massive text corpora is a pressing concern. Specifically, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on the 6M-author dataset (Min et al., 2018), computing coreference in under 4 hours on a single CPU, whereas pairwise approaches inevitably suffer from computationally intractable times. Our results clearly demonstrate the applicability and promise of Hierarchical Coref in large-scale coreference resolution tasks, warranting its exploration in more complex and challenging domains. By targeting both the representational and the computational efficiency of coreference models, we open the path for further improvements in the field of NLP, particularly in resolving complex relationships between entities at diverse scales. In this paper, we elucidate the designt of HierarchicalCoref, introducing a hierarchical model for scalable coreference resolution, elucidating its pertinent features, empirical analysis, and comprehensive evaluation results.

Information Extraction (IE) systems have been widely used to extract structured information from unstructured data, making it possible to automatically recover information from text sources in a wide variety of natural language processing applications. Among these applications, event extraction plays a crucial role in automatically identifying and annotating entities and their roles in the events that they participate in [Sheard et al.,2010;Liu et al.,2010]. One key aspect of extracting reliable information in IE systems is deciding whether a particular phrase or clause is an instance of a particular role or not. The success of this decision is highly dependent on understanding the context surrounding the phrase. This context generally includes both the local setting around the phrase (phrasal context) and the wider setting that encompasses the entire sentence in which the phrase resides (sentential context). Traditional IE systems tend to rely heavily on the local context when making extraction decisions [Finkel et al., 2005;Ritter and Voyager 2011]. In such approaches, the occurrence of a phrase directly adjacent to an event word is a strong indicator that it should be extracted as an instance of a specific role. However, the occurrence of some role fillers may not follow directly from an event word but is instead connected via other information in the sentence. Hence, these traditional approaches may have some limitations in capturing these events in sentences as they may overlook relationships that are important indicators of event extraction. Recognizing this challenge, there is a need for Information Extraction systems that extract role fillers that jointly consider both the local context around a phrase along with the wider sentential context in a probabilistic framework. In this line of research, several researchers have been exploring different approaches to improving IE systems by considering the interplay between the phrasal and sentential contexts. Their work has laid the foundation for moving towards more advanced models that can make better extraction decisions based on the broader context in the available data. Nonetheless, these efforts have so far focused mostly on hand-crafting specific linguistic features to capture the interaction between phrasal and sentential contexts. Another key research thrust has been concentrating on building more sophisticated models that use the qualities of natural language data more effectively. These research developments have highlighted the utility of joint consideration of the phrasal and sentential context of a phrase in extraction processes but more work is required to formalise this process within a probabilistic framework and demonstrate the additional value it brings in the extraction of reliable information.

Abstracts and title statements give a concise indication of the main focus and accomplishment of a paper. In this case, the problem of automatically generating a text from an input Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR) graph is addressed. Given a set of edges representing concepts and their semantic relationships, an AMR graph directly encodes the meaning of a sentence in a form that is closer to the conceptual rather than the propositional representation traditionally found in formal language syntax (Banarescu et al., 2013). Abstracts and summaries of a set of documents convey the main points and key information of the source texts in a compact and readable form (Hovy et al., 1999;Radev et al., 2002). Traditional summarization methods, however, often concentrate on selecting the most salient sentences or keywords from the source texts without group-ing sentences that share strong semantic relationships, making the generated summaries less coherent (Arndt et al., 2005). A coherent summary is one that covers the various aspects and views of a topic presented in the source texts, connecting these views and making the text more readable and understandable (Goldstein, 1997). Consequently, there is an increasing need for new methods that address both coherence and informativeness, which are crucial for effective multi-document summarization. Recently, research has started to focus on visualization methods to aid human writers to generate summaries (Hearst, 2003;Koehler et al., 2004). Another area of exploration is the utilization of more structured layout-based presentations (Varma et al., 2007). Though, these mainstream methods do not perform automatic text summarization, and may lack relevant features for evaluating summaries other than readibility. Meanwhile, there is a growing interest in combining machine learning and certain features intrinsic to natural language, like surface syntax (Titov and Smeman, 2009) or intra-sentence recipients of implicit focus expressions (Ide and Fang, 1999), to the summarization task. However these experiments lack the although successful application to real applications and texts. To bridge this gap, in this paper we develop and explore a novel approach: a graph-based method that uses links between text to generate coherent summaries, and effectively addresses the above-mentioned problems. The key idea here is to form a graph with the source texts and extract a sequence of the most informative sentences that best represent the key information in a coherent way. This approach contrasts with previous methods that simply focus on salience (Titley and Lapata, 2007), and shows more relevance for assessing the importance of sentence selection and coherency within the generated summaries. We perform experiments on the DUC2004 summarization task dataset (Lvosky et al., 2003), a well-established benchmark for multi-document summarization evaluation (Ferro et al., 2004), and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing the generated summaries with those of existing methods using standard metrics based on word overlap. Our results show that the proposed approach achieves top performance in the quality assessments by human judges, while achieving comparative performance in terms of the ROUGE metrics (Lin, 2004).

Despite the impressive advancements of Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) in recent years, current systems are still limited by their reliance on large amounts of parallel training data. This poses a significant challenge for languages with limited resources, where high-quality parallel data is scarce or non-existent. One of the primary obstacles to building effective SMT systems for these languages is the difficulty in translating unknown or out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words. These words often constitute a substantial portion of the source language's vocabulary and, if left untranslated, can seriously degrade the overall translation quality. The current dominance of SMT systems is largely due to the availability of data-rich resources in many well-resourced languages. However, the majority of languages globally lack such resources, which severely restricts the potential of SMT for language pairs not well-covered by parallel data. To alleviate this problem, linguists and machine translation researchers have proposed the use of pivot languages, which can serve as intermediaries for generating paraphrases for low-density languages (Ziemski et al., 2016). The basic idea is to pivot through a well-resourced pivot language to obtain translation equivalents for unseen words in a target language. Although highly effective, this pivot-based strategy has a major drawback: it requires additional parallel texts in multiple language pairs. These extra resources add significantly to the already substantial engineering effort required to develop SMT systems. Furthermore, generating paraphrases by pivoting requires the recipients of two translation components to be in pair with the pivot language, this will degrade the effect of this solutions by adding the although needed resources by the great dimension they need to be dealt with. Moreover, pivoting may also introduce errors from the pivot language, a byproduct of processing through a potentially noisy intermediate language source. Given these constraints, there is a compelling need for alternative strategies that can leverage monolingual resources to augment SMT training data without the need for the recipient of two translation components to be in a pair with the pivot language. Research in distributional semantics and machine learning has shown great promise in leveraging monolingual data for tasks such as word sense induction and semantic text search. This has sparked interest in the potential application of these methods to the field of SMT, with a focus on leveraging monolingually-derived paraphrases to augment the available training data. Recent work in this direction has demonstrated the feasibility of using collocational information based on monolingual corpora to enable the translation of OOV words in SMT systems (Mitkov et al., 2002).

Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in text analysis, information extraction, and machine translation. Despite significant advances in recent years, parsing is still a challenging problem, especially for long-range dependencies, complex syntactic structures, and languages with very different grammatical characteristics. Dependency parsers are typically trained on large annotated corpora and suffer from the related problems of data sparsity and annotation noise. To tackle these issues, a range of strategies have been proposed, including leveraging secondary annotation sources, using perplexity-based evaluation criteria, and incorporating hierarchical models and probabilistic dependency parsing frameworks. While these methods have shown significant improvements in parser accuracy, there is still a need for a deeper understanding of the challenges that underlie the training of efficient and robust parsers. Traditional evaluation metrics, such as precision, recall, and F-score, have been used to benchmark the performance of dependency parsers, and are effective for measuring parser accuracy. However, these metrics are limited in that they do not capture the full gamut of challenges that a parser may encounter during training, such as difficulties in annotating long-range dependencies or the performace metric measured by distance between head and relevant child. This has led to the development of theoretically-flawed method such as a transition-based parser, which has some negative effect. A second approach is to predict the full parse tree in one step. These methods are efficient but difficult to train, particularly with small training sets. Recent work has proposed hybrids of these approaches, such as those that learn the parse tree in stages. While these method have improved the accuracy and robustness of parsers, they also introduce several new challenges: the choice of the optimal parsing strategy, the modeling of complex syntactic structures, and the balancing of parser precision and recall. Moreover, parsing accuracy is only one of the criteria we wish to optimize. This work aims to provide new insights into these challenges, and to develop novel metrics and methods for training more proficient parsers. To do so, we analyze the strengths and weaknesses of a variety of parsing algorithms and discuss their applications in cross-lingual parsing and dependency prediction. We believe that a careful consideration of the strengths and limitations of different parsers is essential for making progress in the field of parsing and machine learning of natural language. Our hope is that the course of this research will bring about better evaluations of various parsing algorithms and that these better evaluations will enable the development of more understandable, interpretable, and generally excellently high-qualityparsers for actual productive use.

Most known stochastic sentence generators use syntactically annotated corpora and perform the projection to the surface in one stage. However, in full-fledged text generation, sentence realization usually starts from semantic (predicate-argument) structures. To be able to deal with semantic structures, stochastic generators require semantically annotated, or, even better, multilevel annotated corpora. The demand for multilevel annotation arises from the fact that sentence generation is a complex task that involves crucial generation issues such as sentence planning, linearization, and morphologization. Traditional sentence generators, which are based on one-stage realization, often rely on an explicit cascade of parse tree transformations and fail to capture the complex interplay between the different levels of linguistic representation. The availability of multilevel annotated corpora has opened up new possibilities for multilingual sentence generation. These kinds of corpora provide detailed annotations not only for the syntactic structure but also for the semantic structure of the sentence, including predicate-argument structure, causal relations, and temporal dependencies. Recent advances in multilevel annotation have made these resources available for multiple languages, and we can now take advantage of them in stochastic sentence generators. In this paper, we propose a multilingual deep stochastic sentence realizer that mirrors the state-of-the-art research in semantic parsing. Our realizer is designed to handle multilevel annotated corpora and to deal with the complex generation issues that arise in this context. At the core of our approach is a sequence of decoders, each responsible for converting a pair of adjacent levels of annotation into a surface string. This modular architecture allows us to learn separate models for different levels of analysis and to combine them into a single generative model. We train our model using a Support Vector Machine (SVM) learning algorithm and evaluate its performance on four languages, namely Chinese, English, German, and Spanish. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and its ability to handle the complexities of multilingual deep sentence generation. To date, our research has been fruitful, and we can generate thousands of sentences in four languages. Our future research will focus on integrating this system with a module for semantic role labeling to improve the coherence and plausibility of the generated sentences. In the following, we will first describe the details of our approach and then present our experimental results.

Human engagement in narrative is a fundamental aspect of storytelling across various forms of media, including film. The ability to understand the relationships between narrative events is crucial to constructing coherent and engaging stories that resonate with audiences (Stein & Glenn, 1979). One critical aspect of this engagement is the reasoning about the contingency of events, i.e., the influence one event has on another and the expectations that arise from such contingency (Wilson & Sperber, 2004). For instance, upon seeing a character walk away from a cliff, a viewer may anticipate a fall because of the expected contingency between the action and the physical environment. Researchers in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have notably addressed the task of modeling such contingency from multiple angles. Some scholars have tackled it as the inference of the CONTINGENT discourse relation, an essential aspect of narrative understanding (Asher & Lascarides, 2003). Others have framed it as a type of common-sense causal reasoning, critical for human inference about narrative events (Mitchell et al., 2013). Against this backdrop, our research delves into modeling likelihood between events to predict contingent event pairs in the context of film narrative understanding. Our work draws on the findings of previous researchers in this area, including the importance of discourse relations in narrative understanding and the crucial role played by common sense in inferring causal relationships between events (Chambers & Jurafsky, 2009). In developing our unsupervised approach to learning contingent event pairs, we differ from previous works in several key aspects. Our primary focus lies in the exploitation of large-scale, readily accessible data sources – in this case, a corpus of film scene descriptions supplemented by web search counts – rather than relying on labeled datasets typically employed by supervised methods (Ji et al., 2017). Specifically, we refine our event pairs through an iterative procedure that leverages these counts to adjust the relative likelihood of event pairs. Our approach has several critical implications for the study of human engagement with narrative. By leveraging web search data, we can augment the efficacy of unsupervised approaches to learning contingent event pairs. This addresses a long-standing challenge in narrative understanding research, namely, the difficulty of assembling large-scale datasets annotated with discourse relations and contingencies. In evaluating our methods, we solicit human judgments of contingency through a controlled user-study, where we compare the performance of our best unsupervised method against a baseline calibrated to achieve 50% accuracy. Our results show that incorporating web search counts significantly improves performance, with an average accuracy of 85.64% achieved by our refined event pair learning method.

The evaluation of machine translation (MT) is a central task in natural language processing. The Measure of Translator Effectiveness Oriented for Recognition (METEOR) (Banerjee and Lavie, 2005) is a state-of-the-art score combining exact and inexact evaluation of translations. METEOR emphasizes the matching between an automatic translation (MT output) and a reference translation by utilizing the F-score, which is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. A match is defined as a word pair that meets a certain criteria, either by being identical, or by being related to each other through lexicosediment and/or morphological processes, such as synonyms or hyponyms. METEOR utilizes WordNet (Miller, 1995) as its primary lexico-semantic resource to identify these relationships. One potential limitation of METEOR is the restrictive assumption that the lexicosediment information is complete and up to date. This assumption is especially problematic for evaluating out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, whose translation in hypothetical word pairs is unknown. Moreover, lexicosing is more relevant to translation tasks involving languages with more complex semantics, but may not be directly relevant for languages with more variable words, such as Japanese and Chinese. With the emergence of distributed word representations, certain methodologies have become possible, including learning differentiable representations for the purpose of capturing semantic relationships. There are many prominent examples of distributed word representations, such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). Word2Vec maps the space of words to a high dimensional space where the proximity between the words is understood as their semantic similarity. By utilizing this technique, a new way to represent word pairs has been introduced offering the possibility of capturing a broader semantic and practical relationship unseen by lexicosediment resources, both morphological and semantically. Distributed representations promise the ability to deal well even with words out of vocabulary and it may be fitted into evaluation metrics more proficiently. To examine whether distributed representations provide a suitable supplement or substitute for lexicosing resources within evaluation runs for assessing the MT quality, several extensions to METEOR will be tested. One includes adding the word pair matching based on their similarity reported by word embeddings. This alternative matching mechanism can evaluate how similar a translation is in the view of a distribution-based meaning representation. Our implementation examines how alternative matching mechanisms aid in the additional capture and detection of the distribution-based semantic relationships in MT evaluations. The growing demand for natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as text classification, sentiment analysis, and information extraction, has sparked interest in utilizing human-based approaches to tackle challenging problems. One such human-based approach is crowdsourcing, which leverages a large and diverse pool of individuals to collect and annotate data. In particular, microtasking platforms, such as Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), provide a convenient and cost-effective way to collect annotations from "Turkers" (workers on AMT). However, the quality and accuracy of crowdsourced data can be compromised by various factors, including worker biases and variability in annotation behavior. This raises the question of whether crowdsourcing is a suitable approach for certain NLP tasks, such as query segmentation, which requires precise and consistent annotations. Query segmentation, also known as query chunking, is a fundamental step towards query understanding and satisfaction, enabling search systems to identify relevant information and provide accurate search results. Given the significance of query segmentation, it is crucial to explore its effectiveness in a crowdsourcing setting and examine potential biases that may affect the quality of annotations. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of query segmentation crowdsourcing, using carefully designed control experiments and novel inter annotator agreement (IAA) metrics to analyze experimental data. Through our research, we demonstrate that certain biases intrinsic to human annotators compromise the quality of crowdsourced query segmentation, rendering crowdsourcing an unsuitable approach for this task. Our study focuses on hierarchical and segmented annotation, examining whether the crowd tends to divide the query into balanced or nested segments. Our investigation reveals that, in fact, the crowd exhibits a strong preference towards dividing the query into roughly equal parts, with a bias towards binary segmentations when possible. We argue that these biases arise from a combination of factors, including cognitive tendencies, such as the need for symmetry and mental categorization, and platform-specific constraints, like rewards and the fear of decreased earnings. Moreover, our results indicate that this bias is particularly evident when relatively long query strings are segmented, suggesting that task complexity adds to the unwanted outcome. Considering the implications of these findings, we contribute to the ongoing discussion surrounding the effectiveness of crowdsourcing for various NLP tasks, highlighting the importance of acknowledging and addressing biases that may distort the quality of crowdsourced data. Our research has practical implications for search systems and platforms that utilize crowdsourced data, highlighting areas where alternative approaches, such as utilizing subject-matter experts or crowd validation mechanisms, may be more suitable.
