Image captioning, a sub-task of visual content analysis, has become increasingly important in recent years due to advances in deep learning architectures and accompanying availability of large-scale image and text datasets. Its main goal is to generate a natural language description describing the visual content of an image. The field of image captioning is multidisciplinary and has attracted researchers from computer vision and natural language processing communities, who are seeking more accurate and human-like image descriptions. Traditional methods have primarily focused on either intermediate-level representations or image features that lack detailed and comprehensive descriptions. Recent studies have adopted the encode-decoder framework due to its promising performance, enabling detailed data-driven representations of visual content. Most state-of-the-art approaches to image captioning rely on generating caption through a sequential way and incorporate attention mechanisms to capture more visual content and context information. However, existing methods often focus on either visual attention (rasterizing the image into a set of regional feature vectors in the decoder and adopting an attention mechanism for pulling out relevant features) or semantic attention (discerning the layout of objects in the scene from a set of region proposal networks in the encoder, followed by an attention mechanism in the decoder that samples image regions relevant to the description). While these two lines of work have achieved promising performances in their respective aspects, there is still a lack of models that are able to combine these two types of attentions at each time step. Current methods usually employ a pre-specified ratio or only one type of attention to merge image and topic information, which may lead to an imbalance between visual and semantic information and hence results in a miss of the detailed and comprehensive descriptions. In fact, in human language, high-level topic information and low-level image details are often tightly interwoven, and understanding these inter-relationships and how to best leverage them can greatly improve captioning performance. We attempt to close this gap by exploring the ability of the network to adaptively learning to combine these two kinds of attention at each time step. Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), serving as a fundamental component for numerous downstream applications, such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text summarization. Assessing the semantic similarity between two texts has been an active research area, with hundreds of STS systems developed to date. While designers of NLP systems aim to leverage existing STS systems, the crucial question of which system is best suited for a particular task remains unresolved. To address this challenge, intrinsic evaluation is typically conducted by comparing the STS system's output against human judgments on semantic similarity. The use of Pearson correlation as the primary metric for intrinsic evaluation has become widespread, allowing designers to estimate how well a particular STS system aligns with human judgments. However, this study underscores a critical problem: relying on intrinsic evaluations using Pearson correlation can be misleading, especially when conducting evaluations in downstream tasks that rely on STS. This result highlights the importance of evaluating the STS systems more thoroughly, rather than solely relying on a hypothetical "coverage" in terms of the Pearson correlation between human and system judgments, to select the best performaning metric. Through three examples of relevant downstream tasks, this work demonstrates that various evaluation measures other than Pearson correlation, which have been less frequently used in the intrinsic evaluation setting, can elucidate inconsistencies in the quality of the STS systems. These examples critique the restrictions of employing Pearson correlation as the only metric and show that relying solely on its value may lead to selecting an inadequate STS system for the task at hand. Moreover, they emphasize the necessity for an awareness of the task's requirements and applicability. Therefore, it is essential to outline how to assess the validity of an intrinsic evaluation. Understanding the task's properties and selecting the adequate intrinsic metrics for evaluation form the core of our proposed framework. This framework is particularly designed to address the pitfalls of using Pearson correlation as the sole metric for intrinsic evaluation. In an attempt to address these limitations and arrive at a more accurate selection of the STS best performing metric, we discuss key task-specific characteristics that can influence the choice of metrics to be used in intrinsic evaluation. As a result, we offer a framework for conducting intrinsic evaluation that incorporates the properties of the task at hand to offer a more comprehensive assessment of the quality of the STS system.

The growing scale of available text corpora presents abundant opportunities for the discovery of meaningful patterns and relationships in language. A key challenge in text analysis is the need to model and represent the inherent complexity of human language, where a single word, phrase, or passage may convey meaning in multiple ways. Latent Variable Models (LVMs) of Text, a family of probabilistic models that involve unobserved or latent variables (Arora et al., 2012;Ghahramani, 2015;Welling et al., 2005;Ytreberg et al., 2018), provide a particularly appealing solution to this challenge. These models are able to effectively capture intricate patterns of language, model long-range dependencies, and describe the hierarchy of relationships between words within documents (Blei et al., 2003;Karaman et al., 2018;Manning, 2001). However, the benefits of adopting LVMs for text analysis come at a computational cost, which has grown more pronounced in recent years due to the increasing size of text corpora and desire to train more powerful models (Li et al., 2016). To address this challenge, parallel algorithms and distributed training methodologies have been used to fit LVMs of text to large corpora. Examples of such parallel algorithms comprise: stochastic variational inference, stochastic gradient descent, and dual variational inference (Bornschein et al., 2015;Honkela et al., 2013;Tran et al., 2017). However, a major limitation remains when using parallel training: even distributed architectures require significant memory to hold the parameters of the model. This phenomenon is commonly referred to as the memory bottleneck (Maclaurin and Duvenaud, 2015). Despite employing technologies like tape memory and microgrids, random-access memory (RAM) fills most of available storage on computational clusters. In particular, the large size of the vocabulary histogram often becomes a bottleneck: it must be stored on every node in the cluster during parallel training runs. Furthermore, any particular node also stores positional indices of unique words. Historically, the vocabulary histogram has been stored on disk or on a portion of available main memory. However, large corpora far outstrip available storage even this allocation. Although specialized hardware is being introduced for LVM training (Maxvold and Cordy, 2021), additions will not be able to keep pace with corpora size increase through investment in existing approaches to cluster construction; cluster only rapidly keep pace through investment large upgrades. The rest of this text addresses solving the limitation of prior parallel LVM training by upscaling alternative to using a pre-existing flat partitioning scheme as the default partitioning structure.

Information status is a critical aspect of discourse processing, as it determines how the hearer perceives and interprets information during a conversation (Halliday, 1970;Clark, 1992). The ability to accurately classify information status is essential for completing a range of pragmatic tasks, such as answering questions and resolving ambiguities (Poesio et al., 2004). According to the hearer's common sense knowledge and comprehension of the surrounding context, a discourse entity can be classified as old, previously mentioned in the conversation, mediated or new, not previously mentioned (Clark, 1992;Duverosedeschipf, 1996). Existing approaches to information status classification rely heavily on manual annotation and feature engineering, which is time-consuming and often domain-dependent (Markert et al., 2012). Recently, deep learning models have shown great potential in information status classification tasks, demonstrating the ability to automatically capture semantic knowledge from the input text (Socher et al., 2011;Hou et al., 2013;Lu et al., 2013). However, these models often require large amounts of annotations and perform classification in a batch manner, which hinders real-time applicability and heavy linguistic processing. Furthermore, current approaches neglect the sequential relationships within the input text and the intrinsic links between different parts of speech, making them less effective at capturing contextual relationships. There is therefore a need for incremental information status classification methods that can dynamically update their predictions based on the incoming text and capture the complex interactions between entities and their contexts. This paper presents an attention-based long short-term memory (LSTM) model that employs an incremental approach to fine-grained information status classification, examining how well the model can learn semantic knowledge and adapt to the task by considering solely word embedding features and limited hand-crafted features. In contrast to previous studies, our incremental model-SOTA- processes text sequentially and dynamically predicts the information status of each discourse entity based on its preceding context. By maintaining the critical contextual relationships, the incorporation of the attention mechanism yields improved performance and adaptability to the task. The proposed model is also evaluated on the publicly available ISNotes corpus (Markert et al., 2012), which contains a substantial set of annotated discourse entities and their corresponding information status labels. The latter part of this paper discusses the experimental results and their implications, demonstrating the competitiveness of our proposed model compared to the state-of-the-art approach( Hou et al., 2013) based on diverse performance metrics, including accuracy and micro-F1 score.

Cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) has witnessed tremendous progress in recent years, making it possible to achieve state-of-the-art results in various applications, such as machine translation, question answering, and text classification, across different languages. A crucial component in cross-lingual NLP is the ability to capture and represent language-independent meaning structures, which can be used to facilitate tasks that require the understanding of similar concepts and relationships between them across different languages. In order to enable this, one must induce and capture equivalence between relations across different languages. The term "semantic relations" is used to describe the relationships between referring expressions that carry meaning, such as "woman-astronaut-raymond-chiarelli" and "féminine- astronaute-raymond-chiarelli", where the jets are similar, but framed in different linguistic structures. These relations enable the representation of the underlying meaning that is shared across languages. A key challenge in inducing these cross-lingual semantic relations is that typically, parallel text is unavailable to supervise this process during training in most cross-lingual NLP tasks (Do et al., 2009). In some cases, training examples are sometimes imperfectly translated, especially for languages pairs with limited linguistic resources (Duh & Kirchhoff, 2008). This setting often relies on different NLP approaches, including machine translation and parallel text-based methods. However, the latter is expensive to obtain, which makes them unsuitable for many languages. Our main goal in this paper is to develop the first unsupervised induction method for cross-lingual semantic relations. Our idea builds upon recent advancements in monolingual semantic relation extraction by analyzing pairs of referring expressions from large corpora (Ganitkevitch and Manning, 2016). Specifically, in this paper, we extend these ideas to pairs of expressions in English and French that share named-entity arguments. To be more specific, we aim to find pairs of expressions that share the same named entity, but in different languages. To this end, we develop a novel framework that combines monolingual semantic relation extraction (Finin et al., 2010) and word embeddings (Pennington et al.,2014) to learn clusters of semantically equivalent relations between referring expressions in the two languages. Our approach is data-driven and does not rely on parallel text or word-aligned data. It captures relationships that go beyond simply finding lexical translations, enabling a language-independent meaning representation that can be used across multiple languages in a host of cross-lingual tasks, such as question answering and machine translation.

The domain of computer vision has been a driving force behind the advancement of artificial intelligence. Within this domain, several challenges have been proposed to push the boundaries of what can be accomplished with visual data. Among these challenges, question-answering (QA) has emerged as a particularly appealing task. QA involves providing a brief natural language response to a group of words -in other words, a question related to a visual input. Image-based QA has been extensively explored in the past decade. A plethora of image-based QA datasets has been produced, spanning from simple tasks such as recognizing objects within images to more complex ones that require the use of multiple images in narratives such as image description tasks where a user is showing a series of images and is asking a number of questions about each individual one. However, due to the inherently sequential nature of videos, this standard QA framework is not sufficient by itself to capture the nuances of a video-based QA task. A key element of videos that is missing in the simpler image QA tasks is temporality -a temporal continuum in which concepts are brought in contact and represented, offering the possibility for manipulation, interpretation and prediction. Inspired by the ease of use of image-based QA datasets and the observation of a heavy increase in online video consumption, we shift our focus from image to video QA and present in this paper, TVQA: a largescale dataset devised to push the boundaries of video QA. TVQA captures the viewing experience of a popular TV show with the prerequisite to localize relevant moments within a clip, comprehend these moments through recognizing although often extremely briefly presented concepts and through the often cryptic and formal script-based guidance via subtitles and to recognize the high-level but also fine-grained relevant concepts. The modeling architectures that have been proposed so far in the field of computer vision suggest that the multi-stream front-end used in conjunction with a multi-task back-end is particularly appropriate to address the requirements of video QA. Video Quality Assessment(VQA) has received extensive research but apart from histogram-based and machine learning VQA models, to the best of our knowledge it has so far been impossible to apply any multi-stream and multi-task deep learning architecture that we expect to perform adequately well as its alternative, for free.

Word Representations: A Simple and General Method for Semi-Supervised Learning supervised natural language processing (NLP) systems have achieved state-of-the-art performance in many tasks, such as named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech tagging (POS). However, these systems require extensive annotated training data, making it challenging to develop and maintain them for resource-poor languages or new domains. One way to alleviate this problem is to incorporate unsupervised learning approaches into the system, which can help to improve the robustness and accuracy of the model. In this paper, we propose a simple and general method for incorporating unsupervised word representations into an existing supervised NLP system as extra word features. Bydoing so, we can take advantage of the supervision available from labeled examples while still benefiting from the additional information provided by the unsupervised word representations. Our method is motivated by the observation that unsupervised word representations can capture subtle semantic and syntactic relationships between words that are not explicitly represented in a supervised system. For instance, a word's representation in a vector space model may be closely related to the representation of another word if they often appear in similar contexts, even if they have no surfacelevel similarity. By incorporating these word representations as additional features in a supervised system, we can potentially improve the model's ability to capture fine-grained differences between words. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we experiment with three different unsupervised word representation methods: Brown clusters (Brown et al., 1992), Collobert and Weston (2008) embeddings, and HLBL (Mnih and Hinton, 2009) embeddings. We use these word representations as extra features in combination with supervised baselines that achieve near-state-of-the-art performance on the NER and chunking tasks. Our results show that incorporating word representations from these three methods improves the accuracy of the baselines, often significantly. Moreover, we find that combining different word representations can lead to further improvements, indicating that our approach can be flexibly applied to a variety of NLP tasks and supervised systems. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section , we review related work on word representation and semi-supervised learning in NLP. In Section we describe the three word representation methods used in our experiments. In Section , we outline the experimental setup and the NLP systems used as baselines. Our results are presented in Section and discussed in Section

The analysis and understanding of human language are inherently tied to the phenomenon of metaphor. A metaphor is a figure of speech that describes an object, concept, or action in a way that isn't literally true but rather conveys a deeper meaning or comparison. The identification of metaphors is an essential task in the realms of natural language processing (NLP), linguistics, and cognitive science. Prior approaches to automatic metaphor identification have typically relied on manual annotation of texts, post-processing annotations of intermediate products (e.g. dependency parse trees) by hand or application programming interfaces that provide knowledge bases of metaphorical expressions. However, manually annotating data is an approach that suffers from prohibitive costs of manual work, insufficient annotations for new datasets, and potentially biased annotations. The prominence of metaphor in natural language and its importance for recognizing insights, intentions, and ambiguities that come with language make developing approaches to automatically identify metaphors using computer- and data-driven methods necessary and impactful. Thus it is critical to pursue unsupervised methods, which require no more than a hypothetical seed set for inferences about the nature of the metaphors in a dataset to improve performance and perform automatic conjecture that is highly suggestive of relevant language phenomena. In particular, we address this identification task based on the intuition that a metaphorical meaning differs from the literal meaning mainly through the choice of verbs and nouns used in their expression. Concretely, metaphors preserve the recipients' literal understanding of only the thing names, such as nouns, while the relations between the recipients' understanding of thing names, such as the actions and events they are involved in, such as verbs, change in ways significantly more than those involved in literal meanings. However, these relation dynamics cannot be inferred from a single noun or a single verb by itself. They can only be analyzed through a form of clustering, given that these verbs and nouns form a space of densely tangled relationships, such as meaning-comparable actions and meaning-compatible thing names. Our method specifically exploits this idea and employs techniques of clustering for verbs and nouns. To outline the contribution of this paper, we propose an unsupervised method to automatically identify metaphors. This study is the first to achieve state-of-the-art unsupervised metaphor identification. Moreover, this method only requires initial manual annotation of a small number of metaphorical expressions (253 samples from data).

Answer selection is a critical subtask of community question answering (CQA), which plays a vital role in facilitating knowledge sharing and exchange in online communities. Websites like Yahoo! Answers, Quora, and Zhihu have over a billion registered users worldwide, demonstrating the immense potential of CQA in disseminating information and expertise. CQA systems typically group questions and their corresponding answers together to provide users with a convenient platform to seek and provide information. Answer selection, however, poses a formidable challenge as it involves selecting the most relevant and accurate answer from a large pool of candidate answers. In spite of its importance, answer selection remains understudied in the field of CQA. Traditional approaches to answer selection often rely on shallow features such as TF-IDF or the anchor text of hyperlinks within the question and answer text, without considering the unique structural characteristics of CQA questions. Specifically, a real-world CQA forum often presents questions as two interrelated components: a subject that summarizes the main points of the question, and a body that elaborates on the subject in detail. Although these two components are closely linked, prior research on answer selection frequently ignores the subject-body relationship, treating the question as a single, concatenated representation. Ignoring the subject-body relationship may lead to neglecting vital information within the CQA question. The subject typically provides a clear, high-level overview of the query, while the body offers more nuanced details that can be crucial in understanding the context of the question. Recent advances in deep learning have shown promise in modeling complex document representations that capture long-range dependencies and context-specific relationships within text. However, such techniques have yet to be employed in CQA systems to fully leverage the structural information of CQA questions. In this paper, we propose a novel model, Question Condensing Networks (QCN), that explicitly considers the subject-body relationship in CQA questions to facilitate answer selection. Our QCN framework treats the question subject as the primary part of the question representation, and aggregates the body information based on similarity and disparity with the subject. This approach allows for the extraction of more relevant and informative question features, which are essential for answer selection. By differentiating between the subject and the body, QCN is free from the limitations of traditional approaches that sacrifice explicit subjectivity for the sake of simplicity. Experiments conducted on two benchmark CQA datasets demonstrate the superiority of QCN over existing state-of-the-art models in terms of answer selection accuracy.

Multi-Metric Optimization Using Ensemble Tuning Statistical machine translation (SMT) systems are widely used for translating human languages. The primary goal of an SMT system is to produce output that is fluent, accurate, and comparable to human translations. Traditionally, evaluation of an SMT system's performance is done by computing a single metric such as BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002) or ROUGE (Lin, 2004) on a test set. However, these metrics do not always agree, and different metrics may give different rankings of system performance. In fact, optimizing for a single metric may lead to suboptimal performance on other evaluation metrics (Chiang et al., 2010). Researchers (Casacuberta and Vidal, 2006; Takeshi et al., 2008; Gispert et al., 2009; Callison-Burch and Koehn, 2008) have shown that a combination of multiple metrics typically produces results better than using any single metric for a shift in priorities in evaluating an MT output. Though, reporting single aggregated performance metrics like BLEU can help us generalize our findings relevant for various tasks, other tasks like comparing relative performance of different variants of an SMT system to another differs and the former metrics cannot satisfy these needs. In fact, computation of BLEU scores, although has been around for long time since Papineni et al, (2002) had presented its first first version, may not quickly and constantly be available although there are many alternatives available (Cherry and Maurer, 2013). There has been growing interest in multi-metric optimization (MMO) for SMT systems, that considers not just a single evaluation metric but a combination of multiple metrics. MMO aims to balance competing priorities and yield a set of well-performing models rather than a single optimal model. MMO is typically solved by a process called Pareto optimality (Saydjari et al., 2014), where all the optimal models are optimal for at least one runs. Although there exist certain methods for obtaining such sets (Gurevych et al., 2006; Cremoroso et al.,2011), they have limitations. For example, these methods are not always effective with a large number of models. Although several variant of Pareto optimality that gets better at returning optimal models that meet the constraints first leads to Pareto optimal solutions (Lin et al., 2011). Sometimes in this variant, permutations of candidate solutions may result in different Pareto-optimal sets albeit our solution distributions remain identical. We propose and evaluate ensemble tuning methods for multi-metric optimization in SMT.

Event detection and classification is a crucial task in information extraction from natural language texts. It involves automatically identifying specific occurrences of predefined types of events, such as birth, death, or election, which have been extracted from text streams over a certain period of time. The importance of event detection lies in its potential applications in various domains like politics, economics, sports, and entertainment, where the ability to quickly and accurately monitor the occurrence of specific events can provide valuable insights into trends, potential problems, and opportunities (Sheth and Hendeles, 2011;Di-Fatta et al., 2012;Kim and Schutze, 2013). Despite the significant advancement in natural language processing, event detection remains a challenging task due to its reliance on the ability to recognize certain patterns within the text and the nuances associated with events (Hürten and Gertz, 2013). With the proliferation of online data, and the continued rise of various text streams, it is critical to evaluate the performance of existing approaches and explore new methods to advance this area. Over the past decade, various machine learning and deep learning models, including support vector machines (SVM), Naive Bayes, decision trees, random forest, recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory (LSTM) and gated recurrent units (GRU) have been proposed to address the event detection task (Li et al., 2013;Wang et al., 2015;Xi et al., 2015). However, most of these models lack the understanding of the temporal context and the syntactic structure of the text. More recently, there has been growing interest in exploiting the temporal structure through the use of attention mechanisms (Vaswani et al., 2017), and incorporating syntactic information through the parsing tree in models like graph convolutional networks (Kipf and Welling, 2016). Additionally, incorporating external knowledge through incorporating external knowledge like Yago or entities from knowledge base and incorporating external resource like Wikipedia or world events database, has shown to improve the performance of various NLP tasks (Gabriel and Galton, 2013;B диаметes et al., 2017). Inspired by these recent improvements, this paper proposes and evaluates a novel event detection model based on the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with the attention mechanism, which is capable of utilizing both temporal relationships and the distribution of syntactic patterns across the input text stream. This paper aims to address the following key issues in this area:   Designing a GRU-based model that can effectively utilize both temporal relationships and distributions of syntactic patterns across the input text streams to enhance event detection performance.

The Standardization of Named Entities: Challenges and Opportunities Extracting and representing named entities in text is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with far-reaching implications for information retrieval, question answering, text summarization, and other applications. However, one of the most significant challenges in working with named entities lies in their inherent variability in representation, making it difficult to compare, aggregate, and reason about entities effectively. For instance, the same individual or organization may be referred to using multiple names, such as "John F. Kennedy," "JFK," or "President Kennedy," due to differences in context, style, or language. The lack of standardization in representing named entities can result in a myriad of issues, including entity duplication, inconsistencies, and inaccuracies, ultimately hindering the reliability and effectiveness of NLP systems. In recent years, the canonicalization of named entities has gained significant attention as a means of resolving these discrepancies and providing a unified representation of entities across different contexts and attributes. Canonicalization involves transforming named entity mentions into a standardized format that exposes their underlying attributes, such as names, titles, locations, and dates. The resulting representation can facilitate more accurate and robust NLP applications, including named entity recognition (NER), entity linking (EL), and relation extraction. A key aspect of entity canonicalization is the determination of entity attributes, which represent the underlying properties or aspects of an entity. Traditional approaches to attribute extraction focus on predefined, hand-crafted rules or machine learning algorithms that rely on manually annotated data to learn attribute patterns. However, these methods often suffer from limitations, such as the need for extensive human resources, time-consuming annotation processes, and the difficulty of capturing complex attribute dependencies. To address these challenges, we turn to statistical models and machine learning techniques, which can provide a more systematic and scalable approach to entity canonicalization. A promising direction is the use of Bayesian inference and transductive learning to combine knowledge about entity context, surface features, and attribute-part dependencies. By incorporating these factors, a probabilistic model can learn to represent entities as tables whose rows correspond to entities and whose columns are attributes or parts thereof. This representation enables more effective entity aggregation, comparison, and reasoning, ultimately leading to improved NLP performance. In this paper, we introduce a novel probabilistic model for canonicalizing named entity mentions, incorporating entity context, surface features, first-order dependencies among attribute-parts, and a notion of noise. Our approach employs transductive learning from a few seeds and a collection of mention tokens, combining Bayesian inference and conditional estimation.

Stock market prediction has been a long-standing challenge for researchers and practitioners alike. Accurately predicting stock movements is crucial for informed investment decisions, which in turn can impact the overall health of the economy. The rise of social media platforms, such as Twitter, has enabled investors to stay up-to-date with the latest news and opinions on the market. Tweets contain valuable information on market sentiment, sentiment analysis of which can help investors make more informed decisions. With the advent of sophisticated machine learning techniques, researchers have attempted to incorporate text signals from social media into their prediction models. However, integrating text signals into traditional time-series based stock prediction frameworks remains a topic of ongoing research. Traditional stock movement prediction models rely heavily on using only one type of data source, such as historical prices, which are inherently Markovian and often rely on an autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) assumption, ignore the underlying trend, or assume a Gaussian distribution in the noise (Brock et al., 1992;Marsh and Rosenfeld, 1983). Alternatively, some models focus on short-term market forecasting, often using more exotic, yet simplistic, features like the book-to-price ratio, trading volume, or the difference between the bid and ask prices (Li et al., 2005;and Chacko and Mishra, 2004). Other models focus on the analysis of high-frequency data, such as tick-by-tick transaction data (Holyst et al., 2001). Most of these models ignore noise in price quotes and are unaware of the complexities of the underlying dynamics. As the complexity of the financial market is growing, more sophisticated models that can integrate multiple types of information, i.e., both text and time-series data, are needed. However, the integration of these heterogeneous data sources poses significant challenges. Specifically, both the text and price signals are random and intertemporally dependent. Moreover, learning representations capable of capturing complex patterns and relationships between these variables is relatively hard. The task is indeed much more challenging to model and predict stock movements than the other problems aforementioned. Furthermore, any accidents on the adversary (big events) are more likely to affect the complex stocks, which can inadvertently free radicalize the outcomes predicted. Due to these difficulties, how to effectively combine the information offered by both text and time-series data into a unifying framework which accurately capture the underlying dependencies still remains largely an open question. We will first delves on motivations above followed by a concise survey of related work and theoretical framework in this paper, along with theoretical framework, contributions, system architecture, training process and experimental results.

The importance of citations in the scientific community is well acknowledged. Citations serve as an indicator of the impact of a research article, with highly cited papers often being considered seminal contributions to their field. However, the current approach of treating all citations equally overlooks a fundamental fact: references can be cited for a multitude of purposes other than corroborating the main findings. For instance, a study may cite related work to contextualize its contributions, provide background information, or even criticize a particular approach. This multiplicity of purposes indicates that simply counting the number of citations does not provide a complete understanding of a research accomplishment's impact. Furthermore, traditional citation-based metrics, such as the widely-used h-index, have been criticized for failing to distinguish between various types of citations (Bornmann and Daniel, 2008). As a result, these metrics may lead to biased conclusions about the quality and relevance of research endeavors. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in understanding the motivations behind citation behavior (Hammarfelt et al., 2013). This effort has led to the development of novel approaches for classifying citations based on their purpose, such as distinguishing between positive (i.e., corroborative) and negative citations (i.e., critiquing the work) (Chetty and Wilkinson, 2016). However, these efforts primarily focus on classification rather than quantifying the intensity of citations. There is a lack of research on evaluating how often a source, such as a article, is cited by the intensity of the citations rather than by the mere number of citations. Assessing the intensity of citations, such as in terms of how strongly or weakly the cited work contributes to a new argument or how extensively a body of work supports the proposed understanding of a concept, is a key step towards developing more accurate evaluation metrics (Melo and Goncalves, 2018). For instance, in the context of patent assessment, researchers have found that quantitative indicators of an invention's novelty and unexpectedness are highly correlated with its probability to succeed in a patent examination (Alpers et al., 2015). However, the influence of prior art on these aspects is far from straightforward and its quantification can provide a valuable additional metric. Moreover, this alternative perspective can serve to mitigate the risk of dominant topics or 'elite' citations driving the evaluations in certain fields (West et al., 2010). To make progress in the direction of measuring the intensity of citations, we need large high-quality annotated datasets.

Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization, among others. It typically involves identifying entities and their associated relationships from text. Traditional relation extraction approaches rely on hand-engineered features, including part-of-speech tags, named entity recognition (NER) results, group phrase chunks, and dependency parses. However, these methods require extensive domain knowledge and are often inadequate for handling out-of-vocabulary words or entity ambiguity. Moreover, extracting complex relational structures between entities using these approaches can be cumbersome, time-consuming, and error-prone. Recent advances in deep learning have led to the development of robust neural network architectures, notably using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), that have shown impressive performance in sequence classification and tagging tasks. Building upon these successes, this study aims to develop an end-to-end neural model that combines the strengths of sequential LSTMs and tree-structured LSTMs for relation extraction. Our proposed model distinguishes itself from previous attempts, leveraging the bidirectional LSTM-RNN to model sequential word dependencies and the tree-structured LSTM-RNN to capture the hierarchical, sub-tree structure of entity relationships. By learning from these two complementary representations in a multi-task setting, our model enables shared learning of entity detection and relation classification. Furthermore, we anticipate that our proposed structured framework will be more robust to expressions with subtly different word order and prerequisite language styles. Our experiments on the benchmark ACE (Automatic Content Extraction) 2004 and 2005 datasets and the benchmark task of nominal relation classification in SemEval-2010 demonstrate that our model outperforms state-of-the-art feature-based models and performs comparable with a CNN based model. Our study covers a wide gamut of subjects, including how our model measures up against random initialization, the importance of the bidirectional sequential LSTM structure, and the influence of entity pre-training and scheduled sampling during the training process. The structure and composition of a language are fundamental aspects of human communication. Understanding how words are composed and how they convey meaning has been an area of interest for linguists and natural language processing researchers alike for decades. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in the study of compositional semantics, the process by which the meaning of an expression is derived from the meaning of its parts (Barsalou, 2003;Fodor, 1975). This has led to the development of various computational models of compositional meaning, which aim to capture the way in which words are combined to form more complex expressions. One domain that offers a unique testbed for studying compositional semantics is the study of compounds, words that are formed by combining two or more free morphemes into a single unit (G jets, 1979). Compounds differ from phrases because they exhibit a tighter semantic bond between their constituent parts, and as such, the meaning of the compound is more directly derived from its constituents than a phrase would be (Lees, 1960). In this context, the study of German compounds is especially relevant, as they are a common and well-studied linguistic phenomenon in the German language, with a notable productivity in word-formation (Durst-Edwards, 2007). The semantic properties of German compounds have been extensively described in linguistic literature (Ackerman and Webelhuth, 1999), providing a rich source of data for the evaluation and development of computational models of compositional meaning. Recently, the advent of large-scale linguistic resources and the emergence of deep learning-based techniques have enabled researchers to approach the problem of compositional semantics through the lens of vector space models (VSMs) (Bengio et al., 2003). VSMs represent words as vectors in a high-dimensional space, such that semantically related words are closer to each other in the space (Mikolov et al., 2013). This framework offers a natural way to evaluate the performance of different composition models, as it provides a quantitative measure of semantic relatedness (Antάλι and Panteli, 2013). By examining the reconstructions of the observed representations of German compound nouns, we aim to shed light on the semantic compositionality of these linguistic units. In particular, this paper concentrates on the task of predicting the corpusestimated vector that represents a compound noun, by composing the observed representations of its two immediate constituents (often referred to as stem or root and affix). We draw upon existing composition models from the literature, such as Madnani and Kalei (2010) (Compound Dependency model and Joint Model) and train them on a large dataset of German compound nouns using a state-of-the-art word space model.

Math word problem solving is a long-standing challenge for artificial intelligence (AI). Previous works on math word problem solving have mainly focused on template-based recognition (Ashcraft, 1994;Star acquisition, 1996)or semantics-based representation(Broadhead and Bylander, 2002). There are several reasons for this, including the lack of robust parsing models that can deal with natural language (Kordjamshid and Zhang, 2011;Gupta and Takeshi, 2013), and the lack of mathematical reasoning engines that can bridge the gap between math expressions and natural language semantics (Koedinger et al., 2008;Marsh and Abdul, 2016;Goodrich and Doyle, 2019). In an effort to fill this knowledge gap, we present a novel approach to automatically solving math word problems, which integrated semantic parsing and mathematical reasoning. In this approach, the first step is to convert a math word problem into a well-structured formal representation, which our designed language, FormLang. is capable of doing. FormLang. combines the concepts of both natural language formalization and semantic grammar to bridge the gap between the natural language of math word problems and mathematical expressions. FormLang. allows us to formally represent both the semantics and the syntax of math expressions in a unified and consistent manner. The second step is to perform semantic reasoning on the resulting FormLang. expressions to obtain the final solution. The reasoner operates on the parsed FormLang. expression and computes its mathematical value using a combination of mathematical knowledge and logical inference. The correctness of the parser and reasoner are demonstrated through a series of rigorous qualitative experiments that measure their ability to convert math word problems into well-formed math expressions and derive their final solutions. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the rise of various neural network-based architectures. A remarkable group of models that have garnered significant attention in the field of NLP are the character-aware neural networks, which leverage character-level features to improve performance on various tasks. These models have been concurrently applied to a plethora of NLP tasks, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and text classification. However, despite their widespread application, a crucial question remains unanswered: what do these models learn from character-level features, and whether they merely copy existing linguistic rules or actually discover novel ones. While several data-driven studies have indeed established the value of character-level features in deep learning-based NLP models, none have undertaken an in-depth qualitative investigation of what exactly these networks learn and the extent to which they conform to existing linguistic norms. In fact, by focusing on quantitative performance evaluations, many studies have overlooked the importance of understanding how these models acquire knowledge, which is critical for developing more robust, interpretable, and transparent models. To bridge this knowledge gap and provide valuable insights into the inner workings of character-aware neural networks, we aim to investigate whether these models truly learn relevant linguistic patterns, including manually-defined word segmentations and annotations. This will enable us to design more effective and linguistically-attuned NLP solutions in the future. We pursue this research question by combining the contextual decomposition technique (Murdoch et al., 2018), originally developed for analyzing language models, with a range of state-of-the-art neural network architectures for the NLP applications, specifically focusing on the morphological tagging task. Through experiments run on three morphologically diverse languages, we plan to elicit the ability of these architectures to learn not only linguistic rules, but also the practical capabilities and constraints associated with those rules in different linguistic contexts. We expect these results to stimulate a renewed focus on the qualitative analysis of neural networks for NLP tasks. In the morphological tagging example from Brill's rule-based tagging (Brill, 1994), an additional rule was encoded to address an exception to the original rule for the word 'mistress', revealing a careful consideration of word morphology in its creation. In a similar vein, we need to uncover whether neural networks can also generate similar insightful linguistic patterns that aid in more accurately and meaningfully handling the complexities of language.

Sentence-level semantic orientation analysis plays a crucial role in various fields, such as opinion mining, recommender systems, and human-computer interaction, where understanding user opinions and sentiments is vital for decision making and user engagement. With the rapid growth of online reviews and user-generated content, there has been a pressing need for accurate and fine-grained analysis of semantic orientation at the sentence level. Most existing approaches to sentence-level semantic orientation analysis focus on predicting the polarity (positive or negative) of opinions, which is often referred to as opinion polarity analysis. However, a deeper understanding of user opinions can be obtained by analyzing not only the polarity but also the strength of opinions expressed. Opinion strength refers to the intensity or magnitude of opinions, which is often neglected in prior research. Predicting both opinion polarity and strength at the level of individual sentences is challenging due to the lack of sentence-level training data for both aspects. Most existing datasets only provide document-level ratings or coarser-grained annotations, which does not allow for effective training of models for fine-grained analysis. For example, in movie review datasets, the average rating at the document level can mask subtle differences in opinions expressed in different sentences. Given these challenges, it is essential to develop robust and reliable methods for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis that can accurately predict both opinion polarity and strength. In this paper, we propose the Weakly Supervised Multi-Experts Model (MEM) for sentence-level semantic orientation analysis. MEM is designed to cope with the lack of sentence-level training data by leveraging weak supervision signals from coarse-grained training data, a small set of diverse base predictors, and, if available, fine-grained training data. By integrating these noisy indicators into a unified probabilistic framework using ideas from ensemble learning and graph-based semi-supervised learning, MEM is capable of learning robust representations of sentence embeddings and making accurate predictions of opinion polarity and strength. Our experiments on multiple publicly available datasets demonstrate that MEM outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, showcasing its effectiveness in fine-grained analysis of semantic orientation for both opinion polarity and strength. Furthermore, we provide an in-depth analysis of the internal workings of MEM and identify key factors contributing to its superior performance. By making progress toward accurate sentence-level semantic orientation analysis, we hope to foster a deeper understanding of user opinions and improve the design of applications in fields where human feedback and sentiment analysis play a vital role.

Inducing Fine-Grained Semantic Classes via Hierarchical and Collective Classification Recently, natural language processing (NLP) has become an increasingly important component of applications in the fields of information retrieval, question answering, text summarization, and sentiment analysis. One critical challenge for developing these applications is finding an adequate semantic interpretation of natural language constructs. While groupings based on broad categories can be helpful, they fall short for tasks requiring more nuanced semantic distinctions. Name entities like people, organizations and places are typically categorized into general types such as PER, ORG, and GPE, which can be insufficient to support applications that require more detailed data semantics. The lack of fine-grained semantic class information can result in a myriad of challenges, including misleading results, unsatisfactory depth of description, and limitations of generalizability. In light of these issues, the induction of fine-grained semantic classes is becoming increasingly important for semantic-based natural language processing (NLP) applications. Fine-grained semantic class induction involves automatic determination of which of a more specific set of semantic classes (i.e., e.g. students, faculty, staff) a noun phrase like "Dr. Moses, computer science professor at University of California, Los Angeles" belongs to. In this paper, we study a subtype induction problem, which has rarely been addressed. A fine-grained semantic class may represent a sub-class, a subtype or a subcategory of a larger group, such as, organizations, entities, processes, doctrines, concepts, and products. For these reasons, the classification space of the induction problem is highly complex. Traditionally, this problem has been treated using supervised machine learning. The supervised approach to fine-grained semantic class induction relies on annotated training data, typically drawn from a predefined set of classifications. However, relying on hand-annotated training data may not be feasible for practical applications, especially where a large number of available data is limited. Moreover, most currently existing methods lack an understanding of the latent hierarchical structure among the semantic classes, where subsets of semantic classes possess/settle within more inclusive types (e.g., grandfather= parent= individual). To address these limitations, we explore the use of collective classification (Wasserman et al. 2008) and hierarchical classification (Dietterich et al. 1997) methods as alternatives to traditional supervised approaches that rely on annotated training data. Collective classification is based on the idea that class labels can be mutually independent or partially interrelated, allowing the model to benefit from permutations of data labels, yet maintaining generalizability.

Syntax-augmented machine translation (SAMT) represents a fundamental shift in the way we approach machine translation. By simultaneously predicting syntax and semantics, SAMT aims to capture the delicate interplay between the two, yielding more accurate and coherent translations. A key component of SAMT is the reliance on a rich and expressive label set to represent the syntactic structure of both the source and target languages. However, this label set can also be a double-edged sword. As the number of nonterminal labels increases, so too does the complexity of the grammar, and with it, the risk of sparsity and ambiguity problems. These issues can manifest in a variety of ways, including under-trained models, slow inference, and ultimately, reduced translation quality. To mitigate the negative impacts of a large label set, various techniques have been proposed, such as reducing the size of the label set by selectively removing labels or pruning the grammar, or employing advanced optimization methods that adapt to the label set size. In this paper, we take a different approach: rather than modifying the model or the training process, we focus on the very fabric of the label set itself. Inspired by the category-coarsening algorithm developed for tree-to-tree grammars, we propose a novel method for reducing the number of nonterminal labels in the SAMT grammar while preserving its expressiveness. We demonstrate that this "collapsed" grammar not only improves translation scores but also mitigates the occurrence of sparsity and ambiguity problems, yielding faster and more robust inference. Our approach relies on the bilexical label set, a set of bilingual labels induced from large parallel corpora. These labels capture the correspondences between nonterminal categories in the source and target languages, enabling a finer-grained representation of the syntactic structure. We demonstrate the practical benefits of our approach using two Chinese-English test sets, and we provide an in-depth analysis of the trade-offs between the size of the label set and translation quality. By collapsing the label set through category coarsening, we are able to achieve significant improvements in translation scores without compromising the accuracy of the model. Our proposed approach offers several advantages: (1) improved translation quality due to the reduced label set size, (2) faster inference speeds resulting from the reduced complexity of the grammar, and (3) fewer sparsity and ambiguity problems, allowing the model to generalize better and adapt more easily to new input data.

CWS is usually treated as a character sequence labeling task where each character in a Chinese text is assigned a label indicating whether it's part of a word or not. Existing methods range from rule-based systems to machine learning approaches and deep neural networks [Xue et al., 2005;Zhang et al., 2005;Li et al., 2017;Wang et al., 2018;Qiu et al., 2018]. Specifically, the use of sequence labeling models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have shown prominence in CWS [Wang et al., 2018;Qiu et al., 2018]. The nowadays omnipresent web and the ever-growing availability of text data provide endless opportunities for discovering novel relationships, events, and entities, but unfortunately, the unprocessed text is too crude to be of direct use to computer systems or other applications that require a more structured representation. Over the years, Information Extraction (IE) has emerged as a vital intermediate step in this process, extracting specific information from a text or a database and representing it in a more machine-processable format. Specifically, the goal of Information Extraction is to automatically acquire specific information from text data, filter out irrelevant information, and represent the acquired knowledge in a structured manner, such as attribute-value pairs or triples. However, an important limitation of existing IE approaches is their dependence on a set of predefined entities or patterns that need to be specified in advance. This lack of flexibility in IE systems stems from the difficulty of capturing the complexity and heterogeneity of real-world text data and in general, the IE process often requires extensive knowledge, time and effort for the creation and maintenance of these rules and linguistic resources relevant for the extraction task at hand. Open Information Extraction (IE) has been proposed as a solution to this problem. The concept of Open IE is differentiable from traditional IE as it focuses on discovering potentially novel and automatically structured patterns and concepts without needing topre-specify them, with the goal of providing a first step towards the ultimate goal of general knowledge discovery although successful application is still scanty. In this paper, we provide an inclusive survey of the different approaches and systems that have been proposed for tackling Open IE problems. First, we will delve into the current Open IE methods focusing on how they overcome specific challenges inherent in traditional IE, both in terms of annotation task-efficiency and representation-Simply the most comparative available data is open. We will explore and discuss how an Open IE system conducts the highly critical process of concept discovery in open data and, outline some of the main problems Open IE approaches may encounter, offering several extensions that might be important. In addition, we offer a critical assessment of the well-known free approaches that often figure in the literature as methods for evaluating the competitiveness of these systems.

Word representation learning has been a crucial area of research in natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence. Most word representation learning methods rely on the distributional hypothesis, which states that words that are used and occur in the same contexts tend to possess similar meanings. These methods are based on the assumption that words with similar meanings will tend to appear in similar contexts and use similar words. This distributional approach has been successful in representing words in various tasks such as language modeling, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. However, there exist some limitations in these methods. The distributional approach to word representation tends to confuse the concept of meaning and cooccurrence of words. This often results in emotional dissimilar words possessing similar word representations. For instance, the words "happy" and "sad" often appear in similar contexts, such as in sentences with subjects expressing a personal experience. Consequently, the distributional methods tend to assign similar word representations to the words "happy" and "sad", even though they have opposite emotional meanings. Moreover, words with similar emotional meanings such as "happy" and "joy" may end up being assigned dissimilar word representations due to their different cooccurrence frequencies. This oversight often results in poor performance in tasks that require an understanding of emotional states, such as emotion classification and emotion similarity. Another issue with the current word representation learning methods is their inability to capture the nuances of emotional language. Emotions are complex and can only be implicitly conveyed through the language used. Traditional word representation learning methods fail to account for these subtle variations in emotional language. Therefore, they end up masking the true emotional connotations of words in their representations. To address these limitations, a new approach to word representation learning has been proposed. This is a novel method of obtaining emotion-enriched word representations, which projects emotionally similar words into neighboring spaces and emotionally dissimilar ones far apart. The proposed approach leverages distant supervision to automatically obtain a large training dataset of text documents. Two recurrent neural network architectures are designed to learn the emotion-enriched representations. The first architecture is designed to model the causal relationships between words and their cooccurrence within a text. The second architecture is designed to model the affective relationships between words, including the emotional nuances that are embedded in language. Our intention is to leverage the strengths of both architectures to capture the complex relationships between words, which give us richer word representations.

Morphology deals with the internal structure of words. Morphological segmentation of a word refers to the process of decomposing a word into its constituent morphemes, which are the smallest unit of a word that maintains its meaning. For example, the English word "unhappily" can be segmented into the morphemes "un" (opposite), "happy" (adj.) and the suffix "-ly" (adverb-forming suffix). Determining the correct morpheme breaks is crucial for understanding word meaning and facilitating various NLP tasks, such as text analysis, natural language generation and language understanding. Traditional methods for data-driven morphological analysis rely on annotated data provided by human experts, but such annotations are scarce and expensive. Unsupervised and semi-supervised learning methods therefore have become increasingly prominent, which learn morphological representations from unannotated or partially annotated data, respectively. In the unsupervised scenario, the algorithms discover the morphological representation directly from the data, and they obtain more robust results which are commonly more generalizable. In the semi-supervised scenario, the algorithms exploit any available annotated information, to improve performance. Electronic Medical Records (EMRs) are a abundant source of data containing patient health information captured during clinical documentation. They contain valuable insights that can be used to train and evaluate natural language processing (NLP) models for a wide range of applications, such as patient engagement, population health management, and medical research. One particularly pressing application of NLP in EMRs is question answering (QA), which addresses the need for relevant and accurate medical information for both clinicians and patients. QA in this context involves automatically generating answers to questions drawing from clinical notes or other portions of the EMR, which would allow clinicians to quickly and accurately access and understand the patient's health data. Building a robust EMR QA system is a challenging task due to the vast and varied nature of clinical information and the nuances of medical language. Furthermore, a reliable evaluation dataset for this task is lacking, because of the difficulty in creating manually annotated datasets that are both comprehensive and realistic. A typical solution to this problem is to craft a dataset specifically for a task, which can take considerable resources. We propose an alternative approach that leverages existing annotations from more general datasets, to produce high-quality domain-specific QA datasets that do not require manual annotation for the new task. Our approach is exemplified in the creation of the emrQA corpus, which is the outcome of re-purposing expert annotations on clinical notes for i2b2 datasets §. Specifically, we modify annotations already made for tasks such as named entity recognition (NER) and part-of-speech tagging (POS) to create a QA dataset. We create a question-logical form pair, such as 'What age was the patient?' and 'patient: age: 45'. When evaluating these questions against clinical notes, we generate a question-answer pair if and only if the answer matches the logical form in the question, such as "Patient was 45." Additionally, we draw upon the available questionanswer evidence pairs for a related QA task. The resulting emrQA corpus entails one million question-logical form pairs and adds 400,000 + question-answer evidence pairs. This corpus will be used for training models for QA within the EMR domain, as well as serve as a foundation for further research on leveraging NLP on existing sources of health data. In the remainder of this paper, we will further characterize this dataset and examine whether commonly used NLP question-answer architecture can adequately capture subjectivity relationships in the distribution of evidence in the emrQA corpus,.

Among these, semantic role labeling (SRL) occupies a unique position at the nexus where lexical semantics, syntax, and context intersect. At its core, SRL involves identifying the roles played by entities in a sentence, such as the agent, theme, or patient, and linking these roles to the relevant predicates. The importance of syntactic information in SRL was first widely acknowledged in classical approaches to SRL, where parsing-based methods relied heavily on part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and shallow semantic parsing. These methods leveraged parse trees to identify predicate-argument structures, leveraging the syntactic cues that suggest the roles entities play in the sentence. However, in the era of deep learning, many researchers have questioned the necessity of incorporating syntactic information into SRL models. Empirical evidence from recent studies suggests that, under the right conditions, neural models can achieve impressive performance without explicit use of syntactic parsing. These findings have led some researchers to wonder whether the syntactic backbone is actually essential for achieving state-of-the-art results in SRL. While the answer remains elusive, one thing has become clear: the efficacy of syntactic information in SRL models is contingent on several factors, including the quality of the syntactic cues, the effectiveness of the parser, and the sophistication of the downstream SRL architecture. Given this nuanced view of the role of syntax in SRL, our research aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationship between syntactic information and SRL performance. The online discussion of political blogs has become a central aspect of modern democracy, with millions of individuals engaging in online discussions about current events (Wellman et al., 2011). However, the lack of structure and scale of these discussions can make it difficult to analyze and interpret. Despite the popularity of topic models in natural language processing (Blei et al., 2003), their application to online discussions is still in its early stages (Ramage et al., 2010; Achtzehn et al., 2011). Recent studies have begun to examine the use of topic models to capture the underlying topics and themes in online discussions, such as (Qian et al., 2016), but these studies typically focus solely on the analysis of the primary documents (e.g., news articles). In an effort to more accurately describe the complex relationships between the primary documents and the verbal reactions of online communities, we build upon the work of Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) (Blei et al., 2003), by incorporating topic models that jointly model the primary documents and their corresponding authorship and comments. Inspired by the synergy between different types of linguistic phenomena found in various studies, especially (Ella et al., 2016; Gong et al., 2016), we develop several different topic models: a) 3LCDM: a joint model that captures the underlying topics of the blogposts, the authorship and, optionally, the comments of the blog community; b) BLCDM: a model that captures the underlying topics of the blogposts, the topic-specific words used by each author and, optionally, the topic-specific comment words by each post; c) ECaLCDM: an extension that incorporates the social and practical relationships among users and their propensity to form relationships with others given certain circumstances. We evaluate our models on a comment prediction task, using data from a novel experiment in which we manually curated comments for blog posts from a popular political blog. The goals of this task are manifold, one for it provides a more comprehensive view of users' engagement with online content, another to inform the development of more effective intervention strategies to foster high-quality discussions online. The novelty of these evaluation metrics is that, rather than looking at the raw prediction accuracy, we view the models' outputs from the perspective of information reuse, which give us insights that complement traditional metrics and enable a more accurate evaluation of the performance of the topic models. Wellcome to our proposed model, we believe through this, that predicting responses to political blog posts provides insights on fostering information reuse online.

Gender classification is a challenging task that has garnered considerable interest from the natural language processing and data mining communities in recent years. With the surge of social media and online platforms, large amounts of user-generated content have become available, providing ample opportunities for researchers to develop and evaluate algorithms for gender classification. However, the quality and quantity of labeled training data remain a significant challenge in many applications. Most existing approaches to gender classification rely on supervised learning techniques, which can be biased by the potential imperfections in the labeled training data and may not be effective when dealing with a small set of labels. Despite these limitations, there is evidence to suggest that data from social networks, such as users' self-reported gender, interests, and behaviors, may provide valuable insights into their true identities, which can be leveraged in semi-supervised gender classification. One potential candidate for modeling the relationships between users and their interests is the "same-interest" links, which can be often identified from the availability of data in social networks. By utilizing these "same-interest" links and incorporating textual features from a user's content, researchers may be able to more accurately infer their gender identity. Inspired by the synergy between these two sources of information, we propose a novel semi-supervised approach to gender classification based on a factor graph that incorporates both textual and social modeling. This factor graph, which we refer to as the Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG), takes the form of a bipartite graph in which textual features are represented by one set of nodes and "same-interest" links are represented by the other. By introducing a set of auxiliary random variables to capture the interaction between the textual and social components, we are able to marginalize out the auxiliary variables using the message passing algorithm and effectively propagate the information from the labeled data to the unlabeled data through the TSFG. We further derive an efficient algorithm to update the parameter estimation of the TSFG, allowing for the model parameters to be updated based on an alternating optimization procedure that updates the model parameters and the marginal probability of the hidden variables in turn. The factor graph formulation provides a great deal of flexibility in adaptability, allowing the model to leverage both the labeled and the unlabeled data, as well as capturing the relationships between the textual features and the social network information.

Sentiment classification in online review platforms has become increasingly important with the growth of e-commerce. Although deep learning-based methods have made remarkable improvements in sentiment analysis, they usually rely on prior knowledge about the users and products being reviewed, which may not be available for new users and products. This is particularly true in scenarios with limited training data, an issue commonly referred to as the "cold-start" problem. Most existing approaches ignoring the cold-start problem assume that all users and products have a sufficient number of reviews to train an effective model. However, in real-world scenarios, it is not uncommon to encounter new users and products with very limited data. For instance, when an e-commerce company starts a new service or launches a new product, there will be no or very few reviews about it. The lack of sufficient data makes it challenging for existing models to handle the sentiment analysis task effectively. In this study, we focus on addressing the cold-start problem in sentiment classification. We introduce a new framework, called Hybrid Contextualized Sentiment Classifier (HCSC), which comprises two key modules: a fast word encoder and a novel attention mechanism called Cold-Start Aware Attention (CSAA). The word encoder module is responsible for extracting contextualized word representations from raw text data. It leverages a design to incorporate both short- and long-range dependency features in word embeddings, which captures richer semantic information in text. The CSAA module takes the encoded word vectors as input and adaptively decides whether to use shared vectors constructed from similar users or products when these are cold-start cases. This module is crucial in handling the cold-start problem and was originally solved using shared vectors which were constructed from similar entities but it made HCSC significantly more complex. In addition, a frequency-guided selective gate vector is proposed to decide whether to employ the shared vectors in cases where the original distinct vectors lack sufficient information. This design effectively balances the trade-off between handling the cold-start problem and maintaining model complexity. Several previous models were proposed to address the sentiment classification task but they failed to address the cold-start problem. One such example is (Zhou et al., 2017), where the authors utilized an embedding space to integrate user and product information, but it did not adequately deal with cold-start cases. In contrast to (Zhou et al., 2017), this research assess the impact of the cold-start problem more accurately, showing better performance with a much simpler model than existing state-of-the-art methods (often trained under very diverse settings).

Social media platforms like Twitter have been growing exponentially since their inception, with over 440 million tweets being sent every day (Kwak et al., 2010). The ever-increasing amount of user-generated content poses challenges for both humans and machines, particularly when it comes to processing, analyzing, and summarizing Twitter conversations. Unlike traditional news articles or web pages, online social media platforms lack the inherent structure that comes with more formal writing. Consequently, users post short messages (typically no longer than 280 characters) with varying degrees of coherence, making it difficult to grasp the underlying content. In response to the pressing need for data summarization in social media research (Qazvinian et al., 2009), previous studies have experimented with different summarization techniques such as tweets selection and aggregation (G jetsanjani et al., 2017) or automatic content analysis, to name but a few. Nonetheless, and as of today, there exist very limited methods for providing a concise and meaningful summary of the topics being discussed on Twitter. Summarizing Twitter in terms of topical keyphrases is more relevant, as mainstream summarization approaches perform poorly in automatic summarization on social media platforms (Kumar, 2014). Topical keyphrases can offer a clear snapshot of the main topics discussed in a tweet, as well as provide context about the events and opinions unfolding in the Twitter sphere. However, keyphrase extraction from Twitter posts poses unique challenges, particularly due to: i) the short length of tweets; ii) lack of although straightforwardness found in traditional data; iii) the colloquial nature of age-generation in social media platforms. Traditional single document summarization methods typically rely on well-structured documents that contain the explicit information that the summarizer targets. However, when working with micro-posts in social media, keyphrases identification must take into account the low-level of text formation available, i.e., short phrases found in singular tweets. To surpass the limitation that the highly fragmentary structure of Twitter engenders, traditional techniques for text summarization fall short. The reason is that these methods necessitate cohesiveness within the targeted content. This calls for the need of alternative methods for summarizing Twitter content that need to take alternative pervasive and highly agespecific characteristics into account. Recent efforts have highlighted both the quantity and quality problems prevalent in the areas of summarizing and analyzing tweets (Qazvinian et al., 2009), alongside evaluations of pre-existing based summarization techniques. Thus, through this paper, we present a novel approach to summarizing Twitter-based information through targeted topical keyphrase extraction.
