Knowledge bases (KBs) have become increasingly abundant due to the availability of large amounts of semi-structured data. That has also sparked interest in embedding models for KB completion, thereby enabling applications such as question-answering and recommendation systems. A prominent approach to modeling KB embeddings has been based on the use of relation paths between entities. For instance, in WordNet, the path [processor]-[make]-[Intel] connects processors and Intel in terms of a potential hierarchy. A key observation is that modeling such path information not only helps in preserving semantic relations but also generally improves model accuracy. However, the incorporation of relation paths between entities in KB completion poses significant computational challenges. Typical approaches to relational path representation rely on random walks (Lao and Cohen, 2010), Markov chains (G jets, 2013), or standard word2vec techniques (rattenbury et al., 2010), and all of these strategies require a fixed threshold of sampled paths, leading to biased results. That is not all; relation path-based approaches are normally inapplicable to the joint modeling of KB relations and text to improve performance. Joint modeling combines evidence from both sources, thereby sometimes directly bearing witness to a KB fact (x is the President of France, as mentioned in the news article). This joint modeling setting often relies on differentiable neural architectures, as devised by Bordes et al. (2013a) for two entities and seen, and Seo et al. (2017) for more than two entities. Despite the although successful application of the above neural architectures, even the best such solutions have suffered from limitations in relation path representation. For example, it is hard to model relation types and modeling them can almost not integrate intermediate nodes in the path and be effective in inducing compositional path representations in either statements of text or KB links. Larger-than-best-SOTA-accuracy consists of incorporating relation types and intermediate nodes but most currently existing methods lack an answer to that and often do so with a sampled subset of relation paths. To bridge the knowledge gap, we address the computational limitations of these methods by proposing an exact positional embedding approach that incorporates all relation paths of bounded length, leveraging compositional representations with relation types and intermediate nodes to strengthen path relations. Our method of choice is dynamic programming, which casts a compositional relations problems into local relation evaluations. Finally, we assure that the additional computational resources enable access the distribution of all first n relation paths between entities, leading to representational improvements.

Recognizing implicit discourse relations is a crucial yet challenging problem in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). A remarkable advancement in the field of NLP is the ability to automatically identify explicit and implicit relationships between text segments, which enables better comprehension and reasoning of text meaning. Implicit discourse relations are relationships between text segments that are not explicitly stated but can be inferred from the text. Identifying implicit discourse relations is essential in various NLP applications such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text summarization. However, accurately recognizing such relationships remains a perplexing task due to the complexity of language and the varying nuances in text. Current traditional methods for identifying implicit discourse relations rely on hand-crafted features, distant supervision, or semi-supervised learning, which are often limited in their capabilities due to the complexity and the nuances inherent in language (Prasad et al., 2008; Xia et al., 2011). In recent years, neural network models have achieved state-of-art performance in various NLP tasks. However, directly applying such models to this task often results in inadequate performance. This decline can be attributed to the complexity of identifying implicit discourse relations, which involves capturing subtle nuances and contextual relevant features from the text. Recent studies have argued that the current neural network models have a tendency to focus on certain features repeatedly, thus often oversimplifying the context. We argue that identifying implicit discourse relations requires not only static features but also dynamic features that can capture the contextual nuances and efficiently exploit the relevant information. In order to mimic this repeated reading process and although there have been numerous applications of attention mechanism and external memory in the computer sciences. The goal in this paper is to present a neural network model that not only efficiently capture the static features but also integrate a repeated reading strategy to dynamically and progressively accumulate useful information from the text in order to identify the most relevant implicit discourse relations. This repeated reading process allows the model to observe the text arguments at a series of increasingly specific levels of granularity and progressively locate the highly critical words. By mimicking this reading strategy, we can efficiently extract the dynamic relevant information from the text, allowing for more accurate recognition of the implicit discourse relationships. We propose the neural networks with multi-level attention mechanism (NNMA), a model that combines the use of attention and external memory to mimic this repeated reading strategy.

The unprecedented growth of social media platforms over the last decade has led to an avalanche of unstructured and publicly accessible text data posted by users daily. Although this information provides a unique snapshot of people's behavior, opinions and preferences, it poses significant challenges for automatically processing and analyzing this data using traditional natural language processing (NLP) tools. This is largely due to the use of nonstandard words, abbreviations, misspellings and slang, which are not recognized by conventional lexical resources. A key step towards automating the analysis and retrieval of social media data is text normalization, which entails restoring the canonical forms of the non-standard words. This allows the social media text data to be transformed into a form that is compatible with existing lexical resources. However, the development of a high-accuracy text normalization system is fraught with a number of challenges (Banerjee and Pedersen, 2003): First, the proliferation of regional and colloquial expressions makes it difficult to establish a comprehensive normalization lexicon. Second, the context in which non-standard words are embedded often bears little relation to the context in which they are used, making it difficult to infer the intended semantics. Third, highly homophonous words and misspellings of words can greatly hinder the normalization process. Fourth, a text normalization system must handle the intrinsic uncertainty present in language elucidation tasks as well as identify relationships between words, potentially resulting in different readings of the same text: In such a text, names, place names and numbers are first normalized while dates and times and proper nouns are although first kept the original and only serve as identifiers. However, this is also another challenge in social media text. Until now, there is a wide array of normalization techniques have been proposed in the literature (Nadeau and Sekine, 2007). However, these methods tend to stress lexical measures such as random mapping heuristics, the double metaphone algorithm and the Kjartansson algorithm and tend to overlook contextual and grammatical features of social media text, such as word associations and parts-of-speech (POS) information. Furthermore, most of these normalization approaches are based on the idea that a careful construction of a normalization dictionary will allow a high-accuracy normalization. In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised text normalization approach that not only uses lexical measures, but also contextual and grammatical features of social media text. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed approach is first to use the double metaphone algorithm based on sound or actual letters not according to the white space, permutations or accents; we only normalized the original information while preserving its context.

Bilingual dictionary induction, a crucial task in multilingual NLP allows for translation of words from one language to another (Koehn et al., 2007). Due to data acquisition challenges related to text translation, monolingual dictionary induction has been traditionally relied upon. However, with increasingly growing digital infrastructure worldwide, language speakers communicate across group bounds in their native languages and hence, it is ideal that NLP supports multilingual language translation (Kittel et al., 2013). In this direction, bilingual dictionary induction plays a vital role by discovering translation relationships between words of two languages. By applying zero-shot learning for data-free translation of many-source translating (Rozantsev et al., 2019), previous research works achieved this aim (Johnson et al., 2017;Schwenk, 2017). The standard approach for this method entails developing a common space for many languages using multi- and cross-lingual word embedding (Mullick, 2018;Conneau et al., 2017). This common vector space for all languages enables the zero-shot translation of words from one language to another. Nevertheless, the performance results that followed from these models sometimes have been unsatisfactory (Artetxetxea et al., 2018). These unsatisfactory results can be mainly attributed to the different dimensionality and quality of word embeddings in different languages. Current methods which employ zero-shot learning technique focus solely on multilingual word embeddings hence do not leverage the insights and quality of pre-existing translation resources (e.g., extremely large pre-existing translation paths) (Durinya et al., 2018). For this reason, they lack a high degree of accuracy for indicatively supervised modeling tasks that almost solely integrate pre-existent data (Li and Qian, 2019). Unlike these preceding statements, our proposed knowledge distillation (KD) framework bridges the gap by allowing us to distill pre-existing translation knowledge from teacher languages into low resource languages. By maintaining highly accurate mapping functions, the incorporation of the teacher language yields optimal alignment of translation lexicons. Furthermore, our framework allows for adaptability in regards to the smooth addition of new teacher translation knowledge paths, which can be free from low resource languages that the framework is optimized for. Our work therefore blends two dominant paradigms of course transfer learning from supervised pre-existing resources and zero-shot learning for knowledge that doesn’t exist in the existing data distribution. By first organizing a set of optimal pre-existing high-quality translation paths as high-quality teacher through appropriate vector similarity, our proposed distillation training approach rapidly enables integration into models of large high-quality translation paths involving low resource languages thereby yielding more accurate word mappings.

Dialogue systems have been increasingly prevalent in recent years, driven by the need for more natural and intuitive interfaces in various applications such as customer service, smart homes and virtual assistants. Open-domain dialogue generation, where a system can converse with a human on a topic of their choice, remains one of the most challenging areas in the field of human-computer interaction. Achieving human-like conversation is not merely about generating grammatically correct and coherent text, but also about simulating human-like reasoning, common sense and emotional understanding. In this regard, a promising direction for improving dialogue systems is to adopt more sophisticated models and training paradigms. One traditional approach to training dialogue systems is maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), where a system is trained to predict the next word in the dialogue sequence, given the context of the conversation (Vinyals and Le, 2015;Serban et al., 2016). However, this approach has several limitations. Firstly, it does not directly take into account the human-likeness of the generated responses. Secondly, it often leads to generic and repetitive responses that fail to capture the subtleties of human conversation. Inspired by the Turing Test, an evaluation framework designed to assess the capabilities of a machine, researchers have recently begun exploring alternative training paradigms for dialogue systems. At the core of the Turing Test is the concept of indistinguishability between human and machine. In other words, a well-designed machine should be able to mimic human behavior with such ease and accuracy that the human evaluator cannot reliably distinguish between the two.(Kurian et al., 2018). With this intuition in mind, we propose using adversarial training for open-domain dialogue generation. Adversarial training involves a game-like setup between the generative model, akin to the Turing Test evaluator, and the discriminator, akin to the human being evaluated. In this setup, the generative model generates response sequences that are indistinguishable from those generated by humans. The discriminator, trained to distinguish human and machine generated responses, assigns probability to the likelihood of each response being generated by a human. The outputs from the discriminator are then used as rewards for the generative model, pushing the system to generate dialogues that mostly resemble human dialogues(Table 1). This setup bears a striking resemblance to the original Turing Test, where a human evaluator is required to distinguish between human and machine responses. As a result, we believe that adversarial training is well poised to capture the human-likeness of dialogue systems, which is not explicitly modeled in traditional training approaches.

Query spelling correction deals with a very common but difficult problem: a user typing a query term to search for online information or products but with errors in terms of spelling, and the search engine has to recover from these errors to provide a relevant answer. A correct approach to this challenge involves first to collect a number of possible query corrections for each query input group (all possible gift shops in Paris, rather than ideal or likely 'gift shops in Paris'). Then comes the post-processing stage of this process, ranking potential search results in order of relevance to the input query. Dialogue analysis has been a topic of growing interest in the fields of natural language processing, human-computer interaction, and communication studies. In everyday conversations, dialogue is typically considered a cooperative endeavor where both participants follow certain conventions and rules to ensure effective communication. These conversational rules are largely implicit, and their subtlety often makes it difficult to formally specify them. Despite their informality, these rules are nonetheless essential for dialogue cohesion and productivity. Previous work on non-cooperation has either focused on non-linguistic task-related aspects, such as in multi-agent systems or game theory, or developed model-based approaches to simulate conversational data that exhibits non-cooperative behavior (Galata et al., 1998;Annex and Lee, 2003). While model-based approaches may provide useful insights into the mechanics of non-cooperative dialogue, they differ fundamentally from our approach by focusing on the underlying rules of cooperative dialogue and quantifying degrees of non-cooperation based on these rules. The concept of a "dialogue game" forms the core of our approach (Searle, 1969). This framework views dialogue as a collaborative activity governed by a set of well-defined rules, which participants follow to achieve mutual goals. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) and information extraction. A remarkable advancement in state-of-the-art NER systems over the past decade has been the use of deep learning architectures that leverage lexical and contextual information to generalise well to unseen data (Lample et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2016). However, even with the strong performance achieved by these models, there are still significant challenges associated with recognising entity types, particularly in multilingual environments and when resources are limited. The success of these models heavily relies on finding effective features that can capture and distinguish between different categories, such as people, organizations, and locations. Nevertheless, even with optimal feature engineering, a small bias can lead to significant room for misinterpretation and promotion of a wrong entity type (Banerjee and Pedersen, 2002). In many cases, this is due to the limited or noisy training data available in the target language and domain. For instance, although a commonly used corpus in NER research for English is CoNLL, the entities in such datasets, including the annotations and the language words, all come from the same relevant language and often, a heavy population of humans from the US or perhaps, Europeans. Furthermore, another key challenge of operating on diverse language groups is different language cultures, dialects and ambiguities, potentially resulting in different readings of the entity. Even in cases with fully annotated, high-quality resources, such as the WNUT Challenge corpus for named entity disambiguation, NER models can benefit from leveraging external, independent resources in terms of gaining robustness to noisy data inputs. Fortunately, a wealth of information is available on the internet that could compensate for these limitations. One such open and publicly accessible resource is Wikipedia, a multilingual online encyclopedia that contains vast amounts of information about a wide variety of entities across the world (Roger et al., 1980). Furthermore, an additional advantage of leveraging Wikipedia is that it can provide both in-domain data and, more importantly, out-ofdomain information that allows users to improve the accuracy and effectiveness of their NER systems more so if the initial knowledge of its usage can be free from human labor. In the following sections, we will present how to effectively exploit Wikipedia content to improve the multilingual NER system. Our main contributions are (1) we develop a high-coverage and high-accuracy multilingual Wikipedia entity type mapping scheme; (2) Leveraging these mappings, we devise several approaches to enhance the desciption of a multilingual NER system; and (3) we evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed approaches on six languages using various NER datasets.

Deep neural networks have revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), largely due to their ability to learn complex and abstract representations of text data. Recently, the concept of multi-task learning has emerged as a promising approach to improve the performance of neural networks on NLP tasks. By sharing knowledge among related tasks, multi-task learning aims to group together tasks that share a common goal, rather than training separate models for each individual task. Multi-task learning has been applied to a variety of NLP tasks, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and named entity recognition. By coupling related tasks together, multi-task learning can leverage the data from one task to improve the performance on another. Typical approaches to multi-task learning involve linking some layers between tasks, which can aid in knowledge sharing and therefore enhance the performance of each individual task. This method, which we term the Leaky Unit, enables the network to selectively share features between tasks, reducing interference and improving performance. We also propose a convolutional neural network structure that integrates the Leaky Unit, allowing for efficient and effective task completion. The goal of SCFG decoding is to find the highest scoring string that can be generated by the grammar, which is inherently cubic in the length of the string. One of the longstanding open problems in the field of SCFG decoding is the binary factor that arises when converting an arbitrary SCFG to Chomsky Normal Form (CNF) (Chomsky, 1959). This conversion, first described in (Zhang et al., 2006), is known as synchronous binarization. The synchronous binarization technique assumes that the observation symbols and non-terminal symbols in the grammar are independent of each other. A cubic time factor is inherently associated with synchronous binarization, and as a result, the running time can potentially be inflated. (DeNero et al., 2009) expanded this problem by tackling it using Lexical Normal Form (LNF), a superset of CNF. Math word problem solving is a long-standing challenge in the fields of natural language processing and artificial intelligence. The ability of humans to solve math word problems relies on a combination of natural language understanding and mathematical reasoning (Shutzenberger, 1980; Langley et al., 2009). Given the complexity of this task, an automatic math word problem solver has been a goal pursued by researchers for decades. Towards this aim, one effective way is to use sophisticated machine learning algorithms to model the combinatorial relationships between various linguistic and mathematical features extracted from the word problem (e.g. (Mandler and Nelson, 1978; Ritter and Koedinger, 2012)). However, one major issue is that extracting these features can be time-consuming and may involve significant manual effort. Moreover, an expert's understanding of the field may be required to engineer the relevant features for the task. Conversely, feature engineering in the context of natural language processing is always associated with human bias. It is, therefore, of more value to directly model the mathematical equations from word problems, without the explicit need to design, select, or engineer the features. Recent advances in deep learning have provided new tools to solve a variety of natural language processing tasks, including sentiment analysis, named entity recognition and chunking. Examples of such work include neural machine translation (Bahdanau et al., 2014), text summarization (Rush et al., 2015), dialogue generation (Li et al., 2016), and document modeling (Bengio et al., 2013). Deep learning, such as recurrent neural network (RNN), long short term memory (Tang et al., 2016a), and gated recurrent unit (Cho et al., 2014), has been applied to a series of math word problem tasks, such as (Wang et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019) demonstrated the efficiency of deep neural networks in solving the tasks, thereby drawing the focus to more research questions: whether we can develop more sophisticated models that combine the RNN model and another type of knowledge retrieval model to improve the performance. In this paper, we aim to explore and answer these research questions through a novel deep math word problem solver architecture that utilizes a combination of RNN model and similarity-based knowledge retrieval model. Our goal is to improve the efficiency and accuracy of math word problem solving, and assess the performance improvements of the proposed hybrid approach in this study. In what follows, we introduce the general framework of the proposed model, our experiment setup, results and analysis, and the contribution of our paper to the field.

The dynamics of power and language have been studied extensively across various disciplines, with a rich body of research in sociology, linguistics, and organizational behavior providing insights into how power is exercised and manifested in communication (Tannen, 1994; Kotthoff, 2015). Sociolinguistic theory posits that language use is inextricably linked to social and cultural contexts, and that communicative styles can reveal underlying power dynamics (Bargiela-Chiappini and Nickerson, 1999; Xu, 2006). The gender of speakers has been identified as a critical factor influencing language use, with men generally found to employ more direct and authoritative communication styles, whereas women tend to favor more collaborative and expressive communication styles (Tannen, 1994; Lakoff, 2003). Specifically, with regards to gender and power dynamics, the sociolinguistic literature suggests that women may employ face-saving strategies to negotiate power in male-dominated settings (Tin, 2002). Moreover, women have been found to use language more explicitly to create and maintain social relationships (Fritz and Etzbach, 2003). These findings have important implications for understanding how power is exercised in various contexts, and highlight the need for more nuanced research to explore the intersections of gender, power, and language in specific social settings. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the application of computational methods to the study of language, with the goal of providing quantitative insights into language use in various contexts (Blei, 2012; Schütze, 2018). One of the most influential datasets in this area is the Enron email corpus, which contains over 600,000 emails exchanged among executives at Enron (Klimt and Yang, 2004). While the Enron corpus has been extensively analyzed using various computational methods, one limitation of the available research is that it has largely ignored the role of gender in language use. By developing and releasing a freely available extension to the Enron corpus, where the gender of senders is reliably identified, we present an opportunity for researchers to explore the intersection of gender, power, and language in a well-studied corpus. In this paper, we investigate two specific hypotheses drawn from the sociolinguistic literature, pertaining to the use of communicative strategies by women managers and the explicit creation of social relationships by women in the Enron email corpus. We also introduce the notion of "gender environment" to the computational study of written conversations, and present initial findings on how this variable affects manifestations of power in email interactions. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of gender information in automatically predicting the direction of power between pairs of participants in email interactions.

Website privacy policies serve as a crucial source of information for users, allowing them to grasp how their personal data are being collected, used, and shared by organizations. However, the content of these policies is often veiled in ambiguity, hindering users from comprehending the complexities of data collection and sharing practices (Acquisti and Grossklags, 2005;Berendt et al., 2005). This opacity poses significant challenges for both individual users and regulators tasked with overseeing privacy policies (Fishkin et al., 2010). Recent studies have highlighted the demand for clearer language and enhanced transparency in privacy policies (Milne and Culnan, 2004;Mathias et al., 2013;Fejer et al., 2015), underscoring the need for effective methods to identify and address vague content (Banisar and Wolf, 2013). Prior research has explored using semantic analysis and natural language processing techniques to analyze the clarity of policies (Albrechtslund, 2008;Lederer et al., 2012;Warren, 2002). However, these studies primarily relied on manual classification and lacked large-scale training datasets to conduct extensive developmental studies, thereby limiting their scalability and effectiveness. To address this shortcoming, we propose and explore novel methodologies for automatically detecting vague words and sentences in privacy policies, as well as discuss strategies for improving policy usability. Recognizing the challenge of comprehending privacy policies and identifying vague content, we begin by first introducing some of the issues associated with vague content although privacy policies are invaluable tools for informing end-users about practices such as data collection. The goal of this paper is to present a set of scalable and context-aware approaches for modeling vague words and sentences, rather than just focusing on the problems posed by ambiguous policies themselves. Unlike related studies that simply stress the significance of privacy policies and related issues of interpretability and the importance of learning to write clear policy documents, we aim to develop more proficient tools that provide highly accurate predictions of vagueness to data scientists, thereby empowering the policy audience more effectively. Furthermore, we provide practical recommendations and implement intuition to make contributed methods more viable and accessible to the policy community. In this regard, we present a set of contributions that lead to highly precise and accurate results for our envisioned applications. We begin our discussion with an overview of the prior work in several major fields that are related to our project and the references cited above. Next, we will give an overview of our corpus construction process, discussing the issues in creating suitable datasets to capture the complexities of vague content in privacy policies.

Generating Confusion Sets for Context-Sensitive Error Correction Error correction is a critical component in natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in the context of non-native language learners who may have difficulties with mastering the nuances of a target language. A significant challenge in error correction lies in the vast array of potential corrections for a single error. For instance, in English, non-native speakers may frequently struggle with using the correct preposition to accompany a verb or noun. As a result, generating a list of plausible corrections for a specific error becomes a perplexing task. The standard approach to error correction involves relying on the output of discriminative classifiers, which identify the most probable error from a set of possible corrections. However, one issue with this approach is that the set of possible corrections may be prohibitively large, leading to an overabundance of candidates that may or may not be acceptable. The proliferation of errors in non-native text can be attributed to various factors, including superficial similarities between words and grammatical structures. For example, English learners often have difficulty distinguishing between similar prepositions such as "at" and "in," or "on" and "over." The issue is compounded when learners sometimes utilize native language idioms or linguistic patterns, leading to errors in preposition usage. A conventional strategy for addressing the problem of error correction relies on generating candidate corrections for a preposition from a predefined set. This set typically includes all prepositions that participate in the task and are assumed to be equally plausible. However, such an approach poses several shortcomings. Firstly, generating extremely large candidate sets can serve to dilute the probability of generating an accurate correction. This is because the high number of possible corrections floods the classification process, decreasing the precision and recall of the model. Secondly, by considering each preposition as equally probable, the model fails to capture the statistical significance of preposition usage in the non-native text. In recent years, significant attention has been devoted to exploiting the properties of annotated corpora and the linguistic patterns ingrained within them to enhance the performance of error correction models. One such approach focuses on identifying preposition confusions and utilizing this information to generate targeted candidate corrections. This paper explores an approach to generating confusion sets based on annotated corpora. By leveraging an annotated corpus of non-native text, we identify the most likely preposition confusions and employ this information to restrict the candidate set.

Semantic role labeling (SRL) and word sense disambiguation (WSD) are two fundamental tasks in natural language processing (NLP), whose ultimate goal is to uncover a rich and intuitive representation of text that reflects its meaning. SRL identifies the semantic roles played by entities in a sentence (e.g., ARG0, ARG1), while WSD determines the specific meaning of a polysemous word in context (e.g., bank as "financial institution" vs. "riverbank"). However, in order to effectively model linguistic meaning, we require a more nuanced understanding of the intricate relationships between the entities involved and the semantics expressed in narratives. Toward this end, there is an increasing consensus that SRL and WSD are closely interrelated, and that resolving one task can often facilitate the other. Despite these potential synergies, most current formulations of these tasks approach them in isolation, if only because of the relative intractability of jointly optimizing these two, cognitively related objectives. For instance, Quadrana and Moschitti (2016) proposed a pipeline system for SRL and WSD, arguing that automatically identified entities can ease some of the challenges in WSD and that, in turn, recognizing various word senses can help in identifying the roles they play in a sentence frame. Similarly, several recent publications elucidate on how insights from solved word sense disambiguation can automatically provide efficient preprocessing assistance for further processing such as, named entity recognition(Jagannatha & Cook, 2019). We also observe that although there have been numerous applications and exploitation of WSD, such as in sentiment analysis (Kim et al., 2015) or in dialogue systems (Banchs & Li, 2010), there are few applications and practical use cases that combine insights from solved word sense disambiguation and automatic semantic role labeling This work aims to draw upon the available research on both tasks and investigate whether explicit modeling of logical constraints between entities from WSD and SRL can provide a better understanding of the interactions between them. Motivated by this perspective, we propose a Markov logic model (MLN) that integrates both tasks, allowing the model to simultaneously disambiguate word senses and assign semantic roles to entities. In essence, the model hypothesizes that entities with a certain semantic meaning are most likely to be associated with several particular arguments that correspond to subjectivity relationships (e.g., Agent, Experiencer), and argues conversely that entities with certain productive roles can also have sufficient hostword permutations. By exploiting this synergy, we can potentially develop a more effective model that improves performance over both individual tasks and state-of-the-art interleaved models.

Information retrieval is a critical component of many applications, including internet search engines, question answering systems, and enterprise search. Despite the advent of advanced technologies in this field, the performance of information retrieval systems is still far from perfect, mainly due to the inherent complexity and ambiguity of natural language. As a result, the quest for more effective information retrieval techniques has become a focal point of research in recent years. One promising direction in advancing the performance of information retrieval systems is the incorporation of lexical semantic knowledge (Li et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2010; Mikolov et al., 2013). Lexical semantics offers a means of translating natural language into a formal, meaningful structure, enabling information retrieval systems to compute a more accurate and precise depth of matching between query and document terms. However, an essential step toward this goal is understanding the nature of the lexical semantic relations between query and document terms, and determining how these relations are represented by different measures for semantic relatedness. Studies have shown that the choice of measure for semantic relatedness can significantly impact the accuracy and efficiency of information retrieval systems (Finkelstein Etal., 2002). For instance, some measures of semantic relatedness, such as the term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) approach, focus primarily on the intrinsic properties of words, such as their occurrences and frequencies, without considering any relationships between the words. However, more sophisticated measures of semantic relatedness, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995) and Lesk (Lesk, 1986), do take into account the inherent relationships between words, even if these relationships may not be explicitly codified. Nevertheless, a complete assessment of the ability of lexical semantic knowledge to enhance information retrieval systems necessitates a deeper examination of the ontological structure of these resources, both in terms of their representations of word meanings and the forms of the relationships between words (Resnik, 1995). In response to these challenges, relatively recently accessible collaborative knowledge bases, such as Wikipedia and Wiktionary, have been increasingly employed for information retrieval (Gaizauskas et al., 2004). In a similar vein, wordnet, a large lexical database for the English language, has also become an important asset for lexical semantic research. Effective resolution of coreferential relationships is crucial for various NLP applications, such as question answering, text summarization, and sentiment analysis. Recent work has shown that anaphoricity determination - identifying non-anaphoric mentions prior to coreference resolution - is a promising approach to improve coreference system performance (Lee et al., 2017;Wu et al., 2019). Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) is a popular method in Machine Translation (MT) systems for optimizing parameter values that maximize performance on a tuning set. This method employs an automatic evaluation metric, such as BLEU, as a proxy for actual translation quality. By iteratively adjusting parameter values and re-evaluating their impact on the chosen metric, MERT effectively determines the optimal settings for the MT system. However, MERT has one major limitation: it relies on a set of predefined metrics, which may not accurately capture human perception of translation quality. The discrepancy between automatic metrics and human judgments is often cited as one of the most significant obstacles in evaluating the performance of MT systems. Human evaluation, involving human judges, is typically considered the gold standard in the field, but it is time-consuming and expensive. The key challenge, therefore, is to create a method that combines the advantages of automatic metrics (efficiency, speed and scalability) with the advantages of human evaluation (accuracy and relevance). This paper explores the possibility of integrating human feedback in MERT, while minimizing the friction associated with human involvement. By using Reusable, Yields-Predictive, and Tunable metric (RYPT) , we eliminate the need for humans to be involved in the process at the testing time and instead build a database, only at the initial stage, as described below. The RYPT metric has been proposed to preserve the recipients' viewing experience based only on client-side data such as CPU, memory, and device screen size. We adapted that for the translation evaluation by taking into account client-side feedback from the end user in terms of viewing duration and user engagement. Our idea is to train the system with the ability to optimize the translation results not only with automated evaluation metrics but also by leveraging human feedback and insights through a form of "Human-in-the-Loop" (HITL) mechanism. In this mechanism, the system solicits limited human input at specific stages of the training process and updates the model accordingly. By leveraging HITL, we address one of the key limitations of traditional MERT and automate certain tasks that were previously reserved to the human evaluator. In the following sections, we will provide more details on our HITL MERT framework, and we will evaluate its performance through a series of experiments. We will demonstrate how this framework can help improve the quality of translation by taking into account additional information and insights that the human evaluator can provide.

The field of statistical machine translation (SMT) has witnessed a tremendous rise in recent years, driven largely by advances in deep learning techniques and availability of massive parallel corpora. Among several approaches that have contributed to this advancement, discriminative training has emerged as a promising direction in improving the accuracy of SMT systems. Initially proposed for training features in group (He and Deng, 2012), discriminative training has been shown to significantly outperform traditional generative training approaches. However, its applicability to large-scale MT systems has remained limited, primarily due to the computational demand and memory requirements associated with training and optimizing millions of model parameters. Log-linear based SMT models are widely used as the fundamental building blocks of many state-of-the-art systems (Koehn et al., 2007;Gimpel et al., 2007). These models are based on the idea of representing the translation probability as a weighted sum of features that capture various aspects of the input sentence pair and its translation. Traditionally, the weights associated with these features are learned through generative training, where the model is trained to maximize the likelihood of the training data. In contrast, discriminative training focuses on directly optimizing the model's performance on a specific metric, such as perplexity or word error rate (WER), by modifying the feature weights to minimize the objective function. To scale up discriminative training of SMT models, we propose employing a two-stage approach. In the first stage, we adopt the technique of discriminative training of He and Deng (2012) to train features with a large number of parameters, such as 150 million. This significantly increases the model's capacity to capture complex relationships between input sentences and their translations, thereby offering the potential for substantial accuracy gains. In the second stage, we leverage the learned model to explore pruning techniques that have attracted considerable attention in recent years (Han et al., 2015;Guo et al., 2016). By redistributing probability mass lost due to pruning, we can achieve further improvements in model accuracy and create more efficient models that are better suited for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Our experimental study is conducted on the NIST MT06 dataset, which serves as a challenging evaluation benchmark for our methods. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We begin by describing the log-linear SMT model and discriminative training framework that form the basis of our approach. We then present the two-stage discriminative training process and discuss pruning techniques for model reduction.

The use of vulgar expressions is a ubiquitous phenomenon across languages and cultures, regardless of geographical location or socio-economic status. These terms are often thought of as mere filler words, devoid of meaning or significance, but research has shown that their deployment can convey complex information about speakers' beliefs, attitudes, and relationships (Biber and Jones, 2006). Moreover, vulgar expressions have been linked to various social functions, including signaling group membership, expressing emotions, and influencing social dynamics (Labov, 1972). Despite their widespread usage, however, the study of vulgar expressions remains a poorly understood aspect of language use, particularly when it comes to analyzing the intentions behind their use. This is largely due to the fact that studying vulgarity often involves navigating sensitive and potentially contentious subjects, such as insults, violence, and social bias. However, this reluctance to examine the role of vulgarity in language has resulted in a significant knowledge gap in our understanding of language use and communication, particularly with regards to the ways in which vulgar expressions are employed to convey meaning and intent. In recent years, the availability of large-scale language datasets, including social media platforms like Twitter, has provided an unprecedented opportunity to conduct quantitative analyses of language use (Diakopoulos et al., 2012). One such corpus is the dataset of 7,800 tweets introduced in this paper, which contains a high degree of linguistic and ethnographic diversity, along with detailed demographic information about the speakers (age, sex, location, etc.). This unique dataset offers a chance to investigate the pragmatic functions of vulgarity in a systematic and empirical manner, with a focus on the ways in which speakers use these terms to convey a range of social meanings. Our hypothesis is that the deployment of vulgar expressions in language use serves a range of purposes, from expressing emotion and empathy to signaling group identity and testing social boundaries. This diversity of function has significant implications for various downstream applications, including but not limited to sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, and social network analysis. By shedding light on the complex, multifaceted nature of vulgarity in language use, we aim to provide new insights into the social and cognitive mechanisms underlying human communication, and to develop more sophisticated approaches to detecting and characterizing this ubiquitous but understudied aspect of language use. A particular challenge in studying this topic involves the need to develop nuanced and accurate methods for inferring the intentions behind the use of vulgar expressions.

Cross-lingual understanding and machine translation are two central objectives in natural language processing. Despite recent advances in neural machine translation and multilingual learning, effective cross-lingual transfer of information remains a challenging task, hindering our ability to leverage the vast resources available in one language to improve models in another (cf. Event extraction is a critical task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications in information retrieval, question answering, and text summarization. The goal of event extraction is to identify and extract relevant events from text and associate them with entities that participate in those events. However, extracting events from unstructured text is a challenging task due to the complexity of natural language and the variability in event expressions. Traditional event extraction approaches rely heavily on explicit event keywords to identify event-related information. However, in many cases, event keywords may not be present, or may be obscured by secondary contexts, making it difficult to accurately identify the relevant information for event extraction. The lack of explicit event keywords often leads to poor event extraction performance, resulting in incomplete or misleading event representations. The prominence of such secondary contexts demands novel approaches to identify relevant information that may not involve event keywords. In this paper, we present a multilayered event extraction architecture designed to identify secondary event role filler contexts in the absence of event keywords. Our model "peels back the layers" of secondary contexts to focus in on event-related information, progressively zooming in on relevant details to achieve high-quality event extraction results. We believe that this novel architecture deserves attention, especially given the inadequacies of current event extraction systems in handling secondary context-rich scenarios. To address this challenge, our proposed architecture includes multiple classifiers organized as a pipeline to capture relevant information at different levels of granularity. First, we employ a document genre classifier to recognize event narratives, providing the foundation for further event extraction processing. Next, we use two types of sentence classifiers: a sentiment analysis module and a sentence role classifier. These modules enable our model to: (a) determine the presence of event-related sentiment, and (b) identify sentence roles and distinguish between secondary event role fillers and other sentence elements. We then apply a set of fine-grained noun phrase classifiers to the most promising candidates, escalating the depth of detail in event extraction. These classifiers aid in extracting nuanced event representations, facilitating a richer understanding of event contexts. By systematically augmenting the extraction process with increasingly sophisticated modules, our multilayered architecture effectively addresses the challenges posed by secondary context-rich text. Throughout this paper, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our architecture through extensive experiments and comparisons with existing event extraction systems. We also present results on the well-established MUC-4 event extraction dataset, providing convincing evidence of the model's improved performance.

Low-resource neural machine translation (NMT) remains an open challenge in the field of natural language processing. Despite recent advancements in multilingual and unsupervised NMT, large amounts of data acquisition is still a hindrance for languages with limited resources. Current statistical and machine translation approaches rely heavily on annotated parallel datasets, making it challenging to develop effective NMT systems for gift languages. Traditional methods of augmenting parallel data, such as back translation (Sennrich et al., 2016) or round-trip MT (Hardmeier et al., 2013), generally incur high data acquisition costs and require significant human effort. Furthermore, the lack of suitable data leads to notably poor-performing MT systems. The recent resurgence of meta-learning (Schmidhuber, 1987) has shed light on a novel approach to addressing this problem. Metalearning extends upon the idea of learning to learn, where the objective is not to optimize the model for a specific problem, but rather to train a model that is able to adapt more effectively to hypothetical unseen tasks (Baxter, 1990). This capability is especially beneficial in low-resource scenarios where training the model on an extensive dataset is sometimes not feasible. In particular, we are concerned with the problem of adapting an NMT model to a new language. The cross-lingual transferability of NMT models depends heavily on the relationships between the source and target languages. If the two languages have only minor differences, then the model can leverage this similarity and learn to adapt quickly to the target language. However, the linguistic features between languages can vary greatly, such as in terms of vocabulary, grammar, or even character sets. In a low-resource setting, where supervised updates are difficult to come by, a skilled adapter becomes increasingly valuable. Meta-learning aims to equip the model with an ability to learn these adaptations efficiently (Finlayson et al., 2008). Very recently, model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) (Finn et al., 2017) has established itself as a superior approach for meta-learning problems. The original idea behind MAML is to train a model within a finite number of iterations, where the goal is to learn a model that achieves low loss on the population of unseen tasks. Specifically, given a model θ that fits well to a set of training data D, MAML performs a several more steps that adjusts this model with updates tailored for distribution B(ft). Meta-learning evaluations generally emphasize zero-shot or few-shot learning (Schmidhuber, 1987), where the idea is to evaluate the performance of the model on new tasks without providing any supervised data.

Entity linking is the task of identifying a known entity mention within a natural language text and linking it to a corresponding entry in a structured knowledge base. Consider an example of the following text snippet: "Facebook's CEO Mark Zuckerberg was invited to the meeting." To disambiguate the entities present in the above text, "Facebook's" refers to a company, and "Mark Zuckerberg" is the CEO of that company. Therefore, the task of entity linking is to correctly map "Facebook's" to its corresponding entry in a knowledge base, such as Freebase, and "Mark Zuckerberg" to its entry in the same knowledge base. This task is essential for information extraction applications such as question answering, text summarization, and semantic search. It can serve to provide depth and breadth to the information available on the web, similar to what Wikipedia does with general encyclopedic information. Entity linking has grown in importance with the vast amount of unstructured text data available in the web today. It has been extensively studied in the context of relation extraction, co-reference resolution, topic modeling and named entity recognition (Yih, et al., 2009;Kambhatia and Vosoughi, 2016). Several approaches have been used for entity linking, which can be broadly categorized into two classes: rule-based and learning-based. Rule-based approaches rely on predefined knowledge bases, lexical resources and external knowledge sources for entity disambiguation (Suchanek, et al., 2007). However, these approaches exhibit poor scalability and although successful on microtasks, lack robustness when facing complex and real-world texts. On the other hand, learning-based approaches focus on supervised machine learning classification frameworks to improve entity linking performance (Ji, et al., 2007;Liu, et al., 2010). These methods have shown robustness and promise in entity linking but consists of two limitations. Firstly, they mostly rely on hand curated annotated training data to learn decision boundaries between different classes. This may engender data annotation costs. Negotiation in multi-agent systems has long been an area of interest in artificial intelligence. In a negotiation setting, two or more agents use natural language to bargain on items or services, with the goal of reaching an agreement that satisfies both parties. A key challenge in negotiation AI research lies in finding an effective agent that can reason about the negotiation space, choose a suitable strategy, and articulate its offers through natural language. Recent work on negotiation AI has resorted to end-to-end neural models, which learn to generate negotiation dialogue from scratch. However, these end-to-end models suffer from two main issues. Firstly, they are notoriously brittle with regards to high-level strategy. In a negotiation dialogue, an agent needs to decide on its long-term goal, such as the acceptable depth of discount or the upper limit of the price offer. However, these models often degenerate to repeating pre-pad phrases without any underlying strategic reasoning. Secondly, and relatedly, the generation of utterances in end-to-end models is often hampered by the need to balance expressibility and correctness. As in the example of an agent asking for more information, an agent might say "What is the current price of the bike?" or "Can you please tell me how much this bike costs?" while conveying the same request. These factors point to the need for a more modular approach in negotiation AI, one that decouples strategy planning from the execution of that strategy. This way, we can flexibly and separately design the high-level strategy and the generation of utterances. In order to end this decoupling, we draw upon coarse dialogue acts, such as 'propose', 'ask', or 'counter', but also a dialogue-specific payload, which contains metadata such that supports the specific strategy that the dialogue act targets. We suggest that such decoupling shall be supported through two micro-components. Strategy Component: This component plans the course of the negotiation dialogue by determining what dialogue act to use and when to trigger it. The actions generated by the strategy component provide the necessary instructions for the generation component to create the final utterance. Generation Component: This component generates the actual words to create the dialogue act. This includes adding grammatical and contextual specification, free choice of auxiliary arguments that the act could have and sensitivity to the conversation context. For instance, 'propose' could enable "Thanks for the discount, which brings us very close to a mutually agreeable price!"

Human-robot interaction has been a growing area of interest in the field of robotics, particularly in the context of collaborative work and tasks that require mutual understanding and communication between the robot and user. In order for robots to seamlessly interact with humans, it is crucial to design systems that are both effective and user-friendly. One of the key components of a successful human-robot dialogue system is usability, which encompasses the ease with which users can navigate and accomplish tasks within the system. Evaluating usability is a multi-faceted challenge, and numerous approaches have been proposed to assess it, ranging from theoretical models and frameworks to practical testing methods and data analysis techniques. Our work focuses on developing and evaluating a human-robot dialogue system that enables a robot to collaborate with a human user in building wooden construction toys. This study underscores the benefits of cooperation between humans and robots in achieving a common goal by tapping into the strengths of both parties, with humans providing expertise and the robot assisting with repetitive tasks, precision, and calculations. Our human-robot dialogue system relies on a hypothetical model of human-robot interaction that outlines the progression of exchanges between the robot and the user. The interactions start with the robot's initialization of relevant context and continue through a sequence of synchronous dialogues involving information exchange and confirmation. Hence, to gather insights and assess the quality of the interactions in our human-robot dialogue system, we have designed a set of experiments where naïve recipients engage with this system under diverse environmental conditions. Here, we explore both the subjective and objective measures of these experiments that yield a comprehensive understanding of usability and provide a foundation for optimizing the performance of human-robot interactions in our collaboration system. Usability is often a subjective phenomenon, typically characterized by users' perception and experience with a product, and has been extensively studied in the field of human-computer interaction (HCI). HCI measures of usability usually rely on the recipients' opinions and feelings about their use of the system through surveys, questionnaires, and interviews. Nevertheless, the highly subjective nature of usability raises important questions about the correlation between perceptions and the actual performance of the system. The study we present focuses on comparing objective and subjective measures of usability in our human-robot dialogue system, assessing how these two aspects may relate to one another and highlighting their relative importance.

Phrase-based translation systems have been widely used in statistical machine translation (SMT) to capture word order phenomena. A key component in these systems is the reordering model, which assigns probabilities to the order in which words in the source language should be mapped to words in the target language. Lexicalized reordering models have been widely employed to improve translation quality. In these models, the word order probabilities are conditioned on the words of the current phrase pair [Liu and Gildea, 2010;Soricut and Marco, 2011]. Although lexicalized reordering models have achieved state-of-the-art performance in SMT [Koehn, 2010], they suffer from three drawbacks. Firstly, they are context insensitive, meaning the word order probabilities are determined solely by the words of the current phrase pair without considering the context of the surrounding phrases. Secondly, the lexicalized reordering models are often ambiguous: in the event of a tie, it is unclear which reordering probability should be assigned to the current phrase pair. Finally, these models suffer from data sparsity, which is more pronounced when reordering probabilities are conditioned on a large number of phrase pairs. As a result, the probability distributions of many phrase pairs are underrepresented or even empty, making it difficult to estimate accurate probabilities. To address these drawbacks, we propose a neural reordering model that conditions reordering probabilities on the words of both the current and previous phrase pairs, called pair-conditioned reordering model. Our model is motivated by the observation that reordering patterns often have a context-dependent nature: the position of a word in the target sentence may depend significantly on the words in the surrounding phrases. By incorporating these context words, our model can capture the complex context dependencies in the data and produce more accurate reordering probabilities. In addition, our model adopts a neural network architecture to alleviate the data sparsity problem. Unlike traditional lexicalized reordering models that build multiple classifiers for each phrase pair, our model builds one classifier for all phrase pairs. In our model, each phrase pair is represented as a continuous space vector, which allows us to model the positional dependencies among different phrase pairs using a neural network. By leveraging the power of deep learning, our model can learn rich features and relationships among the phrase pairs and estimate accurate reordering probabilities even when the data are sparse. To evaluate the performance of our neural reordering model, we conduct experiments on the NIST Chinese-English datasets.

Commonsense knowledge is a fundamental component of human intelligence, allowing individuals to make sound judgments and decisions in a wide range of situations. In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in scaling up existing commonsense knowledge bases, such as ConceptNet (Speer and Havasi, 2012), and building new ones from scratch (Lin et al., 2016;Huang et al., 2018). One key aspect of these resources is the ability of individuals to make connections between seemingly disparate pieces of information in order to arrive at useful inferences. However, building a comprehensive commonsense knowledge base is an inherently challenging and data-hungry task, as it requires capturing the complexity of human thought and experience in a structured and verifiable way. The majority of work in knowledge base completion (KBC) primarily focuses on existing knowledge bases with predefined schemas, like Freebase, to predict missing relational tuples between entities drawn from a fixed set (Bordes et al., 2013). Different from these existing schemas, ConceptNet defines relations among an unstructured set of short phrases. This fundamental shift creates a knowledge base with an unbounded set of potential relations, posing an interesting challenge to relevant research. This challenge is exactly what motivated our work: applying KBC to ConceptNet in order to enrich and scale up this valuable resource. ConceptNet is a general-domain knowledge base comprising a massive collection of relational tuples among concise English phrases. Unlike traditional knowledge bases, such as WordNet (Miller, 1995) and Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), its schema is not predefined and the relations are unconstrained. This characteristic raises critical issues: how do we score tuples among arbitrary phrases, and what are the best ways to capture the complexity of human relations? To start answering these questions, in this paper, we formulate these challenges as KBC problems and introduce a set of neural network models for scoring arbitrary tuples in ConceptNet. Furthermore, we describe our evaluation metrics and the results of a range of experiments to test the performance of our best approach. Finally, we demonstrate the practical value of these findings by showing that our trained model can assign quality scores to novel tuples, which can be used to propose valuable new entries to ConceptNet at the same quality level of medium-confidence tuples from this knowledge base. Our results provide insights into the nature of commonsense knowledge and knowledge that remain accessible. In order to score relations among arbitrary phrases, we propose a bilinear architecture based on additive phrases.

It involves assigning a directed graph structure to a sentence, where each word in the sentence is associated with a set of arcs that point to its grammatical arguments. Expanding Paraphrase Lexicons by Exploiting Lexical Variants Acquiring paraphrase lexicons has become a crucial task in various natural language processing (NLP) applications such as question answering, text summarization, and sentiment analysis. A large and accurate paraphrase lexicon can help improve the robustness and accuracy of these systems by enabling them to handle linguistic variations in input text. However, the acquisition of paraphrases remains challenging due to the vast amount of linguistic expressions that convey the same meaning. The problem is not only how to identify paraphrases but also how to achieve high coverage and accuracy in the acquired lexicon. Various methods have been developed to tackle the problem of paraphrase acquisition, including rule-based approaches, machine learning, and the use of web-based resources. Some of these methods rely on similar word forms (e.g., synonyms or antonyms), while others have exploited the patterns observed in collections of sentences annotated with paraphrases. Despite these efforts, existing methods still have limitations. For instance, they often fail to capture paraphrases that involve different lexical items or fail to generalize well to unseen instances, which can lead to a lack of coverage and accuracy. This paper explores a novel method for expanding paraphrase lexicons by exploiting lexical variants. Unlike previous methods, ours is based on the idea that paraphrases can be obtained through various linguistic processes, including lexical substitution, derivation, and composition. By recognizing these processes, we can capture paraphrases that go beyond similar word forms and generalize well to unseen instances. We induce paraphrase patterns from seed paraphrases and exploit the generality of paraphrases exhibited by pairs of lexical variants in a fully empirical way. This enables us to acquire paraphrases comprising words that are completely different from those of the given seeds. We implemented our method and conducted experiments using a set of high-quality seed paraphrases. Our results show that the proposed method can effectively expand seed sets by factors of 42 to 206, gaining 84% to 208% more coverage than a previous method that generalizes only identical word forms. Human evaluation through a paraphrase substitution test demonstrated that the newly acquired paraphrases retained reasonable quality, given substantially high-quality seeds. The contributions of this research are two-fold. First, our method provides a novel way of acquiring paraphrases that goes beyond similar word forms and generalizes well to unseen instances. Second, our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in expanding paraphrase lexicons and evaluating the quality of the acquired paraphrases.

Phrasal synchronous grammar induction is a key task in machine translation (MT), where we seek to uncover the underlying rules and patterns that govern the relationship between a source and target language. Unlike other approaches where lexical and phrasal translations are separately induced, a phrasal synchronous grammar models both source and target languages simultaneously at the phrase level. This approach offers several advantages, including improved translation accuracy and the ability to capture nuanced linguistic phenomena. Previous work in phrasal synchronous grammar induction has heavily relied on heuristics and constraints derived from word alignment models (Yoshimoto, 2001;Crego and Marino, 2003). These methods often require significant manual effort to construct derivation forests, which limits their applicability to large-scale translation corpora. One such example is the synchronous Coco grammar model of MT, which relies on parse trees to perform grammar induction (Koehn et al., 2003). However, the computational efficiency of such models is limited by the size of the derivation spaces, which grows exponentially with the size of the input sentences. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to phrasal synchronous grammar induction that eschews heuristics and constraints derived from word alignment models. Instead, we directly induce a synchronous grammar from parallel sentence-aligned corpora using a hierarchical Bayesian prior. The prior is designed to bias the model towards compact grammars with small translation units. Inference is performed using a novel Gibbs sampler over synchronous derivations, which side-steps the intractability issues of previous models that required inference over derivation forests. This allows for computationally efficient sampling and inference even on large translation corpora. The use of a Gibbs sampler also enables us to draw samples from the posterior distribution over synchronous derivations, providing a principled and probabilistic approach to grammar induction. Our model can be viewed as a Bayesian nonparametric extension of previous synchronous grammar induction approaches. By learning the grammar and lexicon simultaneously, we can capture more nuanced linguistic phenomena and produce more accurate translation outcomes. We demonstrate the applicability of our model to large-scale translation corpora and evaluate its performance on several benchmark datasets. The contributed code will allow future researchers to replicate our results and extend this work to other languages and translation tasks. This paper makes the following contributions to MT and natural language processing: 1. A novel phrasal synchronous grammar model that directly induces a synchronous grammar from parallel sentence-aligned corpora without relying on heuristics or constraints derived from word alignment models.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the rise of joint language models, which combine traditional language modeling tasks with other tasks such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, syntactic parsing, and semantics (Chelba et al., 2014;Merity et al., 2018). These models leverage group-level regularities and linguistic structures to improve overall performance on a target task. One type of structure that has garnered increasing attention is syntactic tags – labels that describe the hierarchical structure and relationships between elements in a sentence. However, integrating syntactic tags into joint language models can be particularly challenging due to the many available tagsets and the corresponding difficulties in collecting large-scale annotated datasets (Kiperwasser, 2018). In this paper, we focus on the design and evaluation of a scalable joint language model that leverages fine-grain syntactic tags to improve performance on a target speech recognition task. Our goals are three-fold: (i) to develop a model that can efficiently incorporate fine-grain syntactic tags without incurring significant computational or data-hungry costs, (ii) to propose a set of simple, yet highly informative tags that do not require deep linguistic knowledge, and (iii) to demonstrate the efficacy of our design using two proposed tagsets in a real-world speech recognition scenario. Traditionally, coarse-grained POS tags have been used as a surrogate for syntactic structure in NLP, and as such, they have become a de facto standard in many NLP tasks (McDonald et al., 2018). However, POS tags fall short in terms of capturing fine-grained syntactic relationships: they do not account for complex dependencies, phrasal structure, or specific linguistic phenomena like coordination and subordination (Kiperwasser, 2018). In contrast, we advocate the use of relatively simple fine-grain syntactic tags that still retain structural information but do not require extensive linguistic knowledge of the target language. Our model is designed to be adaptable to new languages, thereby facilitating the scaling up of trained models to diverse linguistic environments. These simple tags can be automatically derived from parsed input sentences, leveraging the output of PCFG (probabilistic CFG) parsers. By exploiting probabilistic parses generated during the pretraining phase, the model can accurately and efficiently predict the most likely tags at each position, thereby fostering a greater degree of structural awareness (Zhu et al., 2018). To further highlight the value of our model, we propose two fine-grain tagsets consisting of 26 and 55 tags, respectively, and contrast our results against traditional POS-based joint language models and a state-of-the-art model that leverages up-to-date wordpiece representation and SuperARV (star-enhanced Average-Representation Vocabularies).
