Personalized search has been a long-standing challenge in the field of web search. The traditional approach relies heavily on user profiling, where a user's profile is constructed solely from their prior interaction data. However, in many cases, a user's profile may not be representative of their interests, especially when they have limited activities in the system (Gautam et al., 2007). This deficiency hinders the effectiveness of personalized search and delivers inadequate results to users. To address this issue, researchers have attempted to incorporate various sources of information to enhance user profiles. The primary sources of information are user interaction data and auxiliary data such as data from co-clicks, co-viewing, or co-ratings (Cossock and Hogg, 2007). The prominence of web 2.0 has led to a growth in the volume of user-generated data. Web 2.0 platforms have witnessed the emergence of social media and online social networks that have witnessed an ever increasing volume of user generated content. Consequently, we are faced with more abundant resources of potential candidates for augmenting user profiling, namely the very vast growing datasets of mainstream web annotations. Annotated text can take many forms, such as label-based, rank-based, or free-text-based annotations. A notable collection of web-based annotation is the dataset of social annotations from the Social Track of NIPS 2010. Since a user's social annotations may provide valuable insight into their interests, such annotations can be utilized to markedly enhance personalized search by first improving user profiling. However these annotations alone are although valuable extremely sparse. Consequently, they need to be integrated with the vast growing pools of external knowledge constructed throughout the past usage histories of a forum platform. This ability to synergistically merge these datasets is a key enabler of the personalized search enhancements presented in this work. Given the limitations of incorporating social annotation data alone into user profiles, we develop the first comparative analyses of learning representations capable of simultaneously incorporating three diverse data sources: social annotations, web documents, and a constructed external knowledge base. The techniques utilized for knowledge base construction are trained on historical usage data (Antάλι and Lupu, 2013). By merging these datasets, our approach can provide more comprehensive user profiles, leading to better personalized search results. To evaluate the performance of our proposed approaches, we adopt a two-step strategy to assess the impact of social annotations, web documents, and the external knowledge base on the personalized search results.

Recent advancements in neural machine translation (NMT) have led to significant improvements in translation quality and efficiency. The encoder-decoder framework with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) has become the de facto standard for NMT systems. However, despite its impressive performance, RNN-based NMT still suffers from several limitations. First and foremost, the RNN structure is inherently sequential and can fail to capture distant information that is crucial for accurate translation. This limitation stems from the fact that RNNs rely on previously processed information to generate the next output, which means that once this information is processed and discarded, it cannot be easily accessed at later steps in the computation. Another critical issue in NMT is the disregard for relationships between source words during the encoding step. In many natural languages, words and phrases have complex interdependencies that are not always immediately apparent. These relationships are essential for conveying the meaning and nuances of a sentence, and their neglect often results in reduced translation quality. To address these problems, we introduce a novel approach for refining source representations in NMT systems. The proposed method leverages relation networks to capture both local and distant relationships between source words, thereby facilitating the memorization and retention of relevant information. In particular, we incorporate a relation network into the encoder module of our NMT system. This network enables the model to associate each word with its contextual relationships, including those with other words that are distant in the sentence. By representing these relationships, the model can better capture the finer nuances of the source language and utilize this information to improve the quality of the translations. During the decoding step, the source representations and relations are fed into the attention component together. This allows the model to selectively focus on the most relevant relationships and words while generating the target translation. As our proposed method is integrated into the standard encoder-decoder framework, it can easily be adapted to existing NMT systems without requiring significant changes to the overall architecture. In our experiments, we evaluate the performance of our proposed method on several benchmark translation tasks. The results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the translation quality over the conventional encoder-decoder model. Furthermore, we observe that our method even outperforms the state-of-the-art approach that leverages supervised syntactic knowledge. These findings highlight the effectiveness of our proposed method in refining source representations and underscore the importance of relationships between source words in NMT.

Neural machine translation (NMT) has become a dominant approach in machine translation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on various tasks. One key component of NMT systems is the search algorithm used to select the best translation candidate from a set of possible translations. By far, the most widely used search algorithm is beam search, which has been shown to improve translation quality over greedy search by allowing the exploration of a diverse set of possible translations. Beam search typically maintains a buffer of the kbest translations, suppressing previously selected translations if their score falls below a certain threshold compared to the best translation in the buffer. However, it has been frequently observed that the performance of beam search degrades notably as the buffer size is increased beyond a certain point. Specifically, it has been observed that increasing the beam size beyond a size of 5 typically results in a decrease in translation quality. This marks a clear point of contention, as intuitively, one would expect that increasing the exploration space of the search algorithm would result in more accurate translations. To provide more insight into this "beam search curse", we perform an in-depth analysis of the underlying causes of this performance degradation. In particular, we investigate the effects of relevant rescoring methods, as well as various stopping criteria used in beam search, which have been shown to influence the final outcome of the search process. We demonstrate that these methods, including metrics such as coverage-based re-scoring and sentence-level re-scoring, only subtly improve beam search's performance, leading to the question of why we should not expect that the quality would continue to improve with increasing beam size. Furthermore, we explore various stopping criteria used in beam search, ranging from fixed-length stopping, to weighted ending penalties, and hypothesis length normalization. We show that these stopping criteria are not optimized for unseen data and can unfairly impact model performance. To address these issues, we introduce several novel methods that address the pitfalls of beam search. Our novel methods make no explicit assumptions about the optimal buffersize or histogram's shapes, facilitating a truly universal application to the tasks, thereby dissolving the "beam search curse" once and for all. We implement these methods within the framework of careful hyperparameter tuning and compare its results against those of heuristic approaches often employed in the literature. Surprisingly, we observe that these novel methods far outperform more heuristically equivalent methods like length normalization by 2 BLEU points, showing a +2.0 score-point improvement over the best of the class of standard algorithms based on diverse sourced corpora.

The online news landscape is a rapidly evolving environment where information is disseminated in a multitude of forms and languages. Modern society's increasing reliance on instant access to information necessitates the development of sophisticated methods for news aggregation and analysis. However, the sheer volume of news sources is daunting, with many news outlets publishing concurrently in multiple languages. Traditional methods of group- ing news articles by manually selected keywords or related topics prove inadequate in coping with the scale and diversity of online news streams. A promising approach to addressing this challenge is through clustering, a form of unsupervised learning that groups similar items into meaningful categories based on their inherent properties and data semantics. Clustering applied to multilingual news streams offers the potential for users to engage with coherent and comprehensive stories, even when articles are written in diverse language editions of news sources. Moreover, successful clustering of streaming news enables more efficient media monitoring by integrating relevant information from various sources. Nonetheless, handling an ever-growing news stream poses unique computational challenges for clustering, since it must scale to accommodate a rapidly changing dataset with a hypothetical, but unknown in advance, number of cluster labels. Two traditional clustering algorithms - K-Medoids and Hierarchical Clustering - cannot facilely address these issues as they are designed to operate under either a finite set of cluster labels or with batch mode access to all data. To elucidate these technical problems further, traditional clustering approaches, such as K-Medoids and Hierarchical Clustering, only work in batch modes and do not scale well with infinite number of streaming documents and constantly emerging cluster labels. This paper presents a scalable method for real-time, multilingual clustering of streaming news using Probability Density Estimates. Our proposed method enables a scalable way to process large-scale updates efficiently that supports the aggregation of a story and initialization of new topics with no predefined knowledge of the cluster labels or the size of these topics. Our system leverages low- cost computation of probability density estimates to enable clustering of streaming news and starts detecting an ever emerging number of cluster labels. In the remainder of this paper, we introduce our novel method for multilingual clustering of streaming news, its computationally efficient implementation, experimental evaluation with real-world news data, and comparison against baselines. We also outline future work that seeks to boost our approach and envision potential future applications.

Word representation learning has been a crucial area of research in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Traditional word embeddings such as word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and glove (Pennington et al., 2014) are largely based on general-domain text and fail to capture the nuances of word meanings in specific domains. This is because word meanings vary significantly across domains, and words acquire different connotations in different contexts. For example, the word "bank" refers to a financial institution in the financial domain but a riverbank in the geographical domain. Despite the domain dependence of word semantics, traditional word representation learning methods are deeply rooted in a single domain. As a result, previous methods have limitations when applied to out-of-domain settings. The lack of generalizability leads to decreased performance and efficacy in downstream NLP tasks. Furthermore, the advent of specialized domains has increased the need for word representations that capture domain-specific nuances of word meanings. These challenges motivate us to explore domain-specific word representation learning methods. To overcome existing limitations, a few approaches have been proposed to learn word representations in multiple domains. However, most of these methods rely on labeled data and/or cross-lingual priming, thus involving either human effort or extra resources. These factors severely limit the feasibility and scalability of these methods in real-world applications. Therefore, it is crucial to develop unsupervised domain-specific word representation learning methods that only rely on unlabeled data in each domain. Our work addresses this gap by introducing an unsupervised domain adaptation method for learning word representations across different domains, such as financial, geographical, and social. In this paper, we describe a new method for learning domain-specific word representations that accurately capture the nuances of word meanings in a source-target domain pair. The core idea is to select a small set of pivots (high-frequency words that appear simultaneously in the two domains) to enable knowledge transfer between the domains. The major contributions of our work are: (a) we propose an objective function that leverages the co-occurrence information in each domain to enforce the predictions of co-occurring words by pivot words, (b) we introduce a constraint that encourages the word representations learned for the same pivot words in both domains to be similar, and (c) we develop a novel domain adaptation method using the learned word representations. This method has the potential to improve the generalizability of existing NLP systems on multiple domains, leading to better performance on downstream tasks such as sentiment classification, which is our major focus in this paper.

Machine translation is a challenging task that has garnered considerable interest from the natural language processing (NLP) community. A remarkable advancement in the field has been the widespread adoption and success of neural machine translation (NMT) models, which have largely eclipsed their statistical machine translation (SMT) counterparts. NMT models have achieved state-of-the-art results in several translation benchmarks, and their ability to generalize to unseen data and adapt to new language pairs has been impressive. However, despite these advances, NMT models suffer from a critical limitation: they lack explicit semantic representation and knowledge incorporation, which are essential components of human language translation and understanding. Research in linguistics and psychology has consistently demonstrated that the process of translation relies heavily on semantic and pragmatic knowledge, which includes word meaning, syntactic structure, discourse context, and domain-specific knowledge (Herskovits, 1986; Bloom et al., 2001). This knowledge is not limited to individual words or phrases but extends to the overall meaning and intent behind the message being conveyed. To bridge this gap between NMT models and the rich, semantically-heightened knowledge of human language translation, several researchers have explored incorporating external knowledge sources into NMT models. Incorporating external knowledge can help alleviate the issue of data sparsity and out-of-vocabulary words, improve cross-lingual transferability, and provide the model with access to a potentially limitless source of linguistic and domain-specific knowledge (Xing et al., 2019). One such approach is to leverage knowledge bases (KBs) and semantic space embeddings to connect the source and target languages. A KB is a structured repository of factual knowledge that can be utilized to enrich the representation of words and phrases, capture their semantic relationships, and integrate linguistic and world knowledge into the translation process. In this light, formulating a semantic space that connects source and target languages is a prime requirement to integrate the available knowledge base effectively. Mapping a source sentence into a knowledge-based semantic space can help the model to capture the concept, engender the context, thereby generating the target sentence more accurately. Furthermore, incorporating external knowledge into the translation process through the help of a knowledge base has been explored through incorporating softmax selection (Liu et al., 2018), explicit confidence estimation (Wang et al., 2020), combining the soft attention decoder with knowledge graph attention, (Guo et al., 2019), and the distribution of attention in the sequence decoder towards knowledge graph (Lin et al., 2019).

Phrases are fundamental components of language that contribute to the expressiveness and complexity of natural language. In linguistics, phrases have been studied extensively as a means to describe and analyze the way people think and communicate(Sag et al., 2002;Villavicencio et al., 2005). For instance, understanding phrases is crucial in phraseological analysis and idiom study, and related tasks such as text cohesion and coherence (Halliday and Hasan, 1976;Webber, 1988). Meanwhile, phrases are useful in many applications of natural language processing (NLP), including machine translation, question answering, and sentiment analysis, where the identification and manipulation of phrases can help applications better understand context (Kordjamshidi et al., 2014;Schwartz et al., 2013). However, with the current dominating framework of neural machine translation (NMT) that relies on word-based processing (Bahdanau et al., 2015;Vaswani et al., 2017;Luong et al., 2016;Sutskever et al., 2014), phrases still remain an underutilized resource in NMT, preventing the system from fully leveraging the linguistic information in phrases. A major obstacle to integrating phrases in NMT is its word-based processing: sentences are read and generated word by word, potentially resulting in discontiguous and inefficient phrase translation (Galley, 2006). In this work, we propose a novel NMT architecture by adding a phrase memory into the traditional encoder-decoder structure ( §3), with the aim of leveraging the power of phrases in high-level language representations. We also outline how to dynamically updates the phrase memory using an outside phrase-based statistical machine translation(SMT) system(Sennrich et al., 2016). Our testing results ( §5) demonstrate the significant improvements the proposed model achieves over the baseline on Chinese→English translation tasks. We further analyze and compare the performance of the proposed model in different test scenarios, thereby drawing conclusive evidence that the integration of phrases indeed leads to better translation results. In summary, the unique aspects of our work include the integration of phrase remembering ability into the NMT architecture and the use of an SMT model to dynamically generate phrase target phrases. By targeting both the quantity and quality of phrases, we ultimately provide several major improvements that current word-based NMT models suffer from. By encouraging the direct translation of phrases, this paper fills a gap in high-level linguistic processing in the existing NMT. By collaborating phrase translation with contextual information provided by NMT our model combines the strengths of both NMT and SMT, generating better translations that both have clearness and fluency. The proposed model is tested on the Chinese→English translation test sets and the related improvements prove the recurrent tangible benefit of harnessing phrase memory and helping discover an easier direction in noisy-sparse-high interdependence problems for English and Chinese base

Broad-coverage annotated treebanks remain a scarce resource for many languages, regardless of their relevance to the local culture and society, or their significance in terms of linguistic diversity and importance (Kirchner et al., 2017;Gorn et al., 2009;Murray and May 2001). For instance, Bulgarian has an estimated group of native speakers of about 6-8 million people (Numbers and percentages of population by ethnic category, age group and sex) and has a literary tradition dating back to the 9th century; however, compared to English, annotated Bulgarian data is very limited (Kambanov et al., 2015). Similarly, Spanish is the official language of 20 countries and is spoken by nearly 460 million people (Ethnologue); however, the availability of an annotated Spanish treebank with broad coverage is not ideal by comparison to English (McDonald et al., 2009). One possible solution to this problem is to induce dependency grammars for resource-poor languages from more abundant resources. With the advent of large-scale multilingual parallel text datasets such as Europarl (Koehn, 2008) and the availability of accurate high-coverage English parsers, various grammar induction methods based on transfer learning have been proposed to exploit these resources. Examples include morphological induction (Krakovsky et al., 2011), lexicalized tree projection rules (Vallin et al., 2009), and direct projection from English to the target language (Artzi et al., 2012). However, existing transfer-based methods often assume that there are high-coverage projected parses available for the target language. Unfortunately, generating fully-parsed projections from a source language can be challenging, especially when the source and target languages have distinct ontologies (Gulordava et al., 2012) or when dealing with low-coverage parallel corpora (Roger et al., 2010). Furthermore, an even bigger limitation of current approaches is that they often treat grammar induction as a discriminative problem (Al-Onaizan et al., 2000), focusing on inducing the appropriate tree for each sentence, without considering its native language specification (Löser et al., 2017). This can lead to sub-optimal target grammar fits due to a lack of understanding of the local tree patterns. Unlike previous approaches, our current work tackles these challenges by proposing dependency grammar induction methods that rely on Bitext Projection Constraints based on word-level alignments (Enguehard et al., 2013), where a source language parser (English) constrains the space of distributions over trees for the target language (Voll and Shute, 2015)}}. Our approach does not require full projected parses, allowing partial, approximate transfer through linear expectation constraints.

Argumentation is a pervasive aspect of human communication, playing a crucial role in various aspects of our lives, including politics, education, and daily conversations. Convincing arguments are those that effectively persuade the audience, leaving a lasting impact on their perspective. However, what makes an argument convincing remains a complex and multifaceted question. Despite extensive research in computer science and linguistics, there is still a lack of understanding regarding the attributes of convincingness in arguments. The sophisticated process of creating convincing arguments is often attributed to various factors, including the argument's quality, the persuasiveness of its presentation, and the audience's prior knowledge. Furthermore, the ever-evolving nature of human behavior and opinion, particularly in online platforms, demands a more nuanced understanding of the mechanisms behind argumentation. The role of emotion, logic, and narrative in persuasion has been extensively studied in the field of rhetoric, but the impact of these factors is often evaluated in a qualitative and subjective manner. Recent years have witnessed a surge in online argumentation, with social media platforms and online forums serving as breeding grounds for debates, discussions, and exchanges of information. The sheer volume and diversity of online arguments pose an enormous challenge to those seeking to analyze, classify, or predict their effectiveness. This problem has become even more pronounced with the rise of Web 2.0, which has enabled rapid creation, dissemination, and consumption of user-generated content. In this context, evaluating the convincingness of Web arguments is paramount for resolving online conflicts, improving public discourse, and maintaining social order. However, current approaches to argumentation analysis are largely falling short, often relying on coarse-grained evaluations or computationally expensive methods. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces a novel corpus and framework for the empirical analysis of convincingness in Web argumentation. Our approach focuses on analyzing the statements produced by explainers who assess pairs of arguments on the same topic. These explainers provide evaluative comments regarding which argument is more convincing, typically citing reasons such as the presence of evidence, the persuasiveness of language, or the fallibility of reasoning. By gathering 9,111 argument pairs, each accompanied by a rich set of annotations describing the convincingness of each argument, we establish a comprehensive evaluation framework to assess the attributes of convincingness. Our release of this novel dataset, known as UKPConvArg2, provides a valuable resource for researchers, whose accessible software and permissive license invites the exploration of various machine learning methods and techniques.

Sequential processing models, such as neural sequence-to-sequence models, have become ubiquitous in natural language processing, with applications that range from machine translation and question answering to speech and text generation. One common trait of these models is that their input representation is often determined by some higher-level system, which may be itself a product of other sequential processing systems. Examples of these upstream systems include part-of-speech taggers, named entity recognizers, word segmenters, and speech recognizers. In order to achieve their high accuracy rates, these upstream systems typically work within a deterministic setting, i.e., processes and representations are based on single and data independent steps. However, the accuracy of these systems is never one hundred percent. Depending on the chosen implementation and the specifics of the domain at hand, their error rates can be significant, an effect that leads to substantial consequences for the subsequent processing by downstream systems. This trend of sequential error propagation and build-up results in cascaded drops in performance for down-stream models, culminating in, typically, poor results delivered by hypothetical "artificially perfect" sequence-tosequence models at the end of the processing chain. An effective way to take into account these uncertainty relevant possibilities and their probability distributions is by incorporating them into the model's inputs, which would effectively facilitate and serve certain interpretation improvements, mainly through considering the different sentences as uncertain parses. To that end, this has led to the growing practice of dealing with uncertain expressions seen, and ascertained, through word lattices. Specifically, word lattices are compact symbolic data structures used to provide alternative parses or tag sequences and their corresponding probabilities. The goal here is not only to account but also to minimize the impact of these errors on downstream models. We therefore consider how upstream models can represent and explicitly propagate uncertainty in their output to downstream models. To address these challenges, this paper develops a new family of the encoder-decoders LatticeLSTM architecture which offers several advantages over an encoder-decoder that only receives the 1-best sequence or no information other than the lattice. The main motivation runs as follows. TreeLSTM models adapt child-sum and internal-state gates for node computations, originating from its native tree-structured representations. We leverage these static architecture to our favour and envision a future of more drastic exchange between the 'type' and quantity of data used to build the internal state of a LatticeLSTM.

Variability or intra-class heterogeneity is known to cause a common issue in many computer vision and natural language processing applications such as topic classification, sentiment analysis and action recognition, where extracting consistent features that distinguish related classes remains a crucial problem (Chapelle et al., 2010). Specifically, topic classification is a particularly challenging task, as the group of intra-topic documents exhibits substantial variability, making related topics harder to distinguish (Arampatzis et al., 2005) (Zhang et al., 2012). There are several reasons contributing to such intra-topic variability: (1) varying linguistic features exhibited by documents written in different styles, such as varying vocabulary usage or syntax (Rifkin and Klautau, 2004); (2) diverse content within a single topic, resulting from a range of viewpoints or different meanings (Larkey, 2002); and (3) semantic relationships and entities in the topic causing a deviation from ideal category boundaries (Cореn cambio weekly, 2016), to name a few. Variances from these factors may be captured by more representative, lower-dimensional feature spaces. Consequently, the current state of art in handling intra-topic variability often heavily relies upon robust feature extraction methods like n-gram, TF-IDF, and word embeddings. Examples of such work can be found in (Titov and McDonald, 2008) and (Gottesman Thompson et al., 2014). As with most machine learning algorithms, the final quality of results heavily depends upon whether the quality of the feature extraction method used is satisfactory or not, such as in (Singhal, 2001) (Zhang et al., 2013). However, such methods almost exclusively make use of data-dependent initialization and often rely upon heavy hyperparameter tuning to form a reliable set of feature measures. Furthermore, intra-topic heterogeneity could also arise from available data distribution properties. No matter which strategy we choose, an accurate selection from histogram distributions becomes critical. Some example strategies include subsets of documents, vocabulary selection (Alon et al., 1999) (Zhang et al., 2013). But why not make use of native orthogonal selection ability free from data dependencies. In the following sections, we will present how to enable native dominant direction fits free from both the quantity of data used and native coefficient threshold which several major intra-class variability minimization methods desperately require. We describe an algorithm that is inherently class-ignorant, i.e. inherently not dependent on the availability of either permutations or data size, yet could remarkably well select dominant directions regardless of our choice distributions. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets validate the effectiveness of our proposed intra-class variability minimization algorithm based on linear projection method, as well as how our unique method outperforms related techniques that scale to large datasets.

Language modeling is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), with a wide range of applications in machine translation (Sutskever et al., 2014), speech recognition (Hinton et al., 2012), and text generation (Rumelhart et al., 1986). A language model (LM) is a statistical model that calculates the probabilities over a sequence of words or other discrete symbols (Papineni et al., 2002), which enables it to predict the likelihood of certain words following others in a sentence. The demand for accurate language models has driven the development of various modeling paradigms in the past few decades. Two of the major paradigms for language modeling are count-based n-gram models and neural LMs. The count-based n-gram model, which relies on estimating the probabilities of a given word by counting its occurrences in the training data, is well-known due to its advantages of scalability and test-time speed (Cestnik, 1990). One key reason for this is that countbased models can be computed independently at any time, resulting in faster prediction performance at test time. The count-based approach, however, typically fails to capture more complex linguistic patterns, leading to limited modeling performance. On the contrary, neural LMs have demonstrated impressive performance by considering the entire sequence as input, as opposed to a fixed-sized window (Bengio et al., 2003). Models such as RNNs and its variants (Hochreiter et al., 2001), have enabled the language model to effectively capture long-range dependencies in the text. However, neural LMs typically require a large amount of memory and computational resources to train, which can be challenging to implement on a larger scale and often suffers from slow test-time speed. While either countbased or neural language models have their respective merits, they also have their own drawbacks. The trade-off between scalability and accuracy has long been an issue in the realm of language modeling. Some research have attempted to bridge the gap by using techniques such as caching trained n-gram models (Antάλι and Algoet, 2011) or using word embeddings as n-gram features (Danescu et al., 2011). In this work, we introduce a novel unifying framework combining the desirable features of count-based and neural language models. This framework, which we term as hybridized language model, uses a set of probability distributions over the vocabulary of words, sourced from count-based n-gram models, and dynamically calculates mixture weights over these distributions using neural networks.

Word segmentation is a critical preprocessing step for many Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications, including statistical machine translation (SMT). In languages without explicit word delimiters, such as Chinese, Indian languages, and many others, word segmentation schemes are often handcrafted and require careful design to ensure that they accurately capture the linguistic nuances of the language in question. As a result, the majority of the corpora used for SMT purposes are annotated using these segmenters. However, little attention has been paid to whether the word segmentation schemes used for annotated corpora are suitable for SMT purposes. Word alignment (WA) is a particularly data-hungry SMT task (Galley et al., 2004), and one previous analysis (Chen et al., 2019) suggested that not all WS schemes are similar to those of WA with respect to small clause segments by exhibiting poor alignment performance. Consequently, the hypothesis of this paper was that handcrafted word segmentation (WS) schemes for general purposes are not suitable for SMT purposes in Chinese, a language in which word segmentation is essential for any machine translation (MT) approach. Inspired by a conjecture that an image may resemble relevant language phenomena, the other segmenter accompanies humans modifying the exhibited disorder described by Chen et al., (2019), some cross-lingual elucidations were discussed. We solved the conflicts in the mentioned set by examining which part of the sentence caused trouble. In this paper, we formulate a new WS task as a word splitting task with reference to manually annotated WAs. We use a manually annotated word alignment (WA) corpus for Chinese-English SMT to refine the WS. This enables us to generate WS schemes that capture the linguistic nuances of the specific SMT task and demonstrate its practical benefits in inducing WS schemes suitable for related tasks like Chinese-English MT. We evaluate our WS-SMT-aided MT using various automatic assessment metrics and determine BLEU scores measuring translation quality. Experimental results show that the refined WS indeed exhibits improved word alignment performance and, thereby enhances the quality of the trained SMT model. In particular, our approach addresses a long-standing limitation of many SMT systems, as they are often trained on corpora whose word segmentation schemes were designed for general NLP purposes. Our results demonstrate that this can lead to suboptimal word alignment performance, and, in several cases, word segmentation conflicts. By refining the word segmentation schemes based on the word alignments, we can mitigate these issues and improve the overall SMT performance.

Modelling Sequential Text with an Adaptive Topic Model Topic models have become widely adopted in natural language processing for text analysis tasks, largely due to their ability to capture latent semantic meaning from text data. Among these models, probabilistic latent semantic analysis (pLSA) is a fundamental model that represents text documents as mixture distributions over a shared set of topics (Hofmann, 1999). However, many topic models fail to capture the sequential dependency in text data, a limitation which has motivated the development of models such as the hierarchical topic model (Griffiths et al., 2005) and the dynamic topic model (Blei et al., 2006). Recently, topic adaptation techniques have been proposed to further improve the performance of topic models, which learn topics from one document and apply the knowledge to similar topics in other documents with the aim of learning more general, robust topics (Xu et al., 2010). Nevertheless, these models do not take into account the sequential structure of text, which is commonly found in many types of text such as blogs, e-mails, and books. In this paper, we present an adaptive topic model, referred to as the Adaptive Topic Model (ATM), which is designed to model sequential text while incorporating the advantages of topic adaptation. For certain types of text, the ATM is capable of identifying topics from both the previous segment and the parent document. In this way, the ATM can capture sequential dependencies and learn more coherent topics from the entire document. Our contribution in this paper is threefold: first, by proposing a novel adaptive topic model that combines topic adaptation with sequential text modelling; second, by developing a Gibbs sampler for posterior inference of the ATM; and third, by demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed model through experimental results on sequential text data. Specifically, in this paper, we use the task of modelling the novels of Herman Melville as the primary evaluation task for the ATM. In particular, we investigate whether the ATM can capture the sequential structure of the novel, by adapting topics from both the previous paragraph and the entire novel. Furthermore, we compare the performance of the ATM to a range of alternative models, including static topic models, topic adaptation models, and previous models designed specifically for sequential text modelling. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: we begin by describing the ATM in Section 2, which includes a discussion of the Gibbs sampler and how the model is trained.

Demographic lexica, a collection of words associated with specific demographics such as age and gender, have been gaining attention in recent years due to their vast potential applications in various fields, including social science, economics, and business. These applications range from targeted marketing and advertising to informing public health policies and improving the quality of demographic research. Despite their potential, however, demographic lexica are not yet entirely reliable or widely used, mainly because predicting demographic characteristics using words is an inherently complex task. A key challenge is that the associations between certain words and demographics are not always explicit or straightforward; age and gender labels are not always exhibited through use of stereotypical terms, and the unintended consequences of using such labels to describe users can impede the reliability of a demographic lexica. One approach to addressing these challenges is through the use of machine learning models that identify and weight words predictive of age and gender through the use of extensive datasets with associated demographic labels. Such datasets are increasingly becoming available in the era of social media. Our work, which sets out to create highly accurate age and gender predictive lexica through the use of regression and classification models, reveals the potential of leveraging these models to predict age and gender using relevant language from Facebook, blog, and Twitter. We used extensive training data, which consists of word usage in certain context with associated demographic labels, which our classification models used to identify and weight words that are predictive of age and gender. The results showed remarkable accuracy with which our demographic lexica could predict age and gender, while providing results quickly and efficiently that are although successful extremely valuable. Moreover, they achieved state-of-the-art accuracy in terms age and gender prediction for language based inputs. While there is still scope for further development, the generalization capabilities of our lexica in multiple social media settings is improved across genres such as blog-retweets statements, and micrograbs. Our predictive lexica demonstrate a versatile tool for understanding various predictors that enable researchers and developers alike to integrate age and gender criteria from language into highly critical social media research projects. In the near future, for instance, banks are likely to use demographic lexica to more accurately profile their customer bases. In a similar vein, corporations looking to tailor their advertising campaigns to specific demographics can also leverage the power of these predictive lexica to maximize their impact.

Zero-shot learning has revolutionized the way we approach complex classification tasks by allowing models to generalize to unseen classes with no explicit supervision. This breakthrough is largely attributed to the seminal work of Lampert et al. (2009), which introduced the idea of combining a general feature extractor with a cross-space mapping (CSM) function to project an input representation from its original feature space to a larger, related space where target classes are already labeled. This transformation enables models to transfer knowledge across different domains and achieve impressive gains in various applications, including image captioning (Karpathy et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2014), object recognition (Frome et al., 2013), and natural language processing (Lu et al., 2013). In essence, zero-shot learning relies on a CSM function that maps vectors between two disparate spaces: the source feature space and the target semantic space, where entities of interest are annotated with categorical labels. The ability to accurately project features into the target space is crucial for achieving good generalization performance, as misaligned mappings can lead to suboptimal recognition, reporting pseudo-labeled targets that mislead downstream tasks. While CSM methods have been explored extensively in recent years (xian et al., 2020; Vinyals et al., 2016; Kumar et al., 2013), their performance in practical applications has been limited. Recognizing this challenge, we delve deeper into the theoretical underpinnings of CSM and investigate the intrinsic issues associated with current implementations. Our investigation centers around two key limitations: hubness, which arises from the tendency of certain vectors to have many high-scoring neighbors in the target space, and pollution, which can occur due to contamination by noisy or irrelevant targets. Hubness amplifies the inherent difficulties in learning an accurate CSM, as vectors harboring a multitude of neighbors simultaneously becomes prone to misleading associations. Pollution further exacerbates this problem by introducing an additional noise factor that often skews the semantic space, engendering inaccurate predictions. To address these issues, we develop novel strategies that improve CSM adaptability, positional stability, and resilience to pollution. Specifically, our approach utilizes a hybrid adaptation method that strikes a balance between mapping sources and target similarities. This strategy empowers our CSM model to accurately transfer semantic meaning while minimizing risks caused by hubness and pollution. Our contributions go beyond improving the existing CSM method; we establish a new class of techniques that assess and quantify hubness and pollution, through in-depth experimentation and permutations of data size, embedding spaces, and different models to identify both our strengths and areas requiring elucidation.

Multi-document summarization is a crucial task in information retrieval and extraction applications, where given a set of related documents and a specific query, it aims to automatically synthesize a natural-language summary that best represents the contents of the documents in relation to the query. While general-purpose summarization has made significant strides in recent years, query-focused summarization is particularly important in real-world applications where users are often interested in obtaining the most relevant and concise information related to a specific topic or query. In order to achieve this goal, various techniques have been proposed, ranging from salience-based metrics to machine learning models and even deep learning architectures. However, most of these methods face the challenge of effectively capturing the nuances of relational information across multiple documents and identifying which parts of the text are most relevant to the query. Traditional query-focused multi-document summarization (QFMS) methods are based on ranking the key sentences or phrases that best match the query in the context of the documents. For instance, the MMR (Maximum Marginal Relevance) algorithm (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998) has been widely adopted to compute the relevancy of a sentence in the context of the query and the relevant documents. However, ranking heavy sentences can notwithstanding be useless for QFMS as a condensed version is needed and most compressed sentences represent very high-level surface sentences as factual sentences stating their high-level facts. Thereby is the need for employing sentence compression to reduce redundancy, and as such, convey high-level facts first. Our contribution in this paper addresses the challenging task of query-focused multi-document summarization by leveraging the power of sentence compression techniques. The goal here is not only to succinctly capture the main ideas but also to improve the overall quality and conciseness of the generated summaries. To this end, we develop an innovative sentence-compression-based framework that utilizes learning-based compression models to effectively condense the most relevant information related to the query. Building on top of parse tree structures, we propose a series of compression models that score the probability of the likelihood of compressions being true. An innovative beam search decoder is proposed to efficiently find highly probable compressions. In addition, we explore the integration of various indicative metrics, including linguistic motivation and query relevance, to inform the compression process through a novel formulation of a compression scoring function.

The correction of preposition errors is a crucial task in the realm of natural language processing, as it directly impacts the expressiveness, coherence, and overall quality of written and spoken language. Despite the intuitive nature of preposition use, determining the correct prepositional complement is often challenging, even for human experts. Existing methods for training preposition error correction systems have incorporated a variety of approaches, including utilizing well-edited text and error-annotated corpora. These approaches have demonstrated promising results in certain contexts, but there remains a pressing need to develop more robust systems capable of handling the complexity and variability inherent to real-world language use. One notable limitation of current methods lies in their limited ability to generalize across disparate test sets. In particular, systems trained on well-edited text often struggle to adapt to error-annotated corpora, and vice versa. The performance discrepancies between different test sets have been exacerbated by the lack of comprehensive, annotated corpora specifically designed to capture the full range of preposition errors. This circumstance has been further complicated by the hypothetical "artificiality" inherent to existing corpora, such as artificial, constructed texts crafted with the express purpose of duplicating highly frequent error patterns. These artificial, constructed texts are designed specifically for the sole purpose of testing systems. Furthermore, contemporary approaches to preposition error correction often neglect the fact that language is constantly evolving. As a result, the annotations may not accurately reflect real-world usage, particularly with regards to newly adopted terminology or high-circumstance specifics of expressions whose norms constantly fluctuate although usage extremely rarely exposes any anomalies. In this paper, we propose mitigating these limitations by leveraging a novel corpus of preposition error corrections, extracted from the revisions of Wikipedia articles that contain the corrections rather than just the final and often egregious forms maintained in the others. Specifically, our corpora contains revisions of over 100,000 publications, the changes of prepositions over 2.8 million times and the altered forms made to relatively normal accessible references. In recognizing that Wikipedia engenders the dynamic, constantly evolving landscape of linguistic expression, we demonstrate that our corpus offers several key advantages, including a vast increase in scale, diversity, and representativeness, as well as higher quality annotations that faithfully capture real-world usage. Ultimately, by adopting this novel approach, we seek to develop more robust systems capable of handling the complexities and variability inherent to preposition error correction, and thus improve the overall quality of language processing applications.

The field of Machine Translation (MT) has experienced tremendous progress in recent years, largely driven by the advent of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) systems. NMT models, based on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) or Transformers, have proven to be highly effective in generating high-quality translations directly from source language sequences to target language sequences, with minimal need for feature engineering and multi-technique combination that characterizes traditional Machine Translation systems (Klein et al., 2017). This shift towards end-to-end learning architectures has revolutionized the way MT systems are built and deployed. Nevertheless, despite the significant advancements achieved by NMT models, significant research opportunities persist. One of the key challenges in implementing NMT systems is the so-called Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) problem (Schraft et al., 2013). The OOV issue arises when during the testing phase the system encounters a word or symbol not seen during the training phase. OOV words may arise from various reasons such as, translations of rare_words, rare hypothetical concepts or shift in vocabulary such as newly coined words or name of places, people, things. The inclusion of such words is highly challenging due to the memory constraints, especially for languages such as German where there is a much larger number of compound and multi-word expressions. Dealing with these compound words and expressions exacerbates the issue of managing vocabulary. There are around 15,000 words in German that only exist in combinations with other words and cannot be split into single words. For these reasons, the OOV problem is particularly concerning in German-English translation, and this is also echoed in the commonly used Machine Translation benchmarks: WMT'14 (Raw Data) First Pass Challenge that almost exclusively is populated by English and German language pair (Bojar et al., 2014). In German, these compound words add to the rarity of the words in the vocabulary, escalating the issue further. Consequently, dealing with OOV cases has long been considered a major challenge in MT research, especially when translating from German (Al-Onaizan et al., 2000). The absence of a German word in the dictionary generates an absurd translation, which can have detrimental effects on the quality of the translation as a whole. For this reason, addressing the OOV problem is a pressing requirement for implementing competitive NMT models. Despite several works addressing word-level neural machine translation, few of them have systematically examined the effects on the translation quality and based on that proposed actual solutions.

Answering Opinion Questions on Products by Exploiting Hierarchical Organization of Consumer Reviews Product reviews are increasingly becoming an essential component of the decision-making process for consumers when selecting a product to purchase. Among these reviews, consumer opinions play a crucial role in determining a product's overall quality and desirability (Kim et al., 2006; Hu & Pavlou, 2004). With the proliferation of the web and social media, the sheer volume of product reviews has increased significantly, presenting a challenge for extracting relevant information and providing accurate answers to consumer opinion questions. Typically, these questions are formulated to elicit the opinions and sentiments of consumers with regards to specific product aspects. To effectively answer these opinion questions, one must first understand the product aspects being queried, which are often implicit within the question itself. However, an explicit identification of these aspects is generally required to pinpoint the specific reviews that contain relevant information. Nonetheless, product reviews can often appear disorganized and lack a systematic structure, making it challenging for natural language processing (NLP) models to identify relevant product aspects from consumer reviews. Moreover, even if relevant information is identified, extracting pertinent opinions and sorting them by relevance remains a daunting task. In light of these challenges, various studies have used either explicit or implicit methods to identify product aspects and generate answers for opinion questions. However, most current methods rely on simplistic approaches that fail to leverage the complex relationships among product aspects. To further boost the overall efficiency and accuracy of such processes, more sophisticated approaches that take advantage of the hierarchical organization of consumer reviews are extremely desirable. In this study, we advocate for such an approach by developing a novel framework for opinion question answering that organizes the relationships between product aspects and their corresponding reviews in a hierarchical structure. The proposed framework centers on exploiting the hierarchical organization of consumer reviews to form a tri-dimensional analysis space, encompassing (i) the product aspect hierarchy, (ii) the parent-child relations among these aspects, and (iii) the relevant opinions expressed in the reviews. By leveraging this space, our framework can effectively analyze the question, automatically identify the implicitly expressed product aspects, and select the most salient opinions that are relevant to each product aspect. In order to further improve the quality of our answers, our framework employs a multi-criteria optimization approach to evaluate the retrieved opinions according to their relevance to the question, the coherence among several opinions, diversity of referenced opinions, and relationships among the answer aspects.

The online news landscape is a rapidly growing entity where readers increasingly rely on single-document summaries to help them navigate complex narratives and make informed decisions. However, manually constructing news summaries remains a daunting task that is time-consuming and requires extensive domain knowledge. The advent of artificial intelligence has sparked research into automating news summary generation, particularly focusing on news highlight extraction, where the goal is to condense a long news article into a concise and informative summary consisting of 3-4 highlight sentences. Despite the advances in natural language processing and deep learning, automatic news highlight extraction remains a challenging task due to the vast and varying nature of news topics and data. Research in summarization has relied on conventional approaches such as TextRank, Latent Semantic Analysis, and Principal Component Analysis to capture key information from news articles and extract highlights. However, these methods tend to suffer from generalization issues, rely heavily on the quality of the input data, and often result in low-quality summaries. In this study, we investigate the feasibility of leveraging microblogs to improve automatic news highlights extraction. We propose a novel approach that combines the strengths of traditional summarization methods with the power of social media data. The underlying hypothesis is that microblog posts, often considered as noisy due to their limited length and disorderly nature, hold valuable information and serve as inherently compressed, key fragments of narratives. Specifically, we hypothesize that microblogs can help identify and extract key pieces of information from news articles that capture the essence of the article's content. Our approach revolves around the following methodology: given a news article, we formulate the problem as a rank-then-extract task in two stages. First, we identify a set of indicative tweets through our pairing corpus, which serves as an assistant to the ranking of news sentences for extraction. Our key idea is to leverage microblog-retained statements, although micrograined, to gain a deeper understanding of the most salient aspects of the news article and support the extraction of critical information. In the second stage, we perform a threshold-based selection to identify the top-ranked tweets as substitutes for sentence extraction. This approach capitalizes on the adaptability of deep learning models to leverage both microblog and news article data simultaneously, ultimately bringing out the best from both the summarization methods and the social media landscape. Experimental results based on our meticulously crafted news-tweets pairing corpus suggest that the proposed method yields more precise and informative highlights compared with strong baselines for single-document summarization.

The quest for a universal language model that is applicable across all languages has long been an elusive goal in the field of natural language processing (NLP). The dream of creating a language-independent architecture that is equally effective for any language has been largely hindered by the inherent complexities and variations in the world's languages. Cross-lingual NLP has made significant strides in recent years, enabled by the widespread adoption of deep learning techniques and the availability of large-scale multilingual datasets. However, despite this progress, the issue of language typology remains a perplexing challenge that affects the performance of language models (LMs) across different languages. Language typology, the study of the structural properties of languages, is a crucial area of linguistics that aims to understand the diversity of human languages. The field of typology has primarily focused on identifying the unique characteristics that define a language, including its morphological, phonological, and syntactic features. A key distinction in language typology is the contrast between languages with more complex morphological systems, such as agglutinative and fusional languages, and languages with simpler systems, such as isolating languages. The classification of languages into major typological categories, such as fusional, agglutinative, and isolating languages, has a long history and remains a topic of ongoing research. Agglutinative languages, which include languages such as Turkish and Swahili, exhibit a high degree of morphological complexity, characterized by the use of suffixes and prefixes to express grammatical functions and relationships. Fusional languages, found in languages such as Latin and Russian, are known for their tendency to fuse multiple grammatical functions into single morphemes. Isolating languages, exemplified by Chinese and Vietnamese, are characterized by a relative lack of inflectional morphology, relying instead on lexical statements and word order to convey grammatical relationships. These variations in the typological profiles of languages can significantly impact the performance of LMs, particularly those trained on large-scale text data. In this paper, we aim to address this issue by conducting a large-scale study of LMs on 50 typologically diverse languages, with a focus on examining the implications of language typology on LM performance. We analyze both static and dynamic aspects of LM performance using a range of evaluation metrics, including perplexity, accuracy, and word-level prediction performance. Our study demonstrates that a coarse typology of morphological systems is predictive of absolute LM performance across languages. Image captioning, a subtask of visual content analysis, has become increasingly popular in recent years due to advances in deep learning architectures (Rennie et al., 2017; Venugopalan et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2015). The aim of this task is to automatically generate natural language descriptions that accurately group with the visual content of an image, making it ideal for use in applications such as image search (Kleinberg, 2002), image ranking (Siddiqui et al., 2012), and human-computer interaction (Owen et al., 2006). Despite delivering high performance metrics, such as perplexity and BLEU (Papineni et al., 2002), on publicly available benchmarks, contemporary image captioning models have a problem: they frequently hallucinate objects that are not actually visible in the scene. Hallucination, a well-known phenomenon in the context of machine learning (Laine and Ablin, 2017; Jaderberg et al., 2017), can compromise the reliability and effectiveness of image captioning models, leading to the inclusion of irrelevant objects, image manipulation, or biased labeling. While a great deal of work has been done in improving the robustness of image captioning systems (Das et al., 2017; Vinyals et al., 2015), little is known about the rate of object hallucination seen in such systems, the processes that lead to this outcome, and how quickly these models learn to generate descriptions of the world that contain objects that are not, in fact, present. The goal of this paper is to: (a) propose an image relevance metric that updates the standard metrics to capture image relevance in the presence of hallucinations more effectively; (b) form a better understanding of how these hallucinations arise through a careful analysis of the architecture of available image captioning models and a consideration of the ways in which language models learn object representations and object-attribute associations; (c) inform a new direction for the field of image captioning by quantitatively assessing the effectiveness of current metrics in revealing object hallucination; and (d) offer insights for model developers seeking to minimize the occurrence of these pervasive and highly misleading responses. To estimate object hallucinations more accurately and facilitate this analysis, we will need a relevance metric that is more sensitive to subjectivity and viel gist references than existing metrics. We therefore will use pre-trained visual models to get actual objects in the scene in terms of their desciaptions, only then comparing it to models generated predictions. This allows for the efficient detection of missing and hallucinated objects, such as missing or added image description, alternative possible scene structure based on language priors, as well as how those capture subjectivity.

Morphologically rich languages (MRLs) such as Arabic, Persian, German, Russian, and Turkish pose a challenge for state-of-the-art neural machine translation (NMT) systems. One major obstacle hindering NMT from achieving high quality translations for MRLs stems from the intrinsic complexity of words in these languages. Unlike languages such as English, where words typically follow a simple form-meaning structure, MRLs are characterized by complex words with hierarchical meaning- preserving subunits (Nilofer et al., 2012). In many cases, a single word can be decomposed into smaller meaningful units such as prefixes, roots, and suffixes (Qian et al., 1999), resulting in a rich set of morphological and syntactic relationships between words within and across different languages. Traditional word-based NMT models with their reliance on surface forms may not be able to capture the underlying semantic and syntactic structures often present in these complex words, undermining the quality and accuracy of automatic translations, which directly affect the efficiency and productivity of human interpreters as well as the availability of domain-specific knowledge, such as legal texts and perform language. The issue is compounded when translating relevant language pairs, such as Persian, German, Russian and Turkish into English, where a source word is often mapped to multiple words or even a complete sentence on the target side, resulting in a one-to-many translation problem. Traditional word-based models further fail to capture the variety of inter-word relationships and the internal hierarchical structures of words in MRLs (McDonald et al., 2018). In order to address such limitations in NMT systems, recent advancements have focused on: employing subword units that partition words into a fixed set of subword pieces rather than treating words as atomic units (Sennrich et al., 2016); and micro-modeling discrete word representations as the low-level input consists of characters (Roger et al., 1980 and Luong et al., 2015 and Raffel et al., 2017).This gives the encoder more information about the original text from MRLs and makes full use of the unique properties of MRLs. These advancements have gained fruitful results in capturing more word-internal relationships as well as granularity at the subword level. However, current subword and character-based models still have several limitations. Firstly, they still presume a word is broken into fixed-sized subwords or characters without direct reference to any inherent structure based on word or subword meaning, through appropriate, existing, permutations of subunits, only fixing on their occurrences.

Calibration and Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Processing In natural language processing (NLP), many machine learning models define probabilistic distributions over linguistic structures, capturing the uncertainty associated with different parsing, syntactic, or semantic structures (Chrupała et al., 2015). Model developers and users often evaluate their models based on metrics such as accuracy, precision, and mean average precision (MAP) (Chapelle et al., 2011). These metrics focus on the correctness of the model's output without drawing attention to the model's quality of estimates. However, understanding model quality and estimating uncertainty in natural language processing data is essential in many applied settings (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016). For instance, a mis-calibrated model will assign different probabilities to two events with the same empirical frequencies, misleading downstream applications with their reliance on the model's estimated posterior probabilities. Furthermore, many models rely on the estimates provided by pipeline components to aggregate information, but the impact of miscalibration on these aggregated representations remains unexplored. In contrast to model-agnostic approaches, which focus on evaluating miscalibration aggregated across different tasks (Kuleshov et al., 2018), our work gives primacy to theoretically grounding model calibration in the study of psychology to demonstrate the benefits of intrinsic, task-based calibration (Krueger et al., 2017) of NLP models. Traditional calibration methods evaluating a model's overall accuracy and its error rates do not provide enough insights into understanding the performance of these models (Guo et al., 2018). In this paper, we formalize a framework to assess and improve the calibration of probabilistic NLP models, examining when NLP uncertainty can be projected not only to pipeline components, but also be used in exploratory data analysis to form a sense of trust in these models. Our framework leverages tools from the psychology of decision-making under uncertainty (Hertwig and van Dijke, 2001) to automate model-agnostic checks for violations to the desirable calibrating property of accuracy given probability. Furthermore, we contribute a coreference sampling algorithm to create confidence intervals for tasks where uncertainty cannot be easily quantified, illustrating how our framework can be leveraged to inform exploratory analysis. Our empirical results show how different models calibrated to a set of distributions present varying patterns of miscalibration, providing insights that inform additional model training. By the end of this paper, we demonstrate how calibration can be integrated into diverse NLP pipelines and can also be leveraged in desciptive data analysis, providing actionable guidance to data analysts and scientists.

The quest to endow artificial neural networks with linguistic knowledge has a natural appeal. When a neural machine translation system learns to translate from one language to another, does it learn the syntax or semantics of the languages ? Can this knowledge be extracted from the system to complement existing linguistic research and to fill holes in human scientific knowledge?Linguistic typology, the study of linguistic structures across languages, is a domain that could benefit from advances in neural machine translation. Current typological databases contain relatively full feature specifications for only a few hundred languages, leaving thousands more without comprehensive analysis [Simpson et al., 2015]. One data-rich environment in which linguistic research can be conducted is parallel text, where a text in one language is accompanied by a translation to another language. Large archives of parallel text have been compiled, covering over 1000 languages [Cettolin et al., 2020]. In this work, we build upon these resources to design an approach for predicting features of missing languages. Our overall goal is not only to invent a hypothetical "artificial typologist '', but also to explore whether such an artificial typologist can emulate the performace of current typologists and linguistic researchers relevant for various tasks, especially for linguistic typology. In particular, we concentrate on a design to infer phonological features for all languages, as well as syntax as described by phrase structure grammar and other linguistic theories. We implement this with a massive many-to-one neural machine translation (NMT) system trained from the majority of languages in the world to English and although space constraints limit the features we can predict to the major sound classes in a phonology, and to a limited set of syntactic structures, we outline how our supervised modeling method can eventually generate predictions for a wide array of language features, unseen by linguists or typologists, both morphological and phonological. Our system leverages low-level patterns in the parallel data to learn to predict a wide range of linguistic structures. We further evaluate our system's performance over a baseline model that has access to language neighbors for the languages we are trained on (phylogenetic grandfather effect), showing that our approach is superior for many languages, adding knowledge that native speakers can use for their languages. Thus our architecture has the potential to serve both as a prediction tool that fits well with a linguistic typology data system, and as a typology-informed tool for neural machine translation.
