Machine translation is a challenging task that has garnered significant interest from the natural language processing (NLP) community. A critical component in the development and assessment of machine translation systems is their evaluation. Throughout the years, various evaluation metrics have been proposed to assess the adequacy and fluency of machine translations. Current metrics primarily rely on word-for-word comparisons between the source and target texts and do not effectively capture the nuances of text cohesion and coherence. Given that texts do not consist of isolated words but are composed of sentences that convey a certain meaning, using techniques that capture text relationships could help improve evaluation processes. The meaning and interpretation of a sentence depend not only on the individual words but also on how the sentences are organized. Discourse structure is a field of study that focuses on the description of language in terms of the organization and ordering of units of text with respect to their relationships and their roles in the larger discourse, that is, text entities in which the cohesively connected sentences are grouped with one another into more complex, abstract constructions of more kinds. Discourse theory (Grosz and Sidner, 1986, Reinhart, 1983, Wilson, 1990) assumes that the relationships, especially pragmatic, between discourse units characterize text worlds and, hence, text semantics. For certain interpretation purposes, only very general narratives functions were discussed. We will deepen our treatment, covering also complex composition readings of the recipients' involvement in the interpretation, and, with the prerequisite assumption of discourse completion, differen-tiated solutions by Ishibashi (1992) concerning question-answer functions. Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) (Mann and Thompson, 1987) also provides a well-organized method that distinguishes between a nucleus, the main idea of a sentence, and satellites, supporting sentences, both of which explain, contrast, or prove a point. Moreover, RST classifies the relationships between these units in 22 ways (Mann and Schwartz, 1996, Vincze et al., 2004), enabling the extraction of relevant information about causal/temporal relationships, and adversary/supportive relationships. This study is interested in understanding the role discourse information can play in machine translation evaluation. Specifically, this work aims to investigate whether using discourse structure improves the ability of current evaluation metrics to accurately predict human judgments of translation quality. Our hypothesis is that a greater understanding of the relationships between the components of a sentence leads to more accurate translation quality assessments. In this work, we take the approach of incorporating existing evaluation metrics into a framework that accounts for the organization and ordering of sentences.

The Web has revolutionized the way we create content, find information, and share knowledge. Web documents, with their extensive networking and multiple sources of information, have become the essential element of the digital world. With millions of web pages being created every day, it has become increasingly difficult for users to find the most relevant information on any given topic. Anchor texts in hyperlinks have traditionally played a crucial role in guiding the users' search for relevant content on the Web. Anchor texts provide brief summaries or contexts to describe what the linked content is about, thereby helping users make informed decisions about which links are likely to contain the most relevant and useful information. The creation of high-quality anchor texts is a challenging task, especially for users who are not experienced in content creation and anchor text optimization. While human annotators can create relevant and effective anchor texts, this process is time-consuming, expensive, and requires domain expertise. Consequently, there is an increasing need for automatic methods to create high-quality anchor texts. Various studies have proposed approaches to create anchor texts automatically using different machine learning and natural language processing (NLP) techniques (Fuhry Et Al. 2012) (Zhu and Zhang, 2018). Although these studies have presented theoretically promising methods for anchor text creation, these approaches face significant challenges. The quality of the created anchor texts depends on various factors, including the choice of keywords, keyword extraction methods, and relevance of the extracted expressions to the anchor-related documents. Furthermore, anchor text completion requires sophisticated contextual understanding of document content and the semantics of the anchor-related document. As a response to the need for better anchor text generation, this paper presents a novel approach to automatic creation of anchor texts for hyperlinks in documents that point to similar documents. Our method combines techniques from information retrieval (IR) and NLP, both of which have been extensively used in text summarization, keyphrase extraction, and relatedness assessment tasks. Building on recent advances in IR and NLP, we propose and evaluate several different score functions to rank parts of a document for the creation of anchor texts. Furthermore, we manually evaluate these adaptively generated anchor texts in terms of relatedness to linked documents and compare them to baseline methods consisting of originally inserted anchor texts. Using crowdsourcing for evaluating both original anchors and our generated anchors enables more reliable and scalable evaluation of the generated anchor texts.

Relation extraction is a critical task in natural language processing (NLP), with applications in information extraction, question answering, and text summarization, among others. It typically involves identifying instances of specific relationships between entities mentioned in a text, such as "John is a friend of Mary." Despite the significant advances in NLP over the past few decades, relation extraction remains a challenging task due to its reliance on limited, domain-specific training data and manual annotation. Current models of relation extraction rely heavily on supervised learning, where the goal is to learn a model from a small set of hand-labeled examples. While effective in domains such as named entity recognition (NER), sentiment analysis, and question answering, supervised learning is limited by its dependence on labeled data, which is often scarce, noisy, or domain-specific (Gladkova et al., 2019). For instance, the ACE (Automatic Content Extraction) system, a state-of-the-art relation extraction system, relies on a domain-specific corpus with labeled data, which is difficult to create and maintain (Doddington et al., 2004). In this context, an alternative paradigm to supervised learning is to train relation extraction models without labeled data, leveraging the abundance of unlabeled text data and large knowledge bases. This approach, known as distant supervision (Craven et al., 2000), aims to reduce the reliance on hand-labeled data and has been explored in various NLP tasks, such as text classification and sentiment analysis (Ritter et al., 2010; Mitchell et al., 2011). However, distant supervision for relation extraction has only recently gained attention, with a focus on leveraging large semantic databases, such as Freebase (Bollacker et al., 2008), to provide distant supervision signals. Freebase is a large-scale semantic database that contains statements about entities and their relationships. With over 10 million entities and 200 million statements, Freebase has become a crucial resource for NLP tasks, including relation extraction. In this paper, we propose to leverage Freebase as a knowledge base to provide distant supervision for relation extraction, allowing us to train models without the need for hand-labeled data. Our approach combines the advantages of supervised IE, leveraging the rich semantic information in Freebase, with the scalability of unsupervised IE, which can handle large volumes of unstructured text data. By experimenting with a large corpus of unlabeled text and the Freebase database, we demonstrate the efficacy of our distant supervision approach for relation extraction, outperforming traditional supervised models in terms of scalability and generalizability.

Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a central task in natural language processing (NLP), which consists of automatically translating written text from one language to another. SMT involves several key components including lexical translation models, phrase translation models, and alignment models. These components are used to transform source language (SL) input into a target language (TL) output that preserves the meaning and content of the original sentence. One key aspect of SMT is handling non-contiguous phrases in the source language, which pose significant challenges to machine translation systems. Non-contiguous phrases refer to phrases where words are spread over separate clauses or sentences and may be separated by many other words (Galley et al., 2004), or where there is a gap between the words of a specific syntactic category in a phrase (Fujita et al., 2017) or are multi-clausal expressions with the clauses scattered across the sentence and not in the same co-ordinated or subordinated syntactic structure (Marshman et al., 2013). Traditional phrase-based statistical machine translation models handle non-contiguous phrases using various syntactic reordering techniques (Li et al., 2009;Zhu et al., 2010). However, notwithstanding these efforts, non-contiguous phrases have been shown to cause certain problems for these reordering techniques (Krishnamurthy, 2011), such as reordering ambiguities and difficult-to-model asymmetry between source and target language (Zhu et al., 2010). More recently, there has been work on models based on syntactic structure (Galley et al., 2004;Galley and Manning, 2008;Gormley et al., 2013;Fujita et al., 2017), which consider the syntactic tree structure of both source and target language sentences. These tree sequence-SMT models were found to handle various types of non-contiguous phrases effectively and consistently outperform more traditional models that ignore the syntactic structure (Becker et al., 2019;Al-Onaizan et al., 2009), such as positional phrase-based SMT. One key strength of tree-based models is that they are grounded on the static syntactic constituent structure and can therefore generate more accurate phrase-to-phrase alignments between syntactically equivalent constituents in the source and target languages (Li et al., 2009). However, most tree sequence-based translation models currently developed (Becker et al., 2019;Al-Onaizan et al., 2009;Galley et al., 2004) do not sufficiently account for non-contiguous phrases with very large span due to the demand that all members of a contiguous subtree must be flat and directly embedded in the same parent tree structure. We mitigate these limitations by introducing a novel non-contiguous tree sequence-based model for statistical machine translation.

Document-level sentiment classification is a crucial task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), which involves determining the sentiment of a given document or text, such as positive, negative, or neutral. As the amount of text data available online continues to grow exponentially, automatically analyzing and categorizing sentiment has become increasingly important in many applications, including customer service, marketing, and recommendation systems. With the advent of deep learning techniques, neural networks have achieved remarkable success in sentiment analysis tasks, including sentiment classification. A key contributor to their success is their ability to alleviate the need for manual feature engineering, which can be a time-consuming and labor-intensive process for traditional machine learning models. However, document-level sentiment classification remains a particularly challenging task for neural networks, especially when dealing with long and complex texts. One of the primary limitations is the recurrent architecture's reliance on memory units to capture contextual information. The traditional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) units have a short-term memory, which, although sufficient for modeling shorter texts, can lose important context as the sequence length increases. This issue is further exacerbated in document-level sentiment classification, where we need to capture the overall semantic information and sentiment trends across the entire document, often involving multiple paragraphs and sentences. To address this problem, we propose a novel architecture, Cached Long Short-Term Memory (CLSTM) neural networks, designed specifically for document-level sentiment classification. Our approach revolves around introducing a caching mechanism to the traditional LSTM architecture. By dividing the memory into several groups with different forgetting rates, the CLSTM neural network effectively enables the network to retain sentiment information better within a recurrent unit. This caching mechanism allows the network to adaptively store and retrieve relevant context, alleviating the issues associated with the traditional memory units. The CLSTM architecture consists of two primary components: the micro-memory and the macro-memory. The micro-memory corresponds to the traditional LSTM/recurrent architecture and captures short-term context. In contrast, the macro-memory represents the caching mechanism, which captures long-term context and stores information for extended periods. The key idea behind this design is to leverage the effectiveness of both the micro-memory and macro-memory, allowing the network to simultaneously model both short-term and long-term dependencies. By doing so, the CLSTM neural network is better equipped to handle the complexities and nuances of long texts, making it particularly suitable for document-level sentiment classification tasks.

Visual semantic role labeling (vSRL) is an increasingly important task in the computer vision and natural language processing communities. It involves identifying the participants in an action or event depicted in an image and labeling them with their semantic relation to the event or action. While recent work in this field has achieved remarkable results, most approaches rely on prohibitive amounts of manually annotated data and, in many cases, are limited to specific scenarios or objects of interest. In this paper, we address the challenges of this task and propose an approach to vSRL that leverages noisy data automatically extracted from image captions. By utilizing linguistic semantic role labeling (L-SRL) systems to analyze image captions, we construct a large amount of noisy, yet still informative, labels for the participants in action scenes depicted in images. Our key insight is that these noisy labels can be leveraged to train a vSRL model that learns to associate semantic roles with the corresponding image regions of objects. We represent image regions of interest as vector space embeddings, which we train using a deep neural network architecture that combines elements of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). This combination allows our model to learn spatial relationships between objects in images and their corresponding semantic roles. Moreover, our approach does not rely on frame- semantic annotations for the training data, but can learn the frame semantics from the noisy data extracted from image captions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in experiments with the Visual Genome dataset, which consists of over 1 million images annotated with over 10 million object instances and their labels. We find that our vSRL model achieves significantly better results than previous state-of-the-art models, especially when evaluated on out-of-domain test data. Our comparison to the previous work on supervised visual verb sense disambiguation (VVD) further supports the robustness of our approach. Moreover, we observe that our model can automatically generate a visual representation of the spatial relationships between entities in actions, and induce new frames that have not been annotated in the training data. Overall, our work provides a viable solution to the problem of visual semantic role labeling with limited annotated data, and highlights the potential of leveraging noisy data for training computer vision models. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we review related work in the field of vSRL, image captioning, and linguistic semantic role labeling.

Semantic parsing is the task of mapping natural language to unambiguous, machine-interpretable meaning representations, such as first-order logic or lambda calculus. Considerable progress has been made in scaling up parsing models to larger datasets and improving their accuracy, but efficient lexical representations remain an open research question. CCG (Combinatory Categorial Grammars) (Steedman, 2000) is a widely used formalism for semantic parsing due to its ability to express a range of linguistic phenomena, including quantification and scope. However, CCG lexicons, which assign words and phrases to syntactic and semantic content, often contain multiple entries for closely related words (e.g., "run", "running", "runner"). This redundancy is inefficient and can create conflicts when resolving-word sense and polysemy jets, an essential step in parse generation (Johnson et al., 2016). In many cases, semantic analyzers would benefit greatly from coarser-grained representations, which capture general patterns in word meaning, rather than per-word inventories. To overcome these issues, factored lexicons provide an attractive alternative, including both lexemes to model individual word meanings, and linguistic templates to model systematic variation, as observed in various linguistic phenomena like polysemy, sub-sandhi and chunking. Examples of such templates include garden paths sentences as described by Bever (1970) and scalar implicature readings of words like "some" described by Horn (1969). In this work, we argue that factorization should be part of the CCG learning process. Therefore, we introduce an algorithm, which induces both factored lexicons and a probabilistic parse selection model tailored for semantic parsing. This learning algorithm updates both the CCG grammar and its lexicon by considering how CCG trees are generated given a set of statements about word meaning, testing whether random samples of the data could give rise to such patterns by simulations. We found that this factored approach leads to relatively better parse selection performance, especially when generalizing to unseen words, thereby reducing the number of lexicon entries required to achieve high- accuracy parsing performance. Experiments on different datasets demonstrate the applicability and benefits of CCG grammar induction with lexical factoring for semantic parsing. By reducing lexical redundancy and capturing more general patterns in word meaning, we expect this research to pave the way for more accurate, more general, and more efficient semantic analyzers that can be applied in various domains, such as dialogue systems based onparsers or query-understanding systems through question answering models. In this paper, we only scratch the surface of this critical area and our results point out potential areas to further improve and reinforce the role of factored CCG in NLP applications to achieve learning based semantic language understanding.

With the rising tide of software applications, and the ever-growing demand for bespoke functionalities, there is a stark need for efficient and effective code generation systems. Traditional approaches to code generation, such as template-based systems, rely on predefined templates and can struggle to produce novel, high-quality code (Bruch et al., 2012). Furthermore, much potential of these systems is undervalued, given their rigid template structure. Recent years have seen a significant shift towards machine learning and neural network based approaches to code generation (Allamanis et al., 2016;Johnson et al., 2016). A core aspect of such approaches is the use of prediction models that can map the input code context to the code that should appear next in the output sequence. While this paradigm has brought about impressive results and has opened doors for various applications such as code completion (Raychev et al., 2014), more work is required to fully bridge the gap between the levels of performance seen in language translation, summarisation and other tasks, and those seen in code generation applications relevant to industrial programming, especially heavy, synchronous, theoretically heterogeneous I/O constrained, non trivial design environments. Multi-document summarization is a challenging task that involves extracting the most informative and relevant content from a large collection of documents. Traditional summarization techniques often focus on rank-based and term-frequency measures that ignore the inherent structure and relationships within a document set. A key insight in this paper is that documents belonging to the same category often exhibit common information that can be leveraged to improve summarization quality. This property is widely applicable in multi-document summarization tasks and can be encapsulated by the concept of category-specific importance (CSI). CSI captures the notion that certain categories of documents may demand more importance during the summarization process based on the presence of specific keywords or phrases. The value of CSI lies in its ability to identify category-relevant information and compute a relative importance score for each sentence based on its association with the category. By incorporating CSI into the summarization process, we can improve the selection of informative sentences and generate more coherent and comprehensive summaries. A key challenge in exploiting CSI is the need for accurate document categorization. In practice, manually-curated document-to-category mappings may be unavailable or difficult to obtain. To address this, we propose an approach that performs automatic categorization of document sets using a relevant topic model, such as Non-Negative Matrix Factorization (NMF). Our approach does not require any external knowledge or domain-specific information, making it a promising solution for real-world summarization tasks. We operationalize CSI through the introduction of two new features that can be computed without relying on external knowledge. Our first feature, category-specific frequency (CSF), counts the frequency of category-specific terms within each sentence, such as words or phrases that are commonly used in the category. Our second feature, category-specific relation (CSR), calculates the strength of relationships between sentences in the document set and the category, such as co-occurrence or contextual relevance. We also demonstrate that both features can be easily incorporated into existing summarization workflows, including simple and complex models. Furthermore, we describe the architecture and implementation of our proposed summarization system, called SWING, which integrates CSI and other key features for automatic category detection, sentence selection, and summary generation. Our evaluation on the TAC-2011 guided summarization task demonstrates the effectiveness of SWING, which outperforms all other participant summarization systems as measured by automated ROUGE measures. Our results highlight the importance of category-specific information in multi-document summarization tasks and showcase the value of CSI in improving summarization quality.

Spell checking and autocorrection have been integral components of modern text editors and word processors for decades, ensuring that users input accurate and readable text. Traditional spell checkers and autocorrect systems rely heavily on manually curated dictionaries and annotated training data, which can be time-consuming and expensive to compile. However, the rapidly evolving nature of language, with new words, slangs and colloquialisms emerging continuously, makes manual maintenance of such resources increasingly challenging. Another significant shortcoming of traditional spell checkers is their reliance on language-specific models, limiting their application to a specific language. To address these issues and overcome the language barrier, we propose a novel approach to language-independent spell checking and autocorrection, utilizing the abundant, noisy, and dynamic resource that is the World Wide Web. Our hypothesis is that by leveraging web corpora, we can infer knowledge about misspellings and word usage without the need for manual annotation, thus enabling the development of language-independent spell checking and autocorrection systems. To validate this hypothesis, we designed, implemented, and evaluated an end-to-end system that extracts valuable information from web corpora, learns to model errors and perform language tasks, and evaluates its performance on relevant benchmarks. The proposed system comprises two primary components: an error model and an n-gram language model. The former enables the identification of common misspellings and their frequencies, while the latter helps anticipate the correct spelling of words based on their context. To capture the nuances of language and reinforce accurate predictions, we use noise-tolerant solutions such as decision trees for confidence assignment. Moreover, a secondary set of news articles with inserted artificial errors aids in fine-tuning the confidence classifier to adjust the uncertainty of predicted spellings. This enables our system to make more informed choices and distinguish between likely and unlikely corrections. Since manual annotation is eliminated, our system has significant advantages over traditional approaches: it requires minimal setup and can be easily instantiated for new languages with minimal training and no annotated resources. To demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency, we evaluate our system on human-typed text data containing real-world errors in English and German, achieving an average total error rate (TER) of 3.8% in English, which outperforms baselines leveraging hand-curated dictionaries. Preliminary results on synthetic data for Russian and Arabic also indicate promising gains. With this work, we not only propose a novel approach to language-independent spell checking and autocorrection but also contribute to the broader goal of developing more robust and language-independent natural language processing systems, through the effective reuse and desensitization of web corpora.

Question Answering over Knowledge Bases (KB-QA) has become one of the most critical and challenging tasks in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Its importance stems from its potential to empower various applications, such as virtual assistants, search engines, and decision-making systems, to name a few. KB-QA aims at automatically answering natural language questions by retrieving relevant facts stored in a knowledge base (KB). While significant progress has been made in KB-QA in recent years, most existing approaches suffer from two main limitations. Firstly, they are not able to effectively handle simple questions, which constitute a vast majority of questions queried on the web, yet pose significant difficulties to QA systems. Simple questions, typically phrased using a single subject-verb-object structure, often require more nuanced understanding and context-specific knowledge than complex questions, which frequently involve multiple subtasks and dependencies. Secondly, the trend in existing literature is to employ straightforward fact retrieval mechanisms that fail to mitigate the propagation of errors, culminating in suboptimal performance and efficiency. To tackle these challenges in this work, we propose the PR-SQA, an innovative approach for simple question answering over knowledge bases, focusing on extracting relevant candidate answers by combining pattern extraction, entity linking, and fact selection in an efficient pipeline design. Our approach is characterized by two key components: a pattern revising procedure, designed to address the error propagation problem by iteratively refining the search space of candidate subject-predicate pairs, and a joint fact selection mechanism enhanced by entity detection. This methodology leverages the strength of both pattern extraction and entity linking to perform the candidate answer selection in a hierarchical manner. Specifically, our procedure selects a pattern describing a relation type relevant to the query from the knowledge base, and then further narrows down the search space by inducing entity linking among the subjects, predicates, and objects, yielding an entity-enhanced-SOA- graph that contains available relation types for simple question answering. Following this, we propose to conduct joint fact selection and relation detection using a multi-layer neural model, which learns to rank the top-scoring subject-predicate pairs to enable the retrieval of relevant facts within the graph. By merging the strength of pattern-based and entity-based representations with multi-level encoding and leveraging multi-dimension information, we are able to effectively eradicate the effect of error propagation and facilitate more accurate and efficient information reuse.
